Salt template fabrication of MgO-laden bone-mimetic gyroid scaffolds
abstract: The incorporation of bioactive nanoparticles into polymer scaffolds is essential for enhanced bone regeneration, yet conventional 3D printing is often limited by the rheological constraints of composite resins. High particle loading typically compromises printability, forcing a trade-off between bioactivity and structural fidelity. To overcome this barrier, we employed a salt-templating strategy that decouples the fabrication of complex geometries from the material formulation. This approach enabled the successful shaping of a poly(ϵ-caprolactone) (PCL) matrix heavily reinforced with magnesium oxide (MgO) nanoparticles—a formulation challenging to process via direct additive manufacturing. By infiltrating this high-viscosity composite into sacrificial salt molds, we fabricated gyroid scaffolds that retained precise bone-mimetic architectures while maximizing the functional benefits of the inorganic filler. The incorporated MgO nanoparticles acted as dual-functional agents, serving as nucleating sites to increase polymer crystallinity and mechanical stiffness, while simultaneously altering surface nanotopography to boost protein adsorption. Consequently, the scaffolds provided a potent osteoinductive microenvironment, promoting deep cellular infiltration and significantly accelerating the osteogenic differentiation of human mesenchymal stem cells. Significantly, this work establishes salt-templating as a powerful platform that resolves the long-standing “printability–bioactivity” trade-off. By unlocking the use of “unprintable” high-loading bioactive composites, it enables the fabrication of precise, mathematically defined gyroid architectures that conventional 3D printing cannot achieve, offering a new avenue for next-generation bone tissue engineering.

title: Boosting interfacial OH− turnover via vacancy-hollow synergy for robust oxygen evolution
Effect of ether oxygen atom distribution in the polymer main and side chains on the lithium-ion conductivity of PEG-based polymer electrolytes
abstract: The question regarding the optimal distribution of ether oxygen atoms for enhancing lithium-ion conduction in PEG-based polymer electrolytes—whether on the side chains or along the main backbone—is still unresolved. While understanding this issue is critical for the molecular-level design of high-performance PEG-based polymer electrolytes. The controversy over the contribution of backbone versus side-chain ether oxygen atoms lies in the frequent neglect of keeping the total ether oxygen count per repeat unit constant when comparing their effects on lithium-ion transport. Generally, the higher the total number of ether oxygen atoms per repeat unit (under non-crystalline conditions), the higher the lithium-ion conductivity. To address this, we designed a series of polymers (HPUx-y, where x and y are the consecutive EO counts on the backbone and side chains). Their key feature is that the distribution of EO units varies between the backbone and side chains, while the total number of ether oxygen atoms per repeating unit is kept constant. Lithium-ion transport properties (ionic conductivity and transference number) as well as the dissociation degree of lithium salt in the HPUx-y series electrolytes are comprehensively investigated. Our findings indicate that side chain ether oxygen groups contribute more to lithium salt dissociation, leading to a higher dissociation degree. In contrast, the backbone ether oxygen groups, which have relatively weak solvating power, are more critical for facilitating lithium-ion transport and thus yield a higher transference number. Under non-crystalline conditions, the more ether oxygen atoms on the backbone, the more beneficial it is for lithium-ion transport, as long as the side chains contain at least four ether oxygen atoms each. This work provides a valuable design strategy for developing high-performance PEG-based polymer electrolytes.

Vacancy assisted spin-state modulation strategy for efficient nitrate electrosynthesis
abstract: Electrochemical nitrogen oxidation reaction (NOR) driven by renewable energy (RE) offers a promising alternative to traditional fossil-fuel-based thermochemical nitrate production. However, achieving efficient RE/NOR remains challenging due to the inert nature of N N bonds and the competing oxygen evolution reaction (OER). In this study, we present a novel oxygen-vacancy-rich Ru-doped SnO₂ catalyst (Vo–RuSnOₓ) that addresses these challenges via spin polarization (SP) modulation. Lattice Ru atoms generate asymmetric bonding/antibonding 4d orbitals near the Fermi level, while adjacent oxygen vacancies supply unpaired electrons, synergistically enhancing NOR activity and suppressing OER. Density functional theory calculations reveal that the “Ru + Vo” lowers the energy barrier for *O formation and promotes the *ONN → *ONNO transition step, a critical bottleneck in NOR. Consequently, Vo–RuSnOₓ achieves a remarkable nitrate yield rate of 66.11 μg h −1 mg cat −1 at 1.80 V vs RHE and a Faradaic efficiency of 23.56% at 1.60 V, surpassing the performance of benchmark oxide catalysts under acidic conditions. These findings highlight the potential of spin polarization modulation in OER-inactive hosts to stimulate selective and high-rate NOR. This study has devised a new material design strategy for the next-generation NOR catalysts manipulating the OER-derived intermediates.

title: Engineering catalytic sites in ZnIn2S4 via Mg doping: A S-to-In shift toward enhanced photocatalytic H2 evolution
abstract: Doping engineering has emerged as an effective strategy to unlock the catalytic potential of two-dimensional semiconductors by precisely tailoring their electronic structures and surface active sites for solar-driven H2 evolution. Herein, Mg-doped ZnIn2S4 (ZIS) nanosheets were successfully synthesized via a facile hydrothermal method. The optimal Mg0.1ZIS exhibits an exceptional H2 evolution rate of 9.45 mmol·g-1·h-1 under visible light, which is 4 times that of pristine ZIS, along with excellent stability over five consecutive cycles. Systematic characterizations and DFT calculations reveal that Mg2+ incorporates into the ZIS lattice by occupying In3+ sites. This incorporation effectively modulates the electronic structure, promoting charge carrier separation and accelerating charge transfer kinetics. Furthermore, the Mg-induced electron redistribution renders the In sites electron-rich, shifting the catalytic active site from S in pristine ZIS to In in Mg0.1ZIS (S-to-In shift). This S-to-In shift is corroborated by the optimal hydrogen adsorption free energy (ΔGH*) observed at the In sites. The synergy of enhanced charge dynamics and optimized active sites accounts for the dramatically improved photocatalytic performance. This work provides atomic-scale insights into active site engineering via cation doping for high-performance photocatalysts.

From selection to design: Reshaping aptamer discovery with artificial intelligence
abstract: Nucleic acid aptamers are emerging as powerful “chemical antibodies,” namely synthetic oligonucleotide ligands that emulate antibody-like molecular recognition while retaining the programmability and scalability of chemical synthesis, for precision medicine. Yet their clinical translation has been historically bottlenecked by the stochastic nature of classical discovery methods like SELEX. This trial-and-error paradigm is labor-intensive and often fails to identify binders with optimal therapeutic properties. The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is currently driving a fundamental paradigm shift from empirical screening to rational engineering. This review synthesizes the rapid evolution of this landscape, framing High-Throughput SELEX not merely as a selection tool, but as a critical data engine fueling computational discovery. We categorize current AI frameworks into two distinct paradigms: predictive architectures that decipher complex sequence-structure-function rules from noisy datasets, and generative models (e.g., VAEs, diffusion models, and inverse folding) that enable the de novo design of binders targeting specific geometries. Furthermore, we highlight translational breakthroughs in AI-designed biosensors and chemically optimized therapeutics. Finally, we discuss current challenges in data sparsity and interpretability, outlining a roadmap toward closed-loop ecosystems, that is, iterative design–test–refine workflows in which computational design, experimental validation, and model updating are continuously linked, to accelerate the development of next-generation molecular tools.

Alternating layer-by-layer assembly of cellulose-based composite films via structural design and interfacial engineering for high thermal conductivity
abstract: Traditional thermally conductive composites frequently encounter a bottleneck in reconciling superior heat conduction with mechanical flexibility, primarily stemming from inhomogeneous particulate distribution and randomly oriented micro-structures. We propose a structural engineering-based design strategy to fabricate nanofibrillated cellulose (NFC) based composite films by constructing alternating layer-by-layer structures with graphene (G) and boron nitride nanosheets (BNNS) dual fillers. Through a shear-induced coating process, a highly oriented and continuous in-plane heat transfer "green channel" is constructed. As a result, the composite film containing only 25 wt% filler achieves an in-plane thermal conductivity (TC) of 32.64 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ which is 28.6 times that of pure NFC. This superior thermal performance is synergistically coupled with enhanced mechanical toughness of 4.82 MJ/m³ attributed to the functionalization of BNNS with polydopamine (PDA). The PDA acts as an interfacial "molecular bridge," fostering strong hydrogen bonding with the NFC matrix and ensuring excellent dispersion stability. This work provides a scalable and general method for designing flexible thermally conductive composites with optimized interfacial and structural integrity.

Neuron-targeted selenoprotein-enriched exosomes attenuate ferroptosis in spinal cord injury by stabilizing lipid droplets
abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) induces severe neuronal death, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation, with ferroptosis playing a central role in neuronal loss. Selenium is essential for glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) synthesis and antiferroptotic defense; however, conventional supplementation suffers from poor targeting and a narrow therapeutic window, limiting its therapeutic utility. Inspired by endogenous selenium circulation and homeostatic regulation, we developed an innovative neuron-targeted, selenium-enriched exosomal delivery system (3D-SeExos-RVG) that overcomes the targeting and biosafety limitations of conventional formulations, reduces selenium-associated toxicity, and broadens the therapeutic window for SCI treatment. Through selenium nanoparticle (SeNP) stimulation and 3D culture, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) biotransformed selenium into biogenic selenoprotein P (SELENOP)-loaded exosomes, which were subsequently functionalized with an RVG neuronal-targeting peptide (3D-SeExos-RVG). The resulting 3D-SeExos-RVG exhibited uniform nanoscale morphology, high selenium-loading efficiency, and enhanced colloidal stability, providing biochemical precision and material robustness for neuroregenerative applications. In vitro, 3D-SeExos-RVG significantly reduced erastin-induced ferroptosis in PC12 neurons via the SELENOP-NRF2–GPX4 axis, enhancing antioxidant defenses and ferroptosis resistance. By reinforcing GPX4–lipid droplet interactions, the system stabilized lipid droplets and suppressed ATGL-mediated lipolysis, thereby reducing lipid peroxidation. Moreover, 3D-SeExos-RVG promoted macrophage M2 polarization and directed neural stem cell differentiation toward neuronal lineages, demonstrating anti-inflammatory and neurotrophic effects. In a rat SCI model, 3D-SeExos-RVG efficiently targeted injured spinal cord tissue, reduced iron accumulation, oxidative stress, and lipid peroxidation, and ultimately improved motor function recovery and tissue repair. This study highlights a novel selenium-based exosome therapeutic strategy with significant translational potential for SCI treatment.

abstract: Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to CO and formate holds significant industrial promise for storing intermittent renewable electricity as value-added chemicals and fuels. Herein, we reveal that the surface density of atomically dispersed Sn on Cu lattice modulates the active-site identity from Cu to Cu-Sn, thereby switching product distributions. L-Sn1-Cu, featuring sparse Sn coverage, achieves a CO Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 72.8% at a current density of 300 mA cm-2. Conversely, H-Sn1-Cu with saturated Sn isolation attains a formate FE of 89.3% at a current density of 200 mA cm-2. Operando spectroscopy and DFT calculations show that Sn-deficient locales expose Cu atoms to bind *COOH and favor CO formation, while Sn-congested domains create polarized Cu-Sn pairs that lock *OCHO for formate synthesis. This density-dependent ensemble tuning enables switchable selectivity between CO and formate in CO2 electroreduction at industrially relevant current densities.

Engineering hybrid hydrogels from sticker–spacer peptide and molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) for advanced antimicrobial therapy
abstract: The rapid escalation of antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections poses a severe global health threat, demanding next-generation antimicrobial strategies beyond conventional antibiotics. Herein, we report the development of a hybrid hydrogel constructed through weak intermolecular interactions between a sticker-spacer peptide derivative and molybdenum disulfide (MoS 2 ) nanosheets. The incorporation of MoS 2 within the peptide hydrogel results in nanosheets embedded within a nanofibrous network and intercalation of nanofibers between the nanosheets. This hybrid architecture maintains the mechanical properties while conferring intrinsic, broad-spectrum antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli , Staphylococcus aureus , and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, primarily through mechanisms involving oxidative stress and membrane disruption. Furthermore, in vivo bacterial wound healing studies demonstrated that the hybrid hydrogel remarkably accelerated tissue regeneration, achieving complete wound closure. The histological and quantitative analysis further confirm enhanced re-epithelialization, collagen deposition, and reduced inflammation after the treatment. Overall, this work presents a multifunctional, biocompatible hybrid hydrogel platform that combines antimicrobial activity with regenerative capability, offering a promising strategy for next-generation wound dressings and a potential alternative to traditional antibiotics.

Converting CO2 into carbon nanotubes via sequential CO2 methanation and methane pyrolysis
abstract: This study presents a sequential thermochemical catalytic process for converting CO 2 into carbon nanotubes (CNTs), achieving nearly 99% overall CO 2 conversion and solid carbon yields of up to 49% in a single pass. The overall transformation is divided into two thermodynamically favorable steps: (1) low-temperature CO 2 methanation to CH 4 over a sol-gel-prepared Ni 87 Ce 6.5 Zr 6.5 -SG catalyst, which achieved >95% CO 2 conversion at 250 °C in a single pass, and (2) subsequent methane pyrolysis to CNTs and H 2 over a Ni@Al 2 O 3 -IE core-shell catalyst, which showed improved stability and carbon yield compared with conventional catalysts. Catalyst characterization revealed the synergistic roles of Ce and Zr in the methanation catalyst and the importance of the core-shell architecture in suppressing deactivation during methane pyrolysis. This CH 4 -bridged strategy avoids intrinsic carbon loss through CO 2 regeneration in CO-mediated routes, enabling high single-pass solid‑carbon yield in a gas-phase sequential process. The resulting product consists predominantly of structurally defined CNTs, which were further validated as functional additives in lithium-ion-battery-related systems. Overall, this work establishes an effective route for converting captured CO 2 into value-added CNT materials.

Pilot study of a novel electrochemical approach for NOx removal from flue gas
abstract: This study utilizes a Power-to-X (PtX) mini-pilot to remove NO x impurities from synthesized cement flue gas. The system consists of a combined alkaline scrubber and oxidative electrochemical scrubber. We demonstrate that the oxidative scrubber effectively oxidized NO, while the alkaline scrubber provided additional NO removal and partial NO 2 absorption. The integrated system achieved over 99% NO removal during transient operation, and a 93.95% reduction during steady state operation. The results highlight that an overall ∼79% of NO x removal was achieved. Additionally, as the alkaline solvent reached saturation, CO 2 capture by the system became negligible, proving its suitability as a pretreatment step in carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) processes. Liquid analysis of the alkaline solvent revealed inorganic speciation, including early carbonate/bicarbonate and nitrate formation, followed by a shift toward bicarbonate-rich chemistry. These findings highlight that an electrochemical scrubbing pretreatment system upstream of CCUS plants can successfully reduce NO x concentrations. This could result in mitigation of amine solvent degradation and enhanced process efficiency and longevity, underscoring the system's potential for scalable PtX and CCUS applications.

title: Integrated two-stage catalytic–adsorptive system for efficient removal of O2, H2O, and tritium from molten salt reactor off-gas
abstract: This study describes a two-stage catalytic and adsorptive system for the integrated removal of oxygen (O2), water (H2O), and a tritium surrogate (H2) from a molten salt reactor (MSR) off-gas. The system utilizes a Cu-based catalyst in the initial stage to eliminate O2 and convert H2 to H2O, followed by a zeolite 13X adsorbent in the subsequent stage to adsorb H2O vapor. The performance of each component was optimized in a single-bed configuration. The Cu-based catalyst exhibited exceptional efficiencies for O2 removal and H₂ conversion, surpassing 99% at temperatures of ≥300 °C, with stable cycling performance at the optimal operating temperature of 350 °C. The zeolite 13X adsorbent displayed a high H2O vapor removal efficiency of >99% at 25 °C over a broad concentration range of 500–3000 ppm. The effectiveness of the complete two-stage system was confirmed using a mixed gas stream containing 500 ppm each of O2, H2O vapor, and H2. Operating sequentially, the catalytic stage at 350 °C and the adsorptive stage at 25 °C achieved an overall removal efficiency of >99% for all target species. These findings validate the two-stage strategy as a practical and highly efficient approach for comprehensive off-gas purification, thereby streamlining the system design for advanced MSRs.

Niobium doping enables durable Ni-rich layered cathodes through interfacial and morphological stabilization with data-driven performance validation
abstract: The addition of a small amount of niobium oxide during the synthesis of Nb-modified 9-series Ni-rich layered oxides yields multiple beneficial effects. These include suppression of aluminum segregation from the precursor, refinement of primary particle size within dense spherical secondary particles, mitigation of oxygen release during electrochemical cycling, and reduced structural changes associated with the H2–H3 phase transition at voltages up to 4.3 V vs. Li|Li + . The optimized Nb-doped material with 0.5 mol% Nb addition demonstrates excellent rate capability and improved cycling stability, achieving 85.3% capacity retention after 200 cycles at 1C, even for electrodes with a high active-material mass loading of approximately 8.5 mg cm −2 . The role of Nb in structural and electrochemical stabilization is elucidated using operando X-ray diffraction, ex situ soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy, and complementary microscopy studies. In addition, a gated recurrent unit-based approach enables effective prediction of long-term cycling stability. Overall, this strategy demonstrates a viable pathway toward stabilizing high-energy Ni-rich cathodes while accelerating performance assessment for practical lithium-ion battery applications.

Assessing the full operational potential of solar photo-Fenton plants for microcontaminant removal through economic model predictive control
abstract: This work introduces the use of Economic Model Predictive Control (EMPC) for the automatic operation of solar photo-Fenton plants treating microcontaminants in urban wastewater, establishing a benchmark for assessing operational and techno-economic performance. An EMPC approach was developed for a large-scale solar photo-Fenton plant using a previously validated dynamic process model complemented with real operational data. The proposed strategy was evaluated through closed-loop simulations under representative clear-day (22 June 2022) and cloudy-day (06 April 2022) scenarios, explicitly accounting for forecasted environmental disturbances such as solar UV-A irradiance and water temperature. The results demonstrate that the EMPC effectively adapts operating conditions to strong environmental variability, maintaining near-complete compliance with microcontaminant-removal requirements ( ≥ 80%) and safety-oriented residual hydrogen peroxide constraints ( ≥ 0.147 mM) while minimizing unit operating costs (€ m −3 ). Under clear-day conditions (treatment capacity of 283 m 3 day −1 and mean cost of 0.213 € m −3 ), significant cost reductions are achieved during high-irradiance periods ( ∼ 30%). Under cloudy conditions (188 m 3 day −1 and 0.233 € m −3 ), the controller effectively handles abrupt disturbances and temporary shutdowns with limited performance degradation. To address real-time feasibility, a linearized EMPC formulation based on real-time model linearization was proposed (MAPE < 13%), achieving a reduction in computation time of ∼ 96% (20 vs 1 min) with negligible loss of control performance. Although practical deployment remains constrained by process monitoring requirements, the proposed EMPC framework provides a rigorous benchmark for techno-economic assessment and establishes a structured basis for future implementation of advanced control in solar photo-Fenton plants.

Integrating experiments, numerical simulations and Bayesian optimisation to maximise drug permeability of hollow pyramidal microneedle arrays
abstract: This study presents an experimental–numerical framework integrated with Bayesian optimisation (BO) for the design of hollow pyramidal microneedle (MN) arrays to enhance transdermal drug permeability across the skin. Finite element (FE) simulations have been carried out to model coupled fluid flow and drug delivery in multilayered skin, including convection–diffusion of the drug in HMN and fluid slip condition at fluid (MN tip)–skin (porous) interfaces. The geometric design parameters, including lumen diameter, array pitch, and needle count, have been optimised using a Gaussian process–based BO (GP-BO) framework implemented in Python via the scikit-learn library. Experimental validation has been performed using hollow microneedle (HMN) arrays loaded with ibuprofen (IBU) sodium, applied to ex vivo neonatal porcine skin in Franz diffusion cell setups. Drug permeation has been subsequently quantified using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analysis. The results revealed that approximately 150 μg (≈3%) of the administered drug permeated into the receptor compartment after 24-h, whereas 295.79 ± 148.95 μg remained within the dermal layers, indicating prolonged drug retention and effective localised delivery. The integrated BO methodology significantly improved permeability predictions while minimising computational costs, resulting in optimal HMN geometries that maximised both volumetric flow rate and transdermal permeability. The improvement in performance represents around 5% enhancement over the previously optimised configuration, demonstrating both the effectiveness and robustness of the BO framework.

Biotin-tailored self-assembly conjugate nanoplatform via CD47 blockade and macrophage reprogramming for enhanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma immunotherapy
abstract: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) exploits CD47 overexpression to evade immune surveillance, delivering a dominant “don't eat me” signal that concurrently suppresses phagocytosis and contributing to the maintenance of an immunosuppressive tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) phenotype. To dismantle this dual immunosuppressive axis, we engineered Bio/Met@P820 NPs, a biotin-directed self-assembly nanoplatform integrating a DSPE-PEG-biotin tumor-targeting moiety, metformin, and the paclitaxel-IR820 conjugate drug (P820). Near-infrared (NIR) irradiation triggers P820 activation, enabling spatiotemporally controlled synergistic photothermal-chemotherapy. This induces potent immunogenic cell death (ICD), characterized by apoptosis and calreticulin exposure, thereby priming macrophages for enhanced tumor phagocytosis. Concomitantly, metformin orchestrates metabolic reprogramming: it disrupts mitochondrial respiration, alleviates hypoxia, and downregulates CD47 expression via HIF-1α inhibition, effectively abolishing the CD47-SIRPα checkpoint. This immunometabolic modulation further drives TAM repolarization from protumorigenic M2 to antitumor M1 phenotypes. Leveraging biotin-mediated active targeting, the nanoplatform ensures precise tumor accumulation, minimizing off-target effects. In vivo studies demonstrate that Bio/Met@P820 NPs synergistically amplify macrophage-dependent tumor clearance, promote dendritic cell maturation, and enhance cytotoxic T lymphocyte infiltration, achieving potent antitumor efficacy devoid of systemic toxicity. This self-assembled nanoplatform presents a unified strategy to overcome macrophage-centric immune evasion by synchronizing ICD induction, CD47 blockade, and metabolic reprogramming of TAMs within the tumor microenvironment.

title: Direct regeneration of highly degraded LiFePO4 cathodes enabled by a multifunctional uric acid
abstract: The extensive popularity of lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4, LFP) batteries in electric vehicles and power storage systems has called for efficient disposal and sustainable recycling after their end-of-life to achieve closed-loop utilization of non-renewable resources. Here, a facile one-step solid-phase sintering strategy assisted by uric acid is proposed to rejuvenate highly degraded LFP (D-LFP) cathode materials. It is noteworthy that the pyrolytic products of uric acid are not only conducive to reducing Fe(III) to Fe(II) and rectifying Li/Fe anti-site defects of D-LFP, but also enable to reconstruct an in-situ nitrogen-doped carbon coating on the regenerated LFP (R-LFP) particles, significantly boosting electronic conductivity and lithium-ion transport kinetics. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the introduction of N-doping carbon layer can strengthen Fe-O bonding by elevating d-band center of Fe atoms to enhance structural stability, and improve Li+ diffusion kinetics by lowering the migration energy barrier. As expected, R-LFP exhibits significantly improved electrochemical performance relative to D-LFP, as reflected by high discharge specific capacity of 160.3 mAh g-1 at 0.1 C, superior rate capability and outstanding long-term cyclability (91.2% of capacity retention after 500 cycles at 0.5 C), comparable to those of the fresh commercial counterparts. More significantly, this strategy is well applicable to severely degraded LFP materials, revitalizing their electrochemical performance to the comparable levels as the commercial LFP. Furthermore, technical and economic evaluation underscore substantial economic benefits and minimized environmental impact of the proposed strategy, rendering it to hold significant prospects in sustainable lithium-ion battery recycling.

Degradation mechanism of a newly identified antioxidant AO2246 in groundwater by zero-valent iron-activated persulfate
abstract: AO2246, a synthetic phenolic antioxidant recently identified as a widespread contaminant in industrial cluster groundwater, poses emerging environmental risks. However, its degradation mechanisms remain largely unknown. This study investigates the degradation mechanism of AO2246 using a zero-valent iron-activated persulfate (ZVI/PS) system, which is primarily used for organic pollution remediation, under simulated groundwater conditions. This process achieved 98.59% AO2246 removal in 30 min under optimal conditions. However, it was substantially influenced by the complex aqueous matrix. Visual MINTEQ simulations revealed that alkaline conditions mitigate HA inhibition via electrostatic repulsion, whereas the Mg²⁺–HA interaction triggers antagonism through cation bridging. Mechanistic studies combining electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), radical quenching, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations identified SO₄·⁻ and ·OH as the primary radicals. DFT analyses precisely localized the reactive sites on the phenolic ring and methyl groups. A crucial divergence in reaction pathways was uncovered, i.e., SO₄·⁻ preferentially attacks the aromatic ring via radical adduct formation (RAF), whereas ·OH primarily drives hydrogen atom abstraction (HAA) from alkyl chains. Ecological structure-activity relationship (ECOSAR) modeling demonstrated that the RAF pathway yields significantly less toxic intermediates compared to the HAA route. Therefore, steering the system selectivity towards SO₄·⁻ (e.g., via pH control) is proposed as a key strategy to enhance both degradation efficiency and environmental safety. This work provides fundamental insights into the oxidation mechanisms and interactive effects governing AO2246 degradation, offering a theoretical basis for optimizing persulfate-based advanced oxidation processes for groundwater remediation of persistent organic contaminants.

title: Mechanistic insight into the “intermediate effect”: Competitive adsorption and surface coverage model in controlling hydrate formation in a closed-cell foam–SDS system
Strategies for optimizing dry battery electrode performance
abstract: The growing interest in dry battery electrode (DBE) production as a sustainable and cost-effective alternative to conventional wet coating processes for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) necessitates strategies to enhance electrode performance and fully realize the technology's potential. This study investigates the impact of different current collector pretreatments and an advanced asymmetric calendering process on the electrochemical performance of dry-coated NMC622-based cathodes. We explore how the surface properties of the current collector influence the adhesion and contact resistance of the dry-coated electrodes, deriving guidelines for the design of suitable pretreatments. The asymmetric calendering method, which employs a difference in the circumferential speed of the calender rolls, allows to effectively control electrode thickness and porosity, enabling the production of electrodes suitable for high-energy and high-power applications. Notably, electrodes with a low PTFE binder content of 1 wt% can be produced using this approach, improving electrical conductivity and tortuosity, and consequently leading to enhanced rate capabilities and cycling stability compared to wet-coated electrodes. • Primer- and etched-foils enable robust dry-coated NMC622 cathodes. • Asymmetric calendering controls thickness, loading, porosity. • 1 wt% PTFE lowers tortuosity and improves electrode conductivity. • Dry-coated cathodes outperform wet-coated in rate capability.

Solvent-free extrusion of polymer-based solid-state electrolytes: Formulation, processing and modeling
abstract: Solid-state batteries (SSBs), especially those paired lithium metal anodes with solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) and enabling high-voltage bipolar stacking architectures, promise higher safety and energy density than conventional Li-ion systems. Among candidate electrolytes, polymer-based solid-state electrolytes (PSEs) are attractive for their processability, interfacial compliance, low density, wide form-factor freedom (thin, flexible films), and better air handling than many sulfide/halide systems. Solvent-free extrusion of PSEs has emerged as a promising route for scalable solid-state battery manufacturing. First, we reviewed early foundational research before 2020, including pioneering melt-compounding and hot-pressing studies that established core processing principles and performance baselines, then we surveyed the rapid advances since 2020 in extruding both neat PSEs and composite PSEs. New polymer matrices, inert/ceramic fillers, and refined formulations have expanded the processing window and improved ionic conductivity and interfacial stability. We also detail the extrusion parameters, such as single and twin-screw setups, screw element design, barrel and die temperature profiles, screw speed, residence time distribution, and shear and cooling rates. These parameters determine polymer crystallinity, phase morphology, and ultimately performance. In parallel, we also focus on modeling and simulation approaches (e.g., CFD, SPH, DEM) that predict flow, mixing, and thermal behavior in extruders. Because most current extrusion simulations remain polymer-centric and do not yet encode lithium-salt identity, ion association, and transport closures with sufficient fidelity, the simulation discussion in this review is intended to quantify flow–mixing–thermal histories to guide screw/die and process-window design. So direct prediction of ionic conductivity and Li + transference number now still has to rely on experiments or on separate MD/DFT-type simulations of intrinsic ion transport that do not explicitly resolve the mixing process. Due to fidelity limitations, these tools serve as complementary guides rather than replacements for experiments completely. Key processing–structure–performance relationships are synthesized via comparative radar plots and other graphical summaries, highlighting critical trade-offs to inform design optimization. Finally, we outline future directions, including broadening the range of polymers and fillers, and establishing standardized extrusion protocols. By integrating materials innovation, process engineering, and modeling insights, solvent-free extrusion of PSEs is expected to accelerate the transition from lab-scale feasibility to robust, continuous, scalable production.

An intelligent artificial esophagus with integrated sensing and actuation for sequential peristalsis: Enabled by a mechanically robust, tunable liquid crystal elastomer
abstract: Liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) are exceptional materials for creating artificial muscles, but a persistent challenge impedes their biomedical application: lowering their actuation temperature to a physiologically relevant range often leads to a severe degradation of mechanical strength and performance. This study demonstrates a holistic solution, from molecular design to a functional biomimetic system. Our approach begins at the material level, where we introduce a short-chain reactive additive, HDODA, to precisely tune the nematic-isotropic transition temperature ( T ni ) without significantly compromising the material's integrity (from 64.9 °C to 38.6 °C). This strategy successfully decouples the thermal and mechanical properties, achieving a tunable T ni range while maintaining high tensile strength (>1.5 MPa) and large actuation strain (~45%). Next, we fabricated a Joule-heated artificial muscle fiber from this optimized LCE by integrating a nichrome heating coil. Critically, we utilized these fibers to mimic circular muscles—a key component for peristalsis that is often overlooked in LCE research favoring longitudinal actuation. To impart intelligence, we integrated non-contact capacitive sensors capable of detecting a model bolus. As a final proof-of-concept, we assembled these components into an artificial esophagus, demonstrating programmed sequential peristalsis that effectively propels the bolus, alongside verified mechanoreceptor-like sensing capabilities. This work validates a complete pathway from advanced material synthesis to a functional soft robotic organ, offering a powerful platform for intelligent biomedical devices.

Nitrogen fixation in plasma integrated mixed ionic electronic conducting membrane reactors
abstract: Nitric acid (HNO 3 ) is a key industrial chemical, traditionally produced through the Ostwald process, which relies on ammonia (NH 3 ) derived from the fossil-based Haber–Bosch process. This conventional route is highly energy and carbon-intensive and unsuitable for decentralized or small-scale applications. Since nitric oxide (NO) is the central intermediate in HNO 3 production, developing alternative electrified pathways for direct NO synthesis – bypassing NH 3 – is of growing interest. Here, we present a plasma-enabled mixed ionic–electronic conductor (MIEC) hollow fiber reactor that simultaneously separates oxygen from air and fixes nitrogen into NO in a single step. The design employs Ba 0.5 Sr 0.5 Co 0.8 Fe 0.2 O 3–δ (BSCF) membranes operated at 600 °C under a pressure gradient to achieve oxygen separation efficiencies of up to 98%. In the permeate zone, Radio-frequency (RF) plasma activation generates reactive nitrogen species that react with transported oxygen ions to form NO at rates up to 0.22 μmol s −1 . The observed NO concentrations exceed thermal equilibrium by more than two orders of magnitude, demonstrating the critical role of plasma quenching. Multi-fiber configurations enhance both efficiency and scalability, with extrapolated designs predicted to boost performance. This concept establishes a direct, electrified air–to–NO pathway, offering a sustainable alternative to conventional nitric acid production.

title: In-situ X-ray computed tomographic investigation of the electrochemical interfaces in a miniaturized proton exchange membrane water electrolyzer
abstract: X-ray computed tomography (XCT) provides a non-invasive diagnostic tool for simultaneously analyzing the catalyst-coated membrane (CCM), porous transport layer (PTL), and gas diffusion layer (GDL) of a proton exchange membrane water electrolyzer (PEMWE). In this work, an X-ray-compliant miniaturized PEMWE (mPEMWE) is designed for in-situ XCT visualization of PTL-CCM and GDL-CCM interfaces under electrolyzer operating conditions. Electrochemical testing and visualization of cells with variable land-channel configurations demonstrate that wide lands provide the highest cell performance, resulting from optimal component compression under the channel and land areas. Thin lands cause excessive component compression under the land areas, resulting in poor cell performance, whereas wide channels lack sufficient component support, causing inferior cell performance. The changes in the electrochemical interfaces are investigated at the beginning-of-life and end-of-test stages at 300 h by comparing in-situ XCT images and electrochemical performance using thick Nafion® 115 and thin Nafion® 212 membranes. Severe deformities at the PTL-CCM interface are observed at EOT, with semicircular imprints on the anode catalyst layer resulting from membrane expansion into the PTL crevices. Discontinuity in the anode catalyst layer at the PTL-CCM interface is correlated with increased overpotential, and ohmic and charge transfer resistance at EOT. This interfacial deformation mechanism is consistent across both thick and thin membranes, but is more severe in the thin membrane due to additional indentations and heterogeneity at the PTL-CCM interface. Thus, the stability of the PTL-CCM interface is deemed critical for long-term PEMWE performance and durability.

In situ halide-mediated engineering enabling cascaded alloying-conversion reactions in Ag/Fe3O4/C composite for high-performance potassium-ion batteries
abstract: The large ionic radius of potassium poses fundamental challenges for developing high-energy and high-power anodes for potassium-ion batteries, often leading to sluggish kinetics and rapid structural degradation. Here, we address these challenges through an in situ halide-mediated engineering strategy that orchestrates a cascaded alloying-conversion reaction in a rationally designed AgCl/Ag/Fe3O4/C composite. The key innovation lies in the partial transformation of metallic Ag into an interfacial AgCl phase during pyrolysis, which creates an electronically modulated Ag/AgCl heterojunction. This unique architecture serves a dual function. The AgCl phase facilitates rapid K+ transport while the electron-deficient Ag+ surface, confirmed by a +0.4 eV binding energy shift in XPS, thermodynamically favors K-Ag alloying, effectively lowering the nucleation barrier for the cascaded reaction sequence. When coupled with a KFe[Fe(CN)6] cathode, the full cell delivers exceptional performance metrics. It achieves a high initial Coulombic efficiency of 71.4% and an outstanding rate capability, retaining 63.1 mAh g-1 at a high current density of 2 A g-1. Long-term cycling reveals remarkable stability with 72.5% capacity retention after 1000 cycles at 0.2 A g-1, corresponding to an ultralow decay rate of 0.026 mAh g-1 per cycle. Ragone analysis further quantifies the superior kinetics, yielding an exceptionally high characteristic power density of 7424.5 W kg-1, approaching supercapacitor-level performance, with the cell maintaining 56.3% of its energy density (189.3 Wh kg-1) at 6000 W kg-1. This work establishes a direct quantitative link between interfacial electronic modulation and macroscopic device performance, presenting a versatile strategy for designing multi-functional composites with programmed reaction sequences for next-generation energy storage systems.

In situ synthesis of LaAlO3/SBA-15 from aluminum saline slags for CO2 capture at moderate temperatures
abstract: This study investigates the in situ synthesis of lanthanum aluminate (LaAlO₃) perovskite supported on mesoporous SBA-15 silica (SBA-15) using aluminum (Al) extracted from saline slags with 1.0 M citric acid (CA1.0). The effect of LaAlO 3 loading, synthesis pathway, and thermal conditions on the structural, morphological, and textural properties of the resulting materials was systematically evaluated. X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis shows that CA1.0-derived composites containing 25–50 wt% LaAlO 3 exhibit well-defined perovskite crystallinity, with optimal phase ordering at 25 wt%. In contrast, samples with 100 wt% LaAlO 3 display attenuated silica signals and reduced crystallinity. Materials synthesized using HCl or commercial precursors (PC) fail to develop a well-defined LaAlO 3 perovskite phase, demonstrating that CA plays a dual role as both Al extractant and chelating agent. This dual function promotes the co-complexation of Al 3+ and La 3+ ions and directs perovskite nucleation within the SBA-15 framework. Nitrogen physisorption analysis reveals an inverse correlation between LaAlO 3 crystallinity and surface area. Lower LaAlO 3 loadings (25–50 wt%) in CA1.0-derived materials yield dense perovskite domains with reduced surface areas (17–22 m 2 g −1 ), whereas 100 wt% samples retain higher surface areas (93 m 2 g −1 ) due to the presence of poorly crystalline, dispersed LaAlO 3 phases that preserves mesoporosity. In contrast, PC-derived materials exhibit significantly higher surface areas (252–720 m 2 g −1 ), depending on the hydrothermal treatment temperature (100–160 °C), but fail to develop the targeted perovskite structure, highlighting the importance of precursor conditioning. SEM, HRTEM, EDX, and XPS analyses further indicate that HCl-treated samples maintain the fibrous tubular morphology of SBA-15 but show limited incorporation of La and Al, whereas CA-derived materials display more compact and aggregated morphologies. Overall, the results underscore the critical roles of CA in precursor coordination and phase control, the trade-off between LaAlO 3 crystallinity and porosity, and the effect of hydrothermal conditions and precursor nature on the structural integration of functional perovskite domains. The CO 2 adsorption capacity was evaluated at various temperatures, between 50 and 300 °C, and atmospheric pressure. The results indicate that the materials have a greater adsorption capacity at low temperatures, which corroborates that the interaction is physical in nature. At the same time, the CO 2 adsorption capacity corresponds to the textural properties and the crystalline or amorphous character of the material. A larger specific surface area results in greater adsorption capacity, which is also favored when the material's structure is amorphous.

title: Techno-economic thresholds for solar-assisted photothermal evaporation in lithium recovery from complex brines
abstract: Conventional solar evaporation for lithium recovery from complex brines suffers from slow kinetics, extensive land use, and strong climate dependence, limiting economic feasibility. Solar-assisted photothermal interfacial evaporation offers a promising alternative, yet its practical adoption requires validation of techno-economic viability under realistic brine conditions. Here, we present a scalable solar-assisted interfacial evaporation platform using a monolithic MWCNT/CNF aerogel evaporator designed for efficient heat localization and stable salt management. The photothermal aerogel concentrates heat at the air–liquid interface while sustaining continuous brine transport through interconnected porous pathways, enabling stable evaporation even under high salinity. Large-area fabrication is achieved without compromising mechanical robustness or ionic tolerance. Performance tests using artificial brines representing four major lithium salt lakes—Great Salt Lake, Zabuye Salt Lake, Salar de Atacama, and Salar de Uyuni—show evaporation rates up to 4.5 times higher than conventional pond systems, markedly accelerating brine concentration and lithium enrichment. A techno-economic assessment identifies operational thresholds for economic feasibility. Despite increased capital and operating costs, enhanced evaporation flux improves lithium carbonate productivity and shortens processing time, enabling investment payback within 6 months under favorable conditions. By linking material-enabled productivity gains with system-level economic analysis, this study defines techno-economic thresholds for integrating solar-assisted photothermal evaporation into lithium recovery. The proposed platform provides a scalable, land-efficient, and climate-resilient pathway for sustainable lithium production from complex brines.

Integrated direct air capture and CO2 mineralization using amino acid salt solutions and alkaline solid wastes
abstract: Direct air capture (DAC) technologies are gaining growing attention for climate change mitigation but remain at a very early stage of large-scale deployment. This study proposes and comprehensively demonstrates a novel integrated DAC–mineralization process using five amino acid salt solutions as CO₂ liquid absorbents and cement kiln dust (CKD) as feedstocks for CO₂ mineralization and solvent regeneration. Upon DAC, sodium-based sarcosinate (Na-Sar), prolinate (Na-Pro), lysinate (Na-Lys) achieved desirable atmospheric CO₂ removal efficiencies above 92%, which outperformed sodium-based arginate (Na-Arg) and glycinate (Na-Gly). Solution alkalinity was identified as the key factor governing DAC, with a non-linear relationship observed between CO₂ removal efficiency and pH. At pH > 11.0, all liquid absorbents could maintain atmospheric CO₂ removal efficiencies above ∼60%, whereas a decrease in pH from 11.0 to 10.0 led to a pronounced decline in efficiency. In the integrated DAC–mineralization process, amino acid salt solutions and CKD were examined and characterized by FTIR, XRD, and TGA over six DAC–mineralization cycles. All liquid absorbents exhibited efficient recovery via mineralization, except for Na-Arg. XRD analysis revealed predominant calcite formation upon mineralization, while TGA indicated a CO₂ sequestration capacity of 92–172 g CO₂ kg −1 CKD. Overall, Na-Pro emerged as the most promising candidate for the DAC-mineralization technology. A simplified TEA analysis estimated the integrated process cost at 139–530 USD t −1 CO₂, approximately half that of conventional DAC technologies. For the scale-up of the technology, key technical and economic challenges were also identified and discussed in detail.

Robust interfacial network and ionic conduction of carbon-doped hexagonal boron nitride for dual-mode strain and humidity sensor
abstract: Ionic conducting films garner significant interest as a substitute for traditional rigid electronic conductors due to their inherent flexibility and low power consumption, but simultaneously achieving high toughness, mechanical strength, ionic conductivity, and multifunctionality remains a critical challenge. In this study, we present a novel multifunctional sensor based on ionic conduction in composite films with surface-functionalized, carbon-doped boron nitride (f-BCN) as fillers in polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) matrix. The optimized film exhibits ionic conductivity up to 46 mS/cm under hydrated conditions. The successful formation of proton-conducting channels, attributed to interfacial hydrogen bonding between the functional groups of PVA and f-BCN, is identified as a key factor contributing to the high proton conductivity. Additionally, the f-BCN/PVA composite demonstrates high tensile strength (~44 MPa) and toughness (~73 MJ/m 3 ), while maintaining stable piezoresistive behavior under cyclic strains. As a flexible strain sensor, the composite film achieved a gauge factor of 2.39 for low strains, with remarkable response and recovery of ~0.8 s and ~ 0.6 s, respectively. Furthermore, the composite film is cast on interdigitated silver (Ag) electrodes to prepare a humidity sensor. The sensor demonstrates exceptional sensitivity (718.7 kΩ/%RH and 1268.4 pF/%RH) over a wide humidity range while maintaining fast response and recovery of ~1.5 s and ~ 3 s, respectively. We also studied the cross-interference between strain and humidity sensing and found that strain and humidity can be decoupled via GF calibration. These results demonstrate the potential of f-BCN/PVA composite film, offering high ionic conductivity, dual-sensing functionality, flexibility, high mechanical strength, and low power consumption.

Hierarchical cotton surface engineering via mesoporous silica integration and in situ copper stearate growth for durable superhydrophobicity and enhanced antibacterial activity
abstract: The development of cotton fabrics with multifunctional properties such as superhydrophobicity, self-cleaning, and antibacterial activity without compromising intrinsic characteristics like flexibility, breathability, and comfort remains a significant challenge. In this study, a multifunctional superhydrophobic cotton fabric with amplified antimicrobial activity was fabricated by integrating multiple bactericidal mechanisms into a single platform. The process involved the deposition of copper-doped mesoporous silica nanoparticles (CuMSNs) onto cotton fabrics (CF), followed by in situ synthesis and deposition of copper stearate (CuSA) to impart durable superhydrophobicity. The incorporation of copper in two forms, embedded within the mesoporous structure for sustained release and long-term efficacy, and as copper stearate for immediate contact killing, produces a complementary dual-action effect that enhances both antibacterial performance and durability. Surface characterization by scanning electron microscopy, elemental analysis, and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy confirmed the successful surface modifications. The modified cotton exhibited excellent superhydrophobicity with a water contact angle of 152° and a sliding angle of 7°, along with outstanding antibacterial activity, achieving 99.99% bacterial reduction against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative strains after 24 h. Self-cleaning and air permeability tests further demonstrated the material's suitability for practical and protective applications. This multifunctional coating offers sustained antibacterial performance and robust durability, making it highly promising for advanced medical textiles and protective fabrics. • Facile in situ growth of hierarchical CuSA/CuMSN on cotton surfaces. • Durable superhydrophobicity with 152° contact and 7° sliding angles. • Simultaneous bacterial repellence with dual-mode contact/release killing • 99.99% antibacterial activity against Gram-positive/negative bacteria. • Superior breathability with minimal change in air permeability.

Experimental and modelling studies on the dynamics of the sorption-enhanced methanol synthesis process
abstract: CO 2 hydrogenation to methanol is a promising carbon-utilization pathway; however, it is fundamentally constrained by low equilibrium CO 2 conversion, while accumulation of produced water further limits methanol yield and accelerates catalyst deactivation. This work investigates a sorption-enhanced methanol synthesis (SEMES) process using a physical mixture of an industrial Cu/ZnO/Al 2 O 3 catalyst and zeolite 3 A for in situ water removal. A systematic experimental study was conducted to evaluate the effects of pressure, temperature, and weight hourly space velocity on CO 2 conversion, methanol production, yield, and selectivity. Elevated pressure enhanced CO 2 conversion and methanol productivity through combined equilibrium shifting and stronger water adsorption, while temperature exhibited a convex dependence, with optimal performance observed at 230 °C. To capture the evolving reaction–adsorption environment under sorption-enhanced operation, dynamic reactor models incorporating kinetic formulations by Graaf et al. and Seidel et al. were implemented without parameter refitting. Spatial and temporal rate analyses show that the Seidel model more accurately represents the changing reaction environment induced by water removal, particularly the shifting competition between methanol synthesis and the reverse water–gas shift reaction. A breakthrough-based analysis using gas-phase CO and CO 2 signals enabled clear demarcation of pre-breakthrough and post-breakthrough regimes, allowing quantitative evaluation of conversion, yield, and productivity under transient operation. Overall, the sorption-enhanced configuration increased CO 2 conversion and methanol yield by approximately 200–650% and 150–450%, respectively, relative to the conventional process, demonstrating the potential of coupling selective water adsorption with catalytic methanol synthesis for intensified reactor design.

Mechanism enabled population balance modeling of gold nanoparticle formation
abstract: Gold nanoparticles are useful in many applications and therefore there is interest in having an accurate understanding and model of their growth process. In this work, we utilize the Finke-Watzky model of particle formation to develop a detailed population balance model. The model includes a novel approach to describe partial adsorption of stabilizers on the surface of growing nanoparticles by a modified Langmuir isotherm and takes particle interactions into account. Moreover, we derive a model reduction strategy to significantly decrease the simulation time required. We demonstrate the applicability of our model by estimating unknown model parameters and showing good alignment of the entire particle size distribution to measurement data of the synthesis as a function of time, including equilibrium constants of adsorption as well as growth mechanisms and growth rates.

ZIF-derived nitrogen-doped carbon/silicon composites for asymmetric lithium-ion capacitors
abstract: Lithium-ion capacitors (LICs) are attracting interest as energy storage devices that bridge the gap between batteries and supercapacitors, offering both high energy and power density. However, the challenge lies in developing electrode materials that can combine high capacity with long-term stability. Silicon, despite its high theoretical capacity, suffers from severe volume changes during cycling, while traditional carbon materials are stable but often lack sufficient capacity. Herein, a ZIF-8-derived nitrogen-doped porous carbon (NPC) framework was employed as a conductive scaffold to stabilize silicon nanoparticles (Si NPs) for high-capacity anodes. Si NPs were incorporated into the porous NPC network via solvothermal treatment and anchored by subsequent pyrolysis, producing an NPC/Si composite in which NPC serves as the N-doped carbon matrix and a continuous electron pathway. In the NPC/Si anode composite, the micropore-dominated porosity and mechanical flexibility of NPC provide ion-accessible voids to buffer silicon volume expansion upon lithiation and sustain a robust carbon–silicon contact during cycling, nitrogen doping enhances electronic conductivity and interfacial affinity, and silicon contributes high lithium-storage capacity. These features together enable enhancing electrode stability and capacity retention. The NPC/Si anode electrode with 8.7% silicon content delivered 1053 mAh g −1 at 0.1 A g −1 and sustained 230 mAh g −1 after 1000 cycles at 5 A g −1 . When paired with a high-power ZIF-8-derived NPC-900 capacitive cathode, the NPC-800/Si-8.7||NPC-900 LIC device delivered 244 Wh kg −1 at 395.8 W kg −1 and maintained 71.5 Wh kg −1 at 5789.5 W kg −1 . It retained 80% of its capacity after 5000 cycles, after which the capacity gradually declined to ∼70% with 15,000 cycles. This dual utilization of ZIF-8-derived carbon is a promising way to develop high-energy LIC systems with long-term cyclability.

title: Sterically shielded p-type host via dual adamantane-based molecular engineering for high-efficiency exciplex emission
Investigation of a novel, variable-orientation, pilot-scale mill using positron emission particle tracking
abstract: This study reports the first application of Positron Emission Particle Tracking (PEPT) to a continuous, variable-orientation stirred mill. PEPT is a non-invasive, non-destructive imaging technique that enables direct measurement of grinding media motion using a radiolabelled tracer. While PEPT has previously been applied to stirred milling systems, prior investigations have largely been limited to small, vertical, batch configurations. In contrast, the present work examines a mill operated under both batch and continuous conditions at five separate angles between the vertical and the horizontal. Significantly, the study found that the optimal angle for grinding media dynamics may not be either horizontal or vertical, indicating potential for future exploration of a new design space that could lead to novel, more sustainable processes. Continuous operation was also found to fundamentally alter the motion of the grinding media, inducing clear fluidisation and the formation of persistent recirculation loops. This appeared across all angles and was detrimental to grinding performance.

title: Tuning thermochromic performance of 2D perovskites via Br/Cl doping: Enhanced optical modulation and lowered transition temperature toward building energy efficiency
abstract: Buildings account for a large portion of global energy consumption, driving the need for smart windows that can dynamically regulate solar heat. Two-dimensional (2D) thermochromic perovskites offer promising stability, but their practical application is limited by high transition temperatures and modest solar modulation ability. Here, we employ halide engineering via systematic Br/Cl doping in the 2D perovskite Tha2MAPbI4 (TMPI) to decouple and optimize these key properties. A systematic Br/Cl doping was conducted in TMPI and established a detailed composition-property database. It is found that optimal Cl doping (I: Cl=4:1) enhances the solar modulation ability (Δτsol) to 27.7%, while Br doping effectively lowers the transition temperature to near 40 °C. Spectroscopic analyses correlate these improvements with doping-induced bandgap widening and structural changes. Most importantly, first-principles calculations reveal that enhanced water adsorption energy on doped perovskite surfaces governs the reduced transition temperature and faster response kinetics. A real-world model house demonstration confirms the superior cooling performance of the optimized smart window. This work provides not only high-performance material candidates but also a fundamental mechanistic framework for developing energy-efficient, responsive smart windows.

title: Moderate-field energy storage breakthrough via relaxor-ferroelectric crossover in engineered Sr2Na0.8Ag0.2Nb5O15-based filled tungsten bronze pulsed power capacitors
abstract: The global renewable energy transition demands advanced energy storage technologies, especially pulsed power capacitors capable of operating under moderate electric fields. Tungsten bronze Sr₂NaNb₅O₁₅ (SNN)-based ferroelectrics offer potential for energy storage but are still challenged by the inherent recoverable energy density-efficiency trade-off. Herein, we demonstrate that precisely targeted Bi³⁺/Ti⁴⁺ co-doping effectively regulates the relaxor-ferroelectric crossover in Sr₂Na₀.₈Ag₀.₂Nb₅O₁₅-based filled tungsten bronze ceramics, yielding a drastic enhancement in moderate-field energy storage performance. BT0.3 delivers exceptional metrics under 400 kV/cm—with a recoverable energy density (Wrec) of 6.23 J/cm³ with an energy storage potential (Wrec/E = 0.0155 μC/cm2)—outperforming most lead-free dielectrics and representing the highest performance documented within the filled tungsten bronze ferroelectric family. Multi‑scale characterizations clarify the underlying mechanism that controlled Bi³⁺/Ti⁴⁺ co‑doping stabilizes an incommensurately modulated relaxor architecture in SNN‑based tungsten bronze ceramics, where aperiodic, weakly coupled polar nanoregions replace long‑range ferroelectric order. This transformation is structurally rooted in dual-scale modifications: long-range symmetry evolves from orthorhombic (Im2a) to tetragonal (P4/mbm), suppressing macroscopic polar order, while local BO₆ octahedral vibrational modes soften and broaden, and Sr-site vacancies disrupt lattice periodicity—collectively stabilizing the PNRs configuration. Accompanying microstructural refinement, confirmed by scanning electron microscopy, yields a dense, uniform grain morphology with reduced grain size and porosity, which enhances dielectric breakdown strength and cyclic endurance. This study underscores the engineering of relaxor-ferroelectric crossover as a potent strategy to overcome key limitations in ferroelectric capacitors, providing critical insights for designing high-performance lead-free materials tailored to moderate-field pulsed-power applications.

Ecological functions and bioaugmentation applications of stress-resistant microorganisms under inhibited anaerobic digestion environments
abstract: Inhibition issues are fatal for the efficient and stable operation of anaerobic digestion (AD). Bioaugmentation effectively alleviates AD inhibition by introducing stress-resistant microorganisms, which can be enriched under stressful environments, thereby disrupting the inhibition dilemma. The present review identifies five genera of stress-resistant methanogens and sixteen genera of stress-resistant bacteria based on the succession patterns of microbial communities under stressful environments, and elucidates their ecological functions in adapting to the toxicity of inhibitors. Strategic employment of these stress-resistant microorganisms can maximize their bioaugmentation effects. This review infers that some species assigned to Methanothermobacter, Methanobacterium and Methanoculleus, Methanosarcina, and Methanolinea may be promising as bioaugmentation agents in AD inhibited by ammonium or acids, in AD inhibited by extremely high concentration ammonium or acids or salt, in mesophilic AD inhibited by ammonium or acids or salt, and in AD inhibited by salt, respectively. Furthermore, the introduction of stress-resistant bacteria and methanogens with synergistic effects (e.g., Coprothermobacter and Methanothermobacter, as well as Pseudomonas and Methanoculleus) can establish cooperative relationships in metabolic processes, thereby promoting the enrichment of methanogens. Considering cost-effectiveness and convenience, microbial consortia (such as sewage sludge, digestate, or manure) enriched with specific stress-resistant microorganisms through domestication can be employed as bioaugmentation agents. Another important approach to alleviating AD inhibition lies in reducing inhibitor concentrations. Thus, the simultaneous introduction of stress-resistant microorganisms, porous adsorbent materials, and conductive metal materials can provide a more effective solution for alleviating AD inhibition.

Multifunctional MXene film–embedded GFRP composites: Enabling EMI shielding and efficient electrothermal de-icing
abstract: In this work, we developed an efficient Ti 3 C 2 T x -based MXene film using vacuum-assisted filtration (VAF) and dry casting methods. The manufactured MXene films were embedded into glass fiber reinforced polymer (GFRP) composites via a resin infusion process, eliminating the need for multilayer matrix systems to stabilize MXene. The resulting MXene-embedded GFRP composites feature a unique architecture that imparts substantial surface conductivity to an otherwise highly insulating GFRP substrate, without compromising its structural integrity. The conductive surface enabled by the VAF-produced MXene film (~12 μm thickness) exhibited excellent electrical conductivity (4100 S/cm) and good tensile strength of 52 MPa, resulting in a multifunctional GFRP composite system. The VAF-MXene film embedded GFRP composites achieved an electromagnetic interference shielding effectiveness (EMI SE) of 41.46 dB at room temperature. In addition, the VAF-MXene GFRP composites achieved satisfactory mechanical performance, with tensile strength and modulus reaching up to 141 MPa and 9.2 GPa, respectively, along with an interlaminar shear strength (ILSS) of 31.25 MPa. Beyond their EMI shielding performance, these composites also exhibit good heat dissipation capability, enabling a temperature change of 100 °C within 32 s, making them highly attractive for de-icing applications. Overall, this work presents a promising approach for developing next-generation industrial materials suited to extreme environmental conditions and offers a viable strategy for designing high-performance, structurally stable EMI-shielding systems with integrated de-icing functionality.

Alloyed shell engineered heavy-metal-free quantum dots for efficient photoelectrochemical hydrogen generation
abstract: Heavy-metal-free quantum dots (QDs) based photoelectrochemical (PEC) water splitting has emerged as a promising approach for green hydrogen (H 2 ) production. However, a high density of surface defects/traps substantially limits efficient carrier dynamics and, consequently, overall device performance. In this work, we engineered Cu-Zn-In-Se (Cu-ZISe) QD surfaces by optimizing the alloyed ZnSeS (ZSeS) shell via aluminum (Al) doping to enhance optoelectronic properties and PEC H 2 production performance. The strategic growth of an alloyed ZSeS shell layer effectively passivates surface trap/defect states, promoting a favorable band alignment for efficient carrier dynamics. The incorporation of Al into the alloyed shell layer modulates the electronic band structure and induces the formation of a thin Al-oxide layer, thereby enhancing carrier separation, improving interfacial stability, and enhancing the efficiency of PEC devices. The optimized Cu-ZISe/ZSeS:Al core/alloyed shell QDs-based PEC with polysulfide electrolyte of 0.25 M Na 2 S and 0.35 M Na 2 SO 4 (pH = 14) exhibits a high photocurrent density of 13.91 mA/cm 2 at 1 V under one-sun illumination (AM 1.5G, 100 mW.cm −2 ), which is 65% superior compared to the core Cu-ZISe QDs-based PEC device (8.40 mA/cm 2 at 1 V). Importantly, the PEC device retained 87% and 36% of its initial performance after 2 h and 10 h continuous operation, respectively, under one-sun illumination. This work provides critical insights into alloyed-shell and dopant-assisted engineering strategies for advancing heavy-metal-free QDs-PEC systems toward practical green H 2 production and other QDs-based optoelectronic devices. • Al-ZnSeS alloyed shell passivates core QD surface traps and enhances stability. • Alloyed-shell Al-ZnSeS engineering improves interface quality and carrier dynamics. • PEC device with alloyed-shell QDs yield 65% higher performance than the control QDs. • Stable PEC device with 87% photocurrent retained after 7000 s continuous operation.

Directional molecular design of quaternary ammonium deep eutectic solvents: Enabling low-temperature regeneration for CO2 capture
abstract: Conventional aqueous alkanolamine solutions are limited by low CO2 cyclic capacity and high regeneration energy. Here, a directional molecular design strategy for non-aqueous deep eutectic solvents (DESs) was proposed to decouple high CO2 loading from regeneration temperature. Specifically, a polycationic ammonium salt, [TEPA·3H]Cl3, was employed as a hydrogen-bond acceptor (HBA) framework, while sterically hindered 2-amino-2-methyl-1-propanol (AMP) and ethanol were introduced as dual hydrogen-bond donors (HBDs) to construct a novel DES, [TEPA·3H]Cl3·3AMP·3EtOH, which synergistically regulated CO2 speciation and proton transfer. This DES achieved a high CO2 loading of 2.10 mol·mol-1 and maintained stable cyclic performance during regeneration at 363.15 K, thereby reducing the regeneration duty to 2.77 GJ·t-1 CO2. Characterization studies and quantum chemical calculations elucidated the low-temperature regeneration mechanism. The CO2 absorption proceeded via conventional carbamate formation, whereas regeneration was facilitated by a hydrogen-bond-assisted structural diffusion. Upon CO2 absorption, AMP was protonated to form AMPH+, which strongly interacted with chloride anions and became embedded within the extended hydrogen-bond network as a proton-relay node. Concomitantly, ethanol acted as a catalytic co-HBD that assisted proton shuttling and promoted the conversion of carbamate species into more readily decomposable carbonate-like intermediates. Together with the supramolecular microenvironment that competitively screens and weakens effective C-N stabilization in CO2-bound intermediates, these synergistic effects enabled efficient low-temperature regeneration. In addition, ECOSAR-based screening further suggested acceptable aquatic environmental compatibility. This work provides an explicit, molecularly guided framework for designing non-aqueous DES absorbents that balance high capacity, manageable viscosity, and low-temperature regeneration.

abstract: Integrating hydrocracking with Fischer–Tropsch synthesis (FTS) offers a pathway to overcome the limitations imposed by the Anderson–Schulz–Flory (ASF) distribution and to enhance the yield of middle distillates. Here, we explore a single-pass, non-noble metal catalytic approach of dual bed configurations composed of a Co–CeO2 FTS catalyst and a Ni/Y zeolite for primary synthesis and effluent post-treatment simultaneously. Three reactor configurations were tested—standalone, sequential bed, and physically mixed—under isoconversion conditions across a wide temperature range (235–280 °C and 2.0 MPa). The middle-distillate selectivity peaked at 78 mol% operating at high conversions (XCO > 60%), overcoming reported literature values. The sequential configuration exhibited enhanced isoparaffinic content and promoted olefin oligomerization, while the mixed configuration promoted methane reforming and hydrocracking. In situ DRIFTS, together with comprehensive product-distribution analysis, consistently indicated the presence of three configuration-dependent pathways: olefin oligomerization, hydrocracking of heavier hydrocarbons, and methane reforming, whose relative contributions vary according to the catalyst arrangement. In conclusion, the Ni/Y zeolite has shown activity processing FTS effluents in integrated dual bed configurations by tailoring product distribution and reducing undesired fractions.

Multiple redox system for energy harvesting from ubiquitous temperature fluctuations
abstract: Thermogalvanic cells, which convert heat to electricity, typically require complex thermal and electrical designs to maintain a sufficient spatial temperature difference with low electrical impedance, thereby limiting their practical applications. Herein, we present a multiple redox system (MRS) designed to harvest energy from ubiquitous temporal temperature fluctuations rather than fixed thermal gradients. The MRS employs two thermogalvanic half cells containing an electrolyte composed of a redox pair with reaction entropies of opposite signs, separated by a cation-selective membrane. Cyclic voltammetry and open-circuit voltage measurements demonstrated the fundamental principle of this device, confirming that the electromotive force generated (with a temperature coefficient of ~1.2 mV K −1 ) was consistent with the difference in the temperature-dependent redox potential of each half cell (~1.4 mV K −1 ), with the base temperature located near room temperature. Loading experiments revealed the repeated generation of an alternating current power under cyclic temperature modulations above and below a central base temperature at which the redox potentials of the half cells were identical. Enhanced energy conversion efficiency, with a cumulative energy output of 3.9 mJ from a total temperature-change history of 60 K, was achieved by reducing the electrode gap and modularizing several MRS devices. As a proof-of-concept, the MRS was successfully used to convert ambient air-temperature changes into sufficient electrical energy and activate a direct current (DC)-to-DC converter. Our device-engineering investigations highlight the potential applicability of the MRS beyond a single thermogalvanic cell, with downscaling of the device size leading to marked improvements in power and response speed by suppressing the impedance and heat capacity. This study contributes to the realization of clean, ubiquitous, and self-sustaining power supply systems utilizing ambient thermal energy. • Energy is harvested from temperature fluctuations by a multiple redox system (MRS). • The MRS comprises two galvanic half cells with reaction entropies of opposite signs. • K 3 [Fe(CN) 6 ]/K 4 [Fe(CN) 6 ] and Fe 4 [Fe(CN) 6 ] 3 serve as ideal redox pairs. • Device engineering for maximizing energy conversion is proposed. • The MRS can drive a DC-to-DC converter.

Advances in methane sensor development: From fundamentals to field deployment and future perspective
abstract: Methane plays a dual role in modern society, serving as a valuable energy resource while also being a major contributor to climate change and a serious safety hazard due to its explosivity. As a result, the ability to reliably detect and quantify methane is critical across a wide range of sectors, including mining, oil and gas, agriculture, and waste management. Over the past decades, a diverse array of methane sensing technologies has been developed to address these needs, spanning laboratory-scale devices, field-deployable sensors, and large-area monitoring platforms. This review examines these technologies from a practical, application-driven perspective, covering their underlying sensing principles, material systems, performance characteristics, and typical deployment contexts. Point sensors such as catalytic pellistors, non-dispersive infrared sensors, and chemiresistive devices remain central to localized safety monitoring and leak detection, where fast response and robust operation are essential. At larger spatial scales, mobile and fixed open-path optical techniques enable real-time monitoring of methane over distances ranging from tens of meters to several kilometres, while airborne and satellite-based hyperspectral imaging now plays an increasingly important role in identifying large emission sources and validating regional and global emission inventories. Rather than viewing these approaches in isolation, this review frames methane detection as a complementary, multi-scale sensing hierarchy, in which different technologies address distinct but interconnected monitoring challenges. Particular attention is given to the trade-offs that currently limit widespread deployment, including selectivity, long-term stability, environmental interference, and cost. Finally, emerging trends in sensor integration, data fusion, and the coupling of sensing platforms with Internet of Things (IoT) infrastructure and AI-based analytics are discussed as key enablers for scalable, real-time methane monitoring and more effective emission mitigation strategies.

Dual-polarity, highly responsive broadband photoelectrochemical photodetectors enabled by Ti3CNTx MXene/GO heterostructure
abstract: Dual polarity photodetection devices are an important building block for multifunctional devices. In particular, photoelectrochemical photodetectors (PEC PDs) show great promise due to their ability to control photocurrent polarity by varying the incident light wavelength and the choice of electrolyte. However, achieving broadband dual-polarity PEC PDs that deliver high responsivity and bias switchable operation remains a significant challenge. 2D transition carbides, nitrides, and carbonitrides (MXenes) are emerging materials that combine high electrical conductivity, excellent electrochemical properties, and ease of solution processing, making them suitable for constructing multifunctional PEC PDs. Herein, we report the broadband dual-polarity photoelectrochemical photocurrent switching (PEPS) in Ti 3 CNT x MXene/GO operating under a small external bias. We employ a solid-solution Ti 3 CNT x MXene, which exhibits featureless optical absorption and high electrical conductivity, and hybridize it with semiconducting GO, which possesses abundant surface states and a tunable bandgap, to construct PEC PDs that exhibit the PEPS effect. Notably, Ti 3 CNT x /GO heterostructures show excellent bidirectional photoresponse under UV-to-visible light, with the direction of the and responsivity tuned by the Ti 3 CNT x -to-GO ratio. The optimized heterostructure achieves high photoresponsivity values of 0.16 mA/W (cathodic) and 0.45 mA/W (anodic), corresponding to 360-fold and 4-fold enhancements compared to pristine GO and Ti 3 CNT x , respectively. We untangle that the strong PEPS effect is observed due to the role of Ti 3 CNTₓ facilitating efficient charge carrier transfer and interfacial charge separation at the metal/semiconductor interfaces. These intriguing results highlight the potential of MXenes as building blocks for designing highly sensitive optoelectronic devices with the PEPS effect.
