abstract: Carbon materials have garnered significant interest in CH4/N2 separation owing to their various advantages, such as cost-effectiveness, well-developed porosity, and high stability. Nonetheless, the inherent correlation mechanisms between their pore shapes and CH4/N2 separation efficacy remain inadequately investigated. This study utilized cellulose acetate as a superior carbon precursor to manufacture porous carbon materials with specific pore diameters and surface functional group distributions through a customized regulation technique. By employing a blend of characterisation techniques and molecular simulations, we clarified the regulatory impacts of different alkali activation settings on the microscopic pore architectures and surface characteristics of the porous carbons. Additionally, by adsorption kinetics tests and molecular dynamics simulations, the CH4/N2 separation capabilities of several porous carbons were thoroughly assessed to study the intrinsic correlation between their pore structural characteristics and separation efficiencies. The findings indicate that the CAK-3 sample, created through targeted KOH activation with an alkali-to-carbon ratio of 3, has the most prolific hierarchical micro/mesoporous structure. It attains a BET specific surface area of 1558.9 m2/g, a micropore specific surface area (determined by CO2 adsorption) of 1471.8 m2/g, an IAST separation factor of 6.17, and a column breakthrough time of 14.0 min/g for a 50% CH4/50% N2 gas mixture. Its separation efficacy exceeds that of the majority of already documented carbon-based materials. This study elucidates the mechanisms by which pore scale and chemical properties affect the adsorption and separation kinetics of CH4/N2 in porous carbons, achieved through the integration of macroscopic experiments and microscopic simulations, thus establishing a robust theoretical framework for the advancement of high-performance carbon materials and the optimization of CH4/N2 separation processes.

abstract: Membrane fouling hinders the further expansion of ultrafiltration (UF) technology in water purification, necessitating persistent exploration and development of effective fouling control strategy. Herein, we engineered a high-performance separation-catalysis membrane reactor (SCMR) by functionalizing pore channels with cobalt single-atom catalysts. The hierarchical nanoarchitecture of SCMR, when integrated with peroxymonosulfate (PMS), enabled simultaneous interception of large foulant flocs and catalytic degradation of foulant molecules migrating into pores, which greatly enhanced decontamination performance and alleviated membrane fouling. Foulant migration pathways were systematically explored, including aggregation, accumulation and transformation process of foulants across membrane pore channels. In specific, foulant floc aggregation driven by PMS addition was evidenced at the membrane-front. This phenomenon was beneficial for foulant removal, while highly possible to induce more severe irreversible fouling. Fouling model calculation and tracer tests confirmed the contribution of the functionalized nanochannels within the SCMR on retarding foulant accumulation on the membrane. Fourier transform-ion cyclotron resonance-mass spectrometry (FT-ICR-MS) further validated the structural transformation of aromatic moieties to oxidized products, which enabled regulation of foulant migration pathways via the attenuation of hydrophobic adhesion. Our work exemplified an efficient strategy via nanochannel functionalization for membrane fouling control during ultrafiltration processes.

N-doping strategy and peripheral substituent engineering enable Indolo[3,2,1-jk]carbazole harvesting multi-resonance TADF feature with deep-blue narrowband emission
abstract: Current multi-resonance thermally activated delayed fluorescence (MR-TADF) frameworks are largely limited to B/N- or carbonyl/N-based systems, which rarely achieve deep-blue emission approaching the Rec.2020 standard. Herein, we propose a dual nitrogen-atom doping strategy to construct a novel MR-TADF scaffold. By embedding electron-deficient nitrogen (sp²) atoms into indolo[3,2,1-jk]carbazole (ICz) in a meta-position fashion, a new multiple resonance framework (NICz) is obtained. Combined with peripheral substituent engineering, five derivatives are developed. The N-doping narrows the singlet–triplet splitting (ΔEST) from 0.49 eV (ICz) to 0.38 eV (NICz), and the derived emitters show further reduced ΔEST values of 0.17–0.28 eV. Meanwhile, the four compounds exhibit narrowband MR-TADF emission with wavelength of 426-440 nm and FWHM of 32-45 nm while the tCz-NICz shows donor-acceptor featured blue TADF emission (λem=466 nm, FWHM=45 nm). In OLEDs, PhCz-NICz achieves a deep-blue emission at 436 nm with CIE (0.154, 0.050) and an EQE of 11.1%, whereas tCz-NICz reaches an EQE of 20.9% at 464 nm. This work demonstrates a promising only N-based MR-TADF platform for efficient deep-blue luminescence.

Cost and carbon implications of flexible biomanufacturing to produce bio-based gasoline, jet fuel, and platform chemicals
abstract: Most biorefineries rely on fermentation to produce a single molecule, such as ethanol. This exposes facilities to price volatility and limits their flexibility to respond to market shifts and critical domestic supply chain needs. Reorienting biomanufacturing toward greater flexibility necessitates the development of versatile production platforms and chemicals with multiple upgrading options to broaden the suite of products. This study presents a design that leverages biomass ensiling, ionic liquid pretreatment, industrial microbial hosts, and catalytic upgrading. The result is a platform to convert sorghum to organic acids, indigoidine (an example of a polymer precursor and alternative to a textile dye), and varying ratios of gasoline and jet fuel blendstocks. The facility can reach net average profits above $111 per bone-dry metric ton of biomass, but only if industrial-grade organic acids are recovered and indigoidine can be used as a one-to-one replacement for synthetic indigo dye at current market prices. Results further demonstrate that economic performance is strongly governed by product allocation decisions, particularly the balance between fuels and higher-value chemical products. Rather than relying on single-product optimization, this work highlights a portfolio-based production strategy that enables dynamic adjustment of product outputs in response to market conditions. Overall, the integrated use of flexible feedstock processing, multiproduct upgrading, and selective valorization pathways provides a framework for improving the economic resilience and adaptability of future lignocellulosic biorefineries.

Practical electrochemical production of hydrogen peroxide via paired two-electron oxygen reduction and water oxidation
abstract: Paired electrolysis offers an untapped route towards effective hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) production by harnessing both half-reactions efficiently for a single valuable commodity. Here, we report a localised electrochemical system unifying catalyst innovation, convergent two-electron oxygen reduction (2 e − ORR) and water oxidation (2 e − WOR), and direct H 2 O 2 utilisation. A functionalised and tailored mesoporous carbon catalyst ( o -MC-6) was developed, exhibiting near-total H 2 O 2 selectivity (~99%) and durability (15 h) for the 2 e − ORR at current densities up to 1 A cm −2 across the full pH range, producing H 2 O 2 at a rate of 21.5 mol H 2 O 2 g −1 cat h −1 under continuous flow, consuming 7.8 kWh kg −1 H 2 O 2 , already competitive with the anthraquinone process. Coupling o -MC-6 with a boron-doped diamond (BDD) anode enables synchronous dual H 2 O 2 generation with a record faradaic efficiency of 173.7%, an unprecedented combined rate of 2.27 mmol min −1 , and an energy consumption of only 4.46 kWh kg −1 H 2 O 2 , representing a 75% increase in energy efficiency. Practicality is showcased by oxidising 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) to 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA) with 100% conversion and 98% selectivity under mild conditions using electro-synthesised H 2 O 2 streams. This work establishes a robust and scalable system for decentralised H 2 O 2 production, bridging electrocatalyst design with system-level integration, thus unlocking new avenues for green chemical electro-generation.

title: Integrated experimental, kinetic, and CFD analysis of hydrothermal liquefaction of LDPE-rich plastics waste
abstract: Plastic waste pollutes land and oceans, harms wildlife, and is difficult to recycle, especially when mixed or contaminated. Hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) can convert this waste into oil and other valuable products, offering a sustainable alternative to landfilling and traditional recycling. Therefore, in the present study, the HTL of light-density polyethylene (LDPE)-rich plastic waste was investigated using a combined experimental, lumped kinetic, and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) approach to elucidate reaction pathways, product selectivity, and reactor-scale transport phenomena. Batch HTL experiments conducted at 430–450 °C and residence times of 15–75 min demonstrated strong oil selectivity under moderate conditions, achieving oil yields of 52–61 wt% within 15–45 min. Increasing temperature and residence time shifted product distribution toward gas formation at the expense of oil, particularly at 450 °C, while residue yields remained comparatively stable. The lumped kinetic modelling identified LDPE depolymerization to oil as the governing pathway with a high-rate constant (0.3040 min −1 ) and activation energy (134.7 kJ/mol). Secondary oil-to-gas cracking reactions were negligible at lower temperatures but became kinetically significant at elevated temperatures and prolonged residence times. CFD simulations using COMSOL 6.3 Multiphysics revealed large axial temperature gradients near the wall vicinity, promoting secondary cracking and gas formation, while the reactor core maintained quasi-isothermal conditions favorable for oil production. Overall, this integrated study provides mechanistic and reactor-scale insight into HTL of LDPE-rich plastic waste and establishes a robust foundation for process optimization, reactor design, and scale-up of continuous HTL systems.

Carbonic anhydrase boosts multi-step CO2 conversion: A synergistic approach of co-immobilized enzymes for CO2 valorization
abstract: Carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) is an underutilized industrial byproduct whose conversion into valuable molecules is mainly constrained by slow gas–liquid transfer. Carbonic anhydrase (CA) efficiently accelerates CO 2 hydration to bicarbonate, increasing its availability in the liquid phase. Therefore, integrating CA into CO 2 bioconversion processes is a promising strategy for Carbon Capture and Utilization (CCU). This study investigates CA's role in enhancing CO 2 mass transfer in a multi-enzymatic platform comprising the co-immobilized formate dehydrogenase (FDH) for CO 2 reduction to formate and glycerol dehydrogenase (GlyDH) for in situ NADH regeneration via glycerol oxidation to dihydroxyacetone (DHA). Three microbial CA variants were screened, identifying Bacillus halodurans CA (BhCA) as the best candidate due to boosted formate production, immobilization on Ni 2+ -ReliZyme, and operational stability. Consequently, a novel trifunctional biocatalyst was rationally prepared from crude cell lysates using a one-step purification / co-immobilization strategy, enabling controlled enzyme incorporation at optimal activity ratios and yielding a streamlined, cost-effective, and industrially relevant biocatalyst with high catalytic performance. In the reaction, BhCA significantly enhanced CO 2 reduction to formate by FDH, increasing yield by up to 1.8-fold and reaction rate by up to 4.3-fold. This synergy with FDH arises from CA-mediated stabilization of the CO 2 –bicarbonate interconversion, which enhances gas–liquid transfer and promotes CO 2 reduction. Reusability tests showed remarkable stability with BhCA retaining 63.5 ± 0.8% of its activity and achieving 80.3 ± 1.9% formate yield after five cycles. Overall, CA acts as an effective intensifier for bio-based CCU, boosting both CO 2 capture and its conversion into high-value products within multi-enzymatic platforms.

title: Decoupling zincophilicity and conductivity in electrospun electrodes for high-areal-capacity zinc-iron flow batteries
abstract: Alkaline zinc iron flow batteries are constrained by dendritic Zn growth and membrane-adjacent, surface-confined plating, which accelerates polarization, triggers short circuits, and limits areal capacity. Here, a functionally graded anode is developed that couples zincophilicity and electronic conductivity across the electrode thickness to redirect Zn deposition into the porous bulk. A multilayer composite nanofiber network is fabricated by sequential electrospinning of Cu-doped and N-doped carbon nanofibers onto commercial carbon felt. Strong Zn affinity on the Cu-rich layer promotes rapid, spatially distributed nucleation, while the N-rich layer provides moderated conductivity and abundant secondary nucleation sites to homogenize interfacial fields and suppress near-membrane accumulation. Multi-physical simulations and post-cycling microscopy verify the transition from surface-localized growth to volumetric filling with mitigated dendrite formation. In zinc–iron flow cells, the graded electrode increases areal capacity by 30% relative to pristine felt and sustains 50 mAh cm⁻² cycling with energy efficiency above 76% for 300 cycles at 80 mA cm⁻². This hierarchical coupling of gradient zincophilicity with spatially separated nucleation sites establishes a mechanistic framework for stabilizing metal deposition in flow-battery systems.

abstract: Developing single-ion conducting polymer electrolytes (SICSPEs) with high ionic conductivity and structural homogeneity is critical for high-energy-density lithium batteries. Herein, we propose a ”self-solvation” strategy by designing an artificial pseudo-crown-ether (APCE) functionalized polymer, P(VBS-Li)-g-TEGME. Distinct from conventional synthesis, reversible addition-fragmentation chain-transfer (RAFT) polymerization is employed to precisely control the dispersity (Đ=1.11), which ensured its homogeneous integration into the PEO matrix. Mechanistic studies combining DFT calculations and MD simulations demonstrate that the TEGME side chains form a ”self-solvating” sheath that encapsulates Li⁺ via multi-dentate coordination. These chains simultaneously function as molecular anchors within the PEO matrix, effectively constructing an interconnected Li⁺ percolation network, delivering a near-unity Li+ transference number of 0.92. The resulting PEO/APCE solid electrolyte enables stable Li plating/stripping in Li||Li symmetric cells for over 500 h with low overpotential.

Process intensification via probe sonication in protic ionic liquid pretreatment of biomass
abstract: Protic ionic liquids have proven to be feasible and cost-effective for the fractionation of lignocellulosic biomass into renewable fuels and materials (the ionoSolv process). This study tested probe sonication as a process accelerator for the ionoSolv pretreatment of Miscanthus × giganteus (grass) and spruce (softwood) using the low-cost PIL, N,N -dimethylbutylammonium hydrogen sulfate ([DMBA][HSO 4 ], 20 wt% water content). Treatments were run at moderate temperatures (110 and 130 °C for Miscanthus ; 130 and 150 °C for spruce). Results showed that sonication greatly improved softwood pretreatment, whereas its effect on grass biomass was less pronounced. At 130 °C, spruce displayed high recalcitrance to the conventional ionoSolv process, yielding only 18.1% glucose after 4 h of treatment. In contrast, with sonication, an equivalent saccharification yield was achieved after only 0.5 h of treatment, and the yield further exceeded 40% after 2 h. Monitoring the temperature profile showed that the main driver of this improvement was the temperature rise induced by sonication, rather than enhanced mass transfer. Additionally, sonication was observed to produce two pulp layers, with the upper layer having finer particles. For spruce, this upper layer was markedly more digestible than the lower layer. A preliminary techno-economic analysis indicated that applying sonication during spruce fractionation could reduce the minimum selling price of spruce-derived ethanol relative to the conventional ionoSolv route, although the magnitude of the benefit depends on the extent to which the sonication-induced, laboratory-scale temperature increase can be maintained at an industrial scale.

Understanding and optimizing green synthesis from cellulose to reduced graphene oxide with enhanced photothermal properties
abstract: Reduced graphene oxide (rGO) is a promising photothermal material due to its thermal stability, electrical conductivity, and strong near-infrared (NIR) laser absorption. However, conventional synthesis routes disrupt the sp 2 carbon framework, diminishing photothermal conversion efficiency, and involve environmental hazards. Here, we report a chemical-free reduction-then-exfoliation strategy using cellulose as a renewable precursor to produce high-quality rGO with preserved sp 2 domains. Cellulose is first thermally converted into graphite-like biochar with a high C/O ratio, followed by ultrasonication-assisted exfoliation guided by theoretical calculations. Compared with conventionally synthesized rGO at similar C/O ratios, the cellulose-derived rGO exhibits a 62% lower I D /I G ratio, indicating significantly improved preservation of sp 2 domains. This structural advantage leads to enhanced photothermal performance, with a 10.1–33.0% higher temperature increase under comparable near-infrared irradiation conditions. Simulation-guided optimization of surfactant addition further reduces exfoliation energy, resulting in a 40% increase in yield at the optimal ratio. Life-cycle assessment demonstrates substantial sustainability benefits, including up to 48% reduction in ecosystem impact, 42% reduction in resource depletion, and 48% lower human health damage, together with approximately 50% improvement in cost efficiency compared to conventional methods. This work provides a high-performance and eco-efficient pathway for rGO production and establishes a mechanistic framework linking precursor structure, processing strategy, and functional performance for biomass-derived carbon materials.

Integrated reactive production and functional applications of polyamide 6 micro/nanofiber nonwovens
abstract: Benefiting from the unique physical and chemical characteristics induced by extreme diameter reduction, micro/nanofiber materials exhibit remarkable functional properties and have emerged as a frontier in fiber science and engineering. However, traditional processing approaches for micro/nanofibers mostly rely on previously synthesized high molecular weight polymers as raw materials. This reliance results in manufacturing processes that are either energy-intensive with achievable fiber diameters limited to relatively large micron-scale dimensions, or involve extensive use of organic solvents, leading to low production efficiency and potential environmentally harmful emissions. This paper builds upon our previously reported reactive melt spinning (RMS) technique as a green, efficient and scalable process, and successfully achieves continuous stable operation using polyamide 6 (PA6) as a representative example. We demonstrate herein that the optimal caprolactam monomer/catalyst formulation serves as the starting material, and reactive polymerization, melt extrusion, fiber drawing and web forming are successively taking place within a single integrated process. The resulting PA6 micro/nanofibers and their nonwovens exhibit excellent comprehensive performance, showing significant potential for applications in air purification, hygiene and environmental protection, as well as in creative print design. Furthermore, RMS is presented as a viable alternative to direct spinning technologies currently under active research and development for PA6, and may also be adaptable to other fast-reacting polymeric systems. Therefore, this innovative methodology has opened a promising pathway for the design, preparation and application of high-performance ultrafine fibrous materials.

abstract: Electrochemical CO₂ reduction (ECO₂R) has emerged as a promising approach to address the climate change, store renewable energy while closing the anthropogenic carbon cycle, and it is steadily maturing toward industrial implementation. Carbon monoxide (CO), a strategic precursor for a wide range of polymers and chemicals, along with ethylene (C₂H₄), notable for its high energy density, have been the dominant products in the most efficient electrolyzers. In addition, electrosynthesis of methanol (CH₃OH), a high-energy-density liquid fuel, has garnered significant interest as a sustainable alternative in the pursuit of a methanol economy. For industrial-scale application of ECO₂R, recent studies have focused on high-current-density evaluation of gas diffusion electrode (GDE)-based systems for the production of CO, C₂H₄, and CH₃OH. In the case of CO and C₂H₄, research primarily aims to improve energy efficiency, carbon efficiency, and system stability, while addressing operational challenges such as catalyst deactivation, salt precipitation, and electrode flooding. By contrast, methanol production systems are still striving to enhance Faradaic efficiency and current density. This review provides a unified discussion of highly efficient electrocatalytic systems for the continuous production of CO, C₂H₄, and CH₃OH, examining key aspects of process design. Furthermore, it presents a quantitative comparative assessment of system performance metrics, identifies emerging trends, and addresses existing challenges that warrant further investigation. Finally, the review outlines prospective directions for future research.

A novel CaTiO3/WO3/BiVO4 heterostructured photoanode for simultaneous glycerol valorization and hydrogen evolution
abstract: The development of efficient photoelectrochemical (PEC) systems for glycerol valorization and green hydrogen (H2) production is crucial for advancing sustainable energy technologies. In this work, a novel multilayer CaTiO3/WO3/BiVO4 (CWB) heterostructured photoanode was fabricated via automated spray pyrolysis to enable energy-efficient glycerol photoelectrooxidation, with photogenerated electrons delivered to a dark cathode to enable the H2 evolution reaction (HER). The CWB photoanode operated in a filter-press flow cell, facilitating selective glycerol photoelectrooxidation towards valuable C1-C3 compounds, while H2 was simultaneously produced at a platinum plate dark cathode. At a current density of -10 mA cm-2 under visible light illumination, glycerol conversion yielded dihydroxyacetone (DHA), glyceric acid (GEA), and formate (HCOO-) with an overall Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 64% and achieving a DHA production rate of 124 µmol m-2 s-1. Concurrently, H2 was produced at the cathode with a production rate of 549 µmol m-2 s-1, corresponding to an energy consumption (ECon) of 383 kWh kmol⁻¹ and a cathodic energy efficiency (CEE) of 74%. These findings demonstrate that replacing the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) with glycerol photoelectrooxidation significantly lowers the energy input while enabling the simultaneous production of high-value chemicals. This strategy leverages the glycerol, a low-value byproduct and waste stream from biodiesel production, via the glycerol PEC oxidation reaction (GPEOR) as a more efficient alternative to the sluggish OER in conventional H2 production. Furthermore, this study highlights the potential of multilayered semiconductor heterostructures in PEC electrolyzers for the sustainable co-production of value-added chemicals and fuels.

Denitrogenation of aqueous organic nitrogen by vacuum ultraviolet in tandem with chlorine
abstract: Dissolved organic nitrogen (DON) as an integral part of total nitrogen (TN) is often resistant to conventional wastewater treatment processes, thereby potentially posing risks to receiving water ecosystems. To address this issue, this study proposes vacuum ultraviolet (VUV)/ultraviolet (UV)/chlorine (Cl2) technology to remove TN from DON compounds. Results show that the proposed method reduced TN by 50.4% for adenine, 60.3% for atrazine, and 30.4% for metronidazole within 20 minutes. Through quenching experiments, reactive chlorine species (RCS) were found to be the primary contributors and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) were the second key contributor. Atrazine as an exception was primarily removed by direct UV photolysis. The maximum TN removal was achieved at the Cl2: N molar ratio of 2:1. Decreasing dissolved oxygen (DO) slightly suppressed TN removal rather than enhancing it, suggesting that both oxidizing and reducing components are important in this process. Elevating H⁺, OH⁻, or HCO₃⁻ level reduced TN removals significantly, whereas adding Cl⁻ and Br⁻ had minimal impacts. An assessment of intermediate products revealed that DON was likely degraded to secondary DON and NH4+ firstly, followed by formation of chloramines and conversions into RNS and N2, which eventually led to TN decrease. Overall, these results prove that VUV/UV/Cl₂ is an effective approach for nitrogen control in water treatment.

Enhanced passive micromixing via asymmetric height-variable micropillar arrays at low Reynolds numbers
abstract: Efficient mixing in microfluidic systems is essential for many biological, chemical, and diagnostic applications, yet it remains challenging at low Reynolds numbers, where laminar flow and diffusion-limited transport dominate. Here, we investigate passive micromixing as a function of systematic micropillar height variation along the flow direction over a Reynolds number range of 0.1–10. Four micromixer configurations are examined, including a plain channel without micropillars and three micropillar arrays with uniform, half-square-wave, and backward sawtooth height profiles, implemented in a device comprising two mixing chambers. Mixing efficiency, efficiency ratio, and performance index are quantified experimentally and numerically in both chambers. All micropillar configurations outperform the plain design, demonstrating the effectiveness of three-dimensional geometric modulation for low-Re mixing. Among the tested designs, the asymmetric backward sawtooth configuration provides the most robust enhancement by promoting transverse flow components and sustained interfacial stretching. Mixing efficiency in the downstream chamber consistently exceeds that in the upstream chamber due to cumulative hydrodynamic development and stronger recirculation. The backward sawtooth design achieves a maximum mixing efficiency of approximately 98% at a Reynolds number of about 0.9, while efficiency ratios in the downstream chamber reach up to 1.6 relative to the plain configuration. At a Reynolds number of 0.1, the performance index of the uniform micropillar design is nearly four times higher than that of the plain channel. The close agreement between experimental and numerical results demonstrates that height-graded, asymmetric micropillar arrays offer an energy-efficient and scalable strategy for high-performance passive micromixing under diffusion-dominated conditions, with direct relevance to lab-on-a-chip systems.

From built-in LiDFP to high-stability interface: A targeted and persistent multistage strategy for lithium-rich cathode
abstract: Lithium-rich manganese-based layered oxides (LRM) are promising cathode materials for energy storage applications because of their high specific capacities. However, their cycling stability, even under low-voltage conditions, is often compromised by bulk structural degradation and interfacial side reactions with the electrolyte. Herein, we introduce a targeted and persistent multistage strategy that converts lithium difluorophosphate (LiDFP), pre-implanted within the LRM electrode, into a highly stable interface through three synergistic stages. Initially, during electrode preparation, LiDFP reacts to form conductive fluorophosphate modifiers and simultaneously induce oxygen vacancies in the bulk materials. Subsequently, in the early cycling, the built-in LiDFP absorbs preferentially over carbonate solvents, guiding the formation of a robust inorganic-dominated cathode-electrolyte interphase (CEI). Finally, upon prolonged cycling, the LiDFP reserved within the electrode matrix releases steadily, enabling persistent protection of both stable CEI and matrix material. This multistage strategy endows LRM cathodes with remarkable cycling stability, as evidenced by a capacity retention of 90.7% after 200 cycles in coin half-cells and 89.1% after 500 cycles in pouch full-cells. This work elucidates a novel multistage mechanism for extending the functional longevity of electrolyte additives and provides valuable insights for the application of LRM materials.

abstract: Developing cost-effective, highly efficient, and durable hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) catalysts is critical for the commercialization of anion exchange membrane water electrolysis (AEMWE). However, this remains a significant challenge due to the over-reliance on platinum-based catalysts, especially when operating at ampere-level current densities. Here, we present a Cu electron-networking strategy to create Cu single atom-stabilized Ru clusters on an N-modified carbon support (Ru/Cu@CN), in which bridged Cu sites can efficiently stabilize Ru clusters and promote uniform dispersion of high-density Ru through strong metal-support interactions while weakening the overly strong Ru-H bond via Ru-Cu electron transfer, thereby substantially enhancing the HER activity and stability of Ru/Cu@CN. As a result, the Ru/Cu@CN-based AEMWE achieves exceptional current densities of 5.4 A cm−2 at 2.0 V and 3 A cm−2 at 1.79 V in 1 M KOH with a low Ru loading of 0.3 mg cm−2, fulfilling the US Department of Energy (DOE) 2025 target (3 A cm−2 at <1.8 V) and competing favorably with the state of the art. Moreover, we demonstrate that the Ru/Cu@CN-based AEMWE can be operated at a high current density of 2 A cm−2 for over 600 h without a significant cell voltage decay Ru/Cu@CN thus represents a promising HER catalyst for practical AEMWE applications. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Tight interfacial coupled NiMoO4/In2O3 S-scheme heterojunction hollow hexagonal prisms for efficient charge separation and CO2 photoreduction
abstract: Constructing heterojunction photocatalysts offers a promising approach to realize photocatalytic reduction of CO2 into chemical fuels, where the key lies in proposing a reasonable design for the preparation of effective heterostructure photocatalysts. Herein, NiMoO4/In2O3 S-scheme heterojunction hollow hexagonal prisms with tight interfacial coupling were successfully constructed through a stepwise cation ion etching/anion exchange and pyrolysis strategy using MIL-68(In) hexagonal prisms as template. NiIn layered double hydroxide (NiIn-LDH) nanosheets were first produced by Ni2+ ion etching of MIL-68(In) via a solvothermal process. In this Ni2+ ion etching process, MIL-68(In) hexagonal prisms were hollowed, followed by anion exchange, Mo6+ inserted NiIn-LDH (Mo-NiIn-LDH) was obtained. The resulting Mo-NiIn-LDH/MIL-68(In) precursor was then calcined to yield NiMoO4/In2O3 hollow hexagonal prisms. This strategy facilitates the intimate integration of In2O3 hollow hexagonal prisms with surface NiMoO4 nanosheets and forms a well-defined S-scheme heterojunction interface, greatly accelerating charge carrier dynamics. Meanwhile, this unique hollow hexagonal prism architecture, featuring a high specific surface area, shortens the charge migration distance and supplies abundant reactive sites for CO2 adsorption and activation, while also enhancing light-harvesting capability. Owing to these advantages, the as-fabricated NiMoO4/In2O3 heterostructure exhibits a remarkably boosted photocatalytic CO generation rate of 96.60 μmol g-1 h-1 and a selectivity of 80.5%. Combined electron spin resonance (ESR) analysis, in situ X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) test technique, and energy band alignment confirm the S-scheme charge transfer mechanism. In situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTs) tests reveal the key intermediates of photocatalytic CO2 reduction process. This research introduces a comprehensive approach for the systematic design of advanced heterostructure photocatalysts, enabling effective and selective reduction of CO2 by facilitating close interfacial contact.

title: Role of the nephelauxetic effect in engineering Mn4+ luminescence kinetics for lifetime-based thermometry
abstract: Although the considerable potential of luminescence thermometry based on emission kinetics has been widely demonstrated, reliable tools for the intentional prediction of thermometric performance remain limited. To address this challenge, the present work introduces an approach that enables a theoretical description of the 2E state lifetime of Mn4+ ions, as well as the absolute and relative sensitivities, in terms of the nephelauxetic effect within the group of double perovskites: Sr2InNbO6, Sr2InTaO6, Ba2InTaO6, and Ba2InNbO6. Our results clearly show that, contrary to common assumptions, the Dq/B ratio is not the primary factor governing either the spectroscopic behavior of Mn4+ ions or the thermometric performance of Mn4+-doped phosphors. Instead, the nephelauxetic beta1 parameter plays the dominant role. The empirical analysis carried out in this study led to the development of a predictive model that enables estimation of SAMAX and SRMAX values based exclusively on beta1. This methodology represents a significant step toward the rational design of lifetime-based luminescence thermometers with predefined thermometric characteristics tailored to the requirements of specific applications.

Manipulating tin perovskite microstructures for efficient long-wavelength near-infrared light-emitting diodes
abstract: Tin iodide perovskites, particularly cesium or cesium-rich tin iodide perovskites, offer distinct long-wavelength near-infrared emission (>920 nm) that is of growing importance for applications including night vision, biological tissue analysis, biomedical imaging, sensing and optical communications. However, realizing high-efficiency light-emitting diodes (LEDs) based on these materials remains very challenging, which limits their practical deployment. Here we report a crystallization-control strategy that combines low-temperature preheating with an organic additive to precisely regulate grain and pinhole formation in cesium-rich tin iodide perovskite films. This microstructural control allows for predictable modulation of light trapping and outcoupling in LED stacks, yielding perovskite films that support a broad range of light outcoupling efficiencies and enable perovskite LEDs with record performance. As a result, LEDs emitting at 960 nm with a high external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 9.5% were achieved. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the highest reported EQE for tin-based perovskite LEDs emitting beyond 920 nm. This work provides a viable pathway for efficiency enhancement in perovskite LEDs, which may also spur broader advances in perovskite photonics.

abstract: The ambient laser shock annealing (LSA) strategy enables crystallization kinetics optimization in quasi-two-dimensional (Q-2D) perovskites, yielding photovoltaic devices with high efficiency and stability. This process initiates ultrafast crystallization through the formation of a stable PbI2 intermediate phase, driven by synergistic thermal and shock-wave effects that operate on the timescale of the laser pulse and deliver a peak pressure of 8.91 GPa. The consequent uniform stress field (attenuation below 5% over 500 nm) facilitates the development of a refined microstructure in the Q-2D perovskite, manifested as grain growth, texturing, and dipole moment reduction. Such a microstructure supports a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 20.41%, achieved by suppressing non-radiative recombination and optimizing polaron dynamics via aligned organic cations. Furthermore, reinforced inorganic-organic interactions coupled with an elevated Young's modulus of 28.38 GPa underpin the substantially improved long-term stability. These coordinated improvements demonstrate that LSA is an effective strategy grounded in well-defined mechanisms for advancing perovskite device performance.

abstract: Flexible textile sensors hold enormous potential in the field of wearable flexible electronics owing to their inherent advantages of excellent motion adaptability, superior wearing comfort, and feasible functional integration. However, the application of textile-based sensors in high-temperature environments remains a formidable challenge. In this study, a flame-retardant and heat-resistant core-shell structured triboelectric nanogenerator (CS-TENG) yarn, composed of an aramid yarn outer layer, a polyimide (PI) nanofiber inner layer, and a stainless steel fiber core layer, was successfully fabricated via conjugated electrospinning and winding technology. Subsequently, the CS-TENG fibers were woven into textile sensors with various structures through different weaving methods, and their comprehensive performances were systematically compared. Among them, the 3D CS-TENG textile sensor with a lock stitch structure prepared by knitting exhibited outstanding mechanical properties, flame retardancy, and high-temperature sensing stability due to its unique structural design. Specifically, this sensor achieved an elastic deformation of 160.7% in the weft direction, prevented combustibles from being ignited by flame within 60 seconds, and retained a peak open-circuit voltage of 24.7% at 200℃ compared with that at room temperature, demonstrating tremendous application potential in high-temperature environments. Furthermore, as a self-powered wearable sensor, the CS-TENG textile sensor can be utilized for analyzing human motion states and monitoring personnel safety conditions. The CS-TENG textile sensor prepared in this work features a unique fiber and textile architecture, along with excellent wearability and reliable operability under high-temperature conditions. This research provides a novel strategy for the development of self-powered wearable sensing devices suitable for extreme environments.

Sustainable one-step synthesis of rare-earth-doped carbon quantum dots from agro-industrial and electronic waste precursors
abstract: The key scientific question addressed in this study is whether an agro-industrial biomass precursor and a real electronic-waste-derived rare-earth source can be coupled in a single hydrothermal process to produce carbon quantum dots (CQDs) with preserved carbon-core structure and tunable optical/magnetic properties. A one-step, waste-based hydrothermal synthesis of CQDs directly from cherry-seed biomass and spent fluorescent-lamp phosphor powder is reported, achieving in situ modification with rare-earth elements (REEs). The method simultaneously enables carbonization, nanoparticle formation, and REE coordination without multi-stage post-functionalization Structural and morphological characterization by HR-TEM reveals small graphitic domains (~2–4 nm) preserved upon REE modification. XPS and EDX provide evidence for surface-associated REE species, particularly Dy- and Ho-containing environments, coordinated to oxygen- and nitrogen-containing functional groups. Carbon K-edge XAS analysis indicates that the CQDs preserve a stable sp 2 -dominated carbon framework, with structural features governed primarily by surface-localized oxygen-containing functional groups. FT-IR and UV–Vis spectroscopy indicate changes in the surface ligand environment and the emergence of subtle metal-related electronic states. Photoluminescence studies demonstrate tunable emission: undoped CQDs blue-shift upon dialysis (λₑₘ ≈ 440 nm), whereas REE-doped show red-shifted emission (λₑₘ ≈ 500 nm) and enhanced radiative pathways via metal-ligand charge transfer. Magnetic measurements reveal a three-fold increase in paramagnetic responsiveness in REE-doped CQDs compared to undoped counterparts. These findings establish a sustainable, facile route to multifunctional CQDs with combined optical and magnetic properties, highlighting their potential relevance for future imaging-related applications, provided that cytotoxicity, colloidal stability in biological media, and REE ion-leakage are systematically evaluated.

Dual-responsive injectable hydrogel loaded with DPSCs accelerates diabetic wound healing by promoting mitochondrial transfer to reduce senescent cells
abstract: Accumulated senescent cells in chronic diabetic wounds impede healing, with mitochondrial dysfunction acting as both a hallmark and initiator of cellular senescence. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs)-based mitochondrial delivery holds therapeutic potential but is limited by low transfer efficiency and poor MSC viability in the hostile wound microenvironment. Here, we fabricated a dual-responsive hydrogel (EGCG@MAB) via self-assembly for Dental Pulp Stem Cells (DPSCs) delivery. EGCG enhanced DPSCs viability and upregulated CX43 expression to boost mitochondrial transfer efficiency, thereby restoring senescent cell functions. The underlying mechanism involves elevated autophagic flux via enhanced lysosomal activity and suppressed cGAS-STING pathway. In a diabetic mouse wound model, DPSCs delivered by EGCG@MAB remained viable and active on day 10 post-treatment, effectively reducing senescent cell abundance in the wound bed and accelerating healing. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that the EGCG@MAB-DPSC platform has substantial potential for treating aging- and inflammation-associated diseases.

abstract: Against the backdrop of the growing prevalence of multidrug-resistant bacterial infections and the inherent limitations of the conventional antibiotic therapies, novel wound repair materials that integrate high antibacterial efficacy, anti-inflammatory activity, and excellent biocompatibility have emerged as a critical research focus. In this study, a drug-loaded hydrogel (D-Nap-GFFY-W3BipY8-P) were engineered via the incorporation of the antimicrobial peptide W3BipY8-P into a peptide-based hydrogel (assembled by peptide D-Nap-GFFY), and its physicochemical and biological properties were systematically characterized. Notably, the hydrogel could achieve the sustained release of W3BipY8-P, which protect the internally loaded antimicrobial peptide from the rapid enzymatic degradation, and exhibit favorable biocompatibility. In vitro assays confirmed its potent bactericidal activity. Additionally, this hydrogel could effectively eradicate mature biofilms, and demonstrate hemostatic efficacy in a mouse model of acute hepatic hemorrhage. In mouse wound infection models, the hydrogel could significantly reduce the bacterial burden in wounds, alleviate inflammation, and accelerate tissue healing. These findings underscore the considerable potential of hydrogel dressing materials for treating drug-resistant bacterial wound infections and lay a foundation for the development of highly effective and safe antimicrobial peptide delivery systems.

Plastic-to-jet conversion of plastic waste: A critical review of pyrolysis oil characteristics and aviation fuel compliance
abstract: The global aviation sector is under increasing pressure to decarbonize, while plastic waste continues to accumulate worldwide. Converting waste plastics into sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) precursors through pyrolysis and catalytic upgrading, namely the plastic-to-jet (PTJ) route, offers a potential pathway to couple plastic-waste valorization with aviation-fuel decarbonization. However, plastic-derived pyrolysis oils cannot satisfy SAF-relevant requirements directly. This review critically evaluates recent progress in plastic pyrolysis and systematically maps the major fuel-quality gaps between plastic-derived oils and ASTM D7566/D1655-relevant aviation-fuel requirements. Key parameters, including carbon-number distribution, hydrocarbon composition, oxygen content, chlorine, sulphur and nitrogen impurities, olefins and gum formation, and physical properties, are discussed. The roles of feedstock type, pyrolysis temperature, catalyst type and loading, fractional distillation, and hydrotreating are analyzed in relation to SAF-oriented product regulation, with particular attention given to the trade-offs involved in these strategies. Engineering, techno-economic, and life-cycle considerations are also included to discuss the practical feasibility of PTJ pathways. This review emphasizes that PTJ development is not a single-step conversion process, but a multi-strategy optimization process aimed at satisfying multiple SAF-relevant specifications simultaneously. This process requires a careful balance between fuel-quality improvement and the associated trade-offs in yield, hydrogen demand, energy consumption, process complexity, economic cost, and environmental impact. This review provides a specification-driven basis for assessing the feasibility of PTJ pathways and guiding their development toward SAF-compliant products.

abstract: Polyurea (PUA) is widely used in protective coatings and structural applications owing to its excellent mechanical robustness and environmental resistance. However, intrinsic flammability and severe smoke release significantly limit its use in fire-critical environments. Herein, we report a highly synergistic combination of CuAl-layered double hydroxides (LDH) coated onto the surface of black phosphorus (BP) via high-energy ball milling, with chloro-4,4′-diaminodiphenylmethane (ML) serving as a molecular “bridge” to enhance dispersion and interfacial adhesion within PUA matrix. Beyond the barrier effect of the layered structure, BP contributes to gas-phase radical scavenging while CuAl-LDH acts as an effective catalytic charring agent in the condensed phase. Owing to this multi-synergy effect, PUA/BP@LDH@ML nanocomposite exhibits suppressed melt dripping and reduced combustion intensity achieving a limiting oxygen index (LOI) of 26.5% with a potential to pass the UL-94 rating. Furthermore, the peak heat release rate (PHRR) and total smoke production (TSP) decreased by 39.2% and 52.9%, respectively. Notably, the incorporation of BP@LDH@ML simultaneously enhances mechanical performance of PUA, increasing tensile strength and elongation at break by 64.6% and 39.8%, respectively. This work demonstrates a rational interfacial engineering strategy for developing PUA composites with high fire-safety and mechanical performance for diverse advanced applications.

abstract: As one of the representative intractable chronic complications of diabetes, the global incidence of diabetic non-healing wounds has continued to rise as the diabetic population expands. It not only places 15%–25% of patients at amputation risk but also markedly increases the incidence of life-threatening complications such as infection and sepsis, imposing a heavy burden on patients' quality of life and public health systems. Natural polysaccharide derivatives including oxidized hyaluronic acid and hydroxypropyl chitosan served as raw materials, and these materials were respectively subjected to functional modification via grafting of sepia melanin and phenylboronic acid. Via dynamic covalent interactions (borate ester bonds and Schiff bases) together with hydrogen bonding, a supramolecular hydrogel with multi-responsive characteristics to glucose level, pH and ROS level was constructed. Using a diabetic rat model of infected wounds, in-depth investigations were conducted into the wound repair efficacy and underlying mechanisms. Results demonstrated that the hydrogel markedly suppressed the activation of NOD-like receptor and Toll-like receptor signaling pathways, modulated macrophage polarization from the M1 to M2 phenotype, and reversed adverse pathological factors such as hyperglycemia-induced damage, oxidative stress and chronic inflammation via multi-targeted synergistic regulation, thereby effectively promoting wound healing. Focusing on remodeling the pathological microenvironment of diabetic wounds as the core premise, this study developed a specialized dressing for diabetic wounds capable of reversing the adverse microenvironment. It offers a targeted novel strategy for microenvironment modulation to overcome diabetic wound healing barriers, with scientific innovation for addressing clinical challenges and promising translational potential.

Defect-mediated enhancement of TiO2 photoanodes with potassium-poly(heptazine imide) for enhanced solar-driven biomass oxidation and synergistic degradation of organophosphorus pesticides
abstract: In this work, we report the development of TiO 2 -based photoanodes modified with potassium-poly (heptazine imide) (K-PHI). By screening various weight percentages of this polymeric carbon nitride, we initially prepared the photoanodes as thin films and evaluated their performance based on photocurrent response from methanol oxidation reaction (MOR) under simulated solar light. Our results show that incorporating up to 5 wt% of K-PHI leads to a five-fold increase in photocurrent compared to pristine TiO 2 . However, higher concentrations (10% and 20%) resulted in a performance decline. This suggests that while K-PHI introduces beneficial defects into the TiO 2 lattice that enhance photoelectrocatalytic activity, exceeding a specific threshold creates recombination sites for photogenerated charge carriers. After optimizing the K-PHI ratio, we investigated the effect of film thickness. A photoanode with 30 deposited layers achieved a significant current density of approximately 5 mA cm −2 . Furthermore, degradation assays demonstrated that the photoelectrocatalytic (PEC) process is far superior to standalone electrochemical or photocatalytic methods. Specifically, the system achieved a catalytic increment 10 7 times higher than the spontaneous degradation of paraoxon (POX), successfully degrading both the pesticide and its byproduct, p-Nitrophenol (p-NP). These findings highlight the potential of TiO 2 -K-PHI photoanodes as a versatile platform for simultaneous anodic biomass substrate oxidation and advanced environmental remediation.

Dual-functional chitosan nanoparticles enhance berberine bioavailability and alleviate mastitis-associated Staphylococcus aureus infection via synergistic antioxidant and antibacterial mechanisms
abstract: Bovine mastitis represents a major economic and clinical challenge in the dairy industry, primarily managed with antibiotics that contribute significantly to the global crisis of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). There is an urgent need for non-antibiotic therapeutics that can reduce bacterial burden while simultaneously mitigating the inflammation and oxidative stress associated with mastitis. In this study, we developed a synergistic nanoplatform by encapsulating berberine (BBR) within gallic acid-grafted chitosan nanoparticles (GA-g-CSNPs). The covalent grafting of gallate was designed to enhance the antioxidant, antibacterial, and anti-inflammatory properties of the complex. Computational analysis via molecular docking and dynamics simulations confirmed that BBR exerted multiple pharmacological effects through stable, energetically favorable interactions with hub proteins central to the mastitis inflammatory response. The BBR@GA-g-CSNPs demonstrated significantly enhanced antibacterial and antioxidant activity compared to free BBR, effectively reducing the bacterial-driven inflammatory response in bovine mammary epithelial cells (BMECs). The nanoplatform reinforced the compromised blood-milk epithelial barrier by restoring the E-cadherin/β-catenin junctional complex. Critically, the system promoted mitochondrial homeostasis by enhancing PINK1/P62-mediated mitophagy, facilitating the targeted clearance of damaged mitochondria under oxidative injury. This study establishes BBR@GA-g-CSNPs as a robust, antibiotic-free alternative for treating bovine mastitis. By combining direct bacterial suppression with the restoration of cellular quality control mechanisms, this engineered nanoplatform offers a comprehensive strategy for mammary tissue repair, providing a blueprint for the use of nanoparticle-mediated delivery of bioactive compounds to preserve animal health and mitigate the risks of antibiotic abuse.

title: Polymer-packed bed reactors enhance photocatalytic efficiency by utilizing multiple light reflections in heterogeneous photocatalysis
abstract: Efficient light utilization is a central challenge in flow photochemistry, which strongly influences catalytic performance. Here, we improve photocatalytic performance by controlling the optical properties of packing materials in the packed-bed flow reactor. Synthetic polymer particles were selected as reactor packings because their size and refractive index can be readily tuned. A Ru(bpy)₃ photocatalyst was covalently immobilized on polymer particle surfaces and mixed with catalyst-free co-packing particles, poly(methyl methacrylate) or poly(styrene), possessing different refractive indices. The mixtures were packed into columns and evaluated in the blue-light-driven oxidation of 9,10-diphenylanthracene. By systematically varying particle size, refractive index of packings and solvent, we clarified how the optical properties govern multiple light reflection and photoreaction kinetics by experiments, modelling, and theoretical simulation. The optimized reactor design enhanced photocatalytic performance and showcased successful synthesis of juglone, demonstrating a practical strategy for advancing sustainable photochemical processes.

Deciphering Er3+ energy level population in La2Sn2O7 nanocrystals via tailored short-range energy transfer for multidimensional applications
abstract: Er3+-activated upconversion (UC) materials enable color-tunable emission through their multiple radiative channels, offering promising potential in advanced optical applications. However, achieving precise color control at low doping levels remains challenging due to weak cross-relaxation (CR). Herein, we introduce a “cross-relaxation engineering” strategy based on the synergy of short interionic distances and abundant intermediate level populations to selectively enhance a specific CR pathway (4F7/2 + 4I11/2 → 4F9/2 + 4F9/2). The strategy is implemented by employing pyrochlore La2Sn2O7 nanocrystals, in which the short La3+-La3+ distance (3.79 Å) establishes the structural foundation for Er3+-Er3+ cross‑relaxation, along with Yb3+ gradient sensitization to precisely regulate the population of the intermediate level (4I11/2). The enhanced CR pathway is experimentally verified through luminescence dynamics analysis and theoretically supported by rate equation modeling, which confirm the selective promotion of red and near infrared II emission alongside green emission suppression. Leveraging this tailored emission, we demonstrate a multimodal optical thermometer and a high capacity “temperature–spectrum–chromaticity” photonic barcode for sensitive thermometry and multidimensional information encryption. This work provides a sophisticated strategy for tuning UC emission, offering a design paradigm to advance intelligent optical materials for next generation optical applications.

Application of a three-phase fluidized bed electrode for an electro-enzymatic batch process with the peroxygenase AaeUPO
abstract: Electrification of biological syntheses offers a sustainable route to decarbonize chemical production. This requires innovative reactor concepts that combine efficient electrochemical reaction steps with selective biocatalysts. Unspecific peroxygenases (UPOs) are attractive because they hydroxylate non-activated C H bonds and need only hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) as co-substrate. However, excess H₂O₂ rapidly deactivates UPOs. Electrochemical reactors must therefore generate H₂O₂ in-situ at low, uniform levels while maintaining strong mixing and mass transfer — a capability conventional electrochemical cells struggle to provide. Here, we present the first three-phase electrochemical fluidized bed reactor (gas–liquid–solid) for combined electro-enzymatic synthesis. This reactor utilizes conductive graphite particles as a fluidized electrode on which oxygen reduction generates H₂O₂ throughout the particle bed, while air sparging resupplies O₂ and drives mixing, enhancing mass transfer. Using the unspecific peroxygenase from Agrocybe aegerita ( Aae UPO) as a model enzyme, we successfully optimized the electrochemical H₂O₂ generation rate to maintain non-inhibitory H 2 O 2 concentrations below 0.2 mM and achieved a high current efficiency of 54.5 ± 12.5% for enzymatic product formation. Moreover, the batch process demonstrated scalability, as increasing the enzyme concentration enabled a Y HEBA / EBA of ~100% at even higher H₂O₂ generation rates, resulting in a space-time yield (STY) of 38.83 ± 0.32 g/(L·d) for the hydroxylation of 4-ethylbenzoic acid (EBA) to 4-(1-hydroxyethyl)benzoic acid (HEBA). These results establish the electrochemical fluidized bed reactor as a highly efficient platform for electro-enzymatic synthesis, particularly for processes requiring in-situ co-substrate generation.

abstract: Silicon offers exceptionally high theoretical capacity for lithium-ion battery anodes but suffers from large volume variation and unstable interphase evolution. Here we upcycle end-of-life photovoltaic (PV) silicon into a plasma-activated Si/C composite (P-Si/C) via dielectric barrier discharge plasma-assisted ball milling. Plasma activation promotes interfacial reactions and strengthens Si C coupling, thereby improving charge transport and suppressing mechanically driven degradation during cycling. P-Si/C delivers an initial Coulombic efficiency of 80.52% and stable cycling at high current density, retaining over 1700 mAh g −1 at 3 A g −1 with negligible decay over 100 cycles and a Coulombic efficiency approaching 100%. This work provides a practical route to convert PV waste into high-performance Si-based anodes for sustainable energy storage.

Synergistic interfacial modulation enables efficient and stable air-ambient fabricated perovskite solar cells
abstract: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have reached remarkable power conversion efficiencies (PCEs), yet the simultaneous attainment of high performance and long-term operational stability under ambient processing conditions remains a critical challenge. Here, we report a synergistic strategy that integrates functional layer optimization (SnO2 by chemical bath deposition) with interfacial dipole engineering using cyclohexylmethylammonium iodide (CHMAI) for stable air-ambient fabricated formamidinium lead iodide (FAPbI3) PSCs. CHMAI treatment induced the formation of a low-dimensional quasi 2D/3D perovskite heterostructure, evidenced by new X-ray diffraction peaks at 5.24° and 10.5°, corresponding to layered 2D-perovskite phases. Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) measurements confirmed that the CHMAI interlayer introduced an interfacial dipole, shifting the valence band maximum of the perovskite and facilitating improved energy-level alignment with the hole-transporting material (HTM) TOP α-3, which is further supported by first-principles DFT calculations. This modification reduced non-radiative recombination, improved charge transport, suppressed interfacial defects, and enhanced moisture resistance, resulting in a champion PCE of 23.55% with negligible hysteresis. Notably, CHMAI-modified devices retained nearly 90% of their initial efficiency after 5600 hours of storage in the dark and were measured periodically in high humidity, demonstrating substantial air stability. This work highlights the critical role of interfacial dipole engineering in achieving simultaneously efficient and stable PSCs through scalable, ambient-compatible processes that use less explored and cost-effective HTM. To the best of our knowledge, this is the highest reported PCE to date with this HTM.

Supramolecular assembly-driven N-type surface reconstruction for efficient and scalable perovskite solar cells
abstract: Surface defects, energy-level misalignment, and residual stress remain critical bottlenecks limiting the efficiency and scalability of perovskite solar cells (PSCs). While conventional passivation mitigates isolated defects, it seldom addresses the coupled electro-mechanical vulnerabilities inherent at the perovskite interface. Herein, we report a surface reconstruction strategy mediated by the supramolecular assembly of piperazine diiodide (PDI) and 3-(methylthio)-1-propylammonium iodide (3MTPAI). Such synergistic assembly, governed by strong intermolecular interactions, suppresses disordered aggregation during film formation and triggers beneficial secondary crystallization. The resulting morphological reconstruction effectively alleviates residual stress, thereby enhancing the structural integrity of the perovskite lattice. Simultaneously, the targeted anchoring of formamidinium vacancies and undercoordinated Pb2+ sites creates a highly ordered surface dipole layer. This dipole arrangement modulates the surface work function, inducing a distinct N-type inversion that ensures energy-level alignment with the adjacent electron transport layer. Consequently, the synergy of enhanced built-in potential and suppressed non-radiative recombination yields a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 25.73% (certified 25.02%) with improved stability. Furthermore, the exceptional spatial uniformity afforded by such electro-mechanical reconstruction enables a 12.8 cm2 mini-module to achieve an efficiency of 23.76%. Our work establishes a robust supramolecular framework for multi-dimensional surface optimization in high-efficiency, scalable perovskite photovoltaics.

title: A-site Yb-doped CaMnO3-δ perovskite as a Co-/Sr-free oxygen electrode with enhanced conductivity and stability for solid oxide fuel cells
abstract: Perovskite oxides (ABO3-δ) are widely used as oxygen electrodes in solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) because of their high activity toward the oxygen reduction reaction. Nevertheless, many state-of-the-art Co- and Sr-containing perovskites suffer from large thermal expansion and interfacial degradation, which hinder scale-up and long-term operation. Herein, we develop a Co-/Sr-free oxygen electrode based on A-site Yb-doped CaMnO3-δ (Yb0.1Ca0.9MnO3-δ, denoted Yb0.1CMO). Yb incorporation stabilizes an orthorhombic perovskite phase, decreases the thermal expansion to match gadolinium-doped ceria (GDC), and markedly increases electrical conductivity at 750–850 °C. As a cathode for solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs), Yb0.1CMO delivers exceptional electrochemical performance, achieving a peak power density of 1.83 W·cm-2 at 800 °C and maintaining long-term stability for over 400 hours, surpassing most reported cathode materials. Combined ex-situ/in-situ characterizations and density functional theory calculations indicate that A-site Yb incorporation enhances electronic transport by shifting the electronic states toward the Fermi level while enabling fast oxygen migration, thereby reducing polarization losses and improving overall cell efficiency. This work demonstrates an effective A-site doping strategy to realize high-performance and durable Co-/Sr-free oxygen electrodes for SOFCs.

title: Nanostructured Fe2(MoO4)3 cathodes: Enhancing ion and electron kinetics for high-rate and low-temperature sodium-ion batteries
Piston-type triboelectric-electromagnetic hybrid nanogenerator for wind energy harvesting in self-powered laboratory environmental monitoring systems
abstract: This paper proposes a piston-type electromagnetic-triboelectric hybrid nanogenerator (P-TEHG) based on a star‐engine model for wind energy harvesting. The device converts irregular wind energy into stable and continuous power output, significantly improving energy capture efficiency. The electromagnetic generator (EMG) employs a multi‐coil lateral arrangement and parallel connection strategy, while the triboelectric nanogenerator (TENG) utilizes a wool and PTFE/PET/FEP multi‐layer polymer combination to optimize charge density and durability. The soft texture of wool minimizes sliding friction and charge leakage by maintaining close contact with the film within the rectangular frame, thereby enhancing the output performance of the TENG. Under a rotational excitation of 300 rpm, the optimized TENG and EMG achieved output powers of 2.13 mW and 190.2 mW, respectively. In addition, a self-powered environmental monitoring system was also constructed. This system operates continuously at a wind speed of 5 m/s, providing power to gas sensors and wireless temperature/humidity sensors while supporting real-time sound-light alarms for gas leaks and transmission of temperature-humidity data. This work proposes an innovative, self-sustaining solution for laboratory environmental monitoring, capable of achieving continuous autonomous operation to effectively ensure the stability and reliability of the experimental environment.

A new sintering mechanism, “silver-zipping”, for low-temperature sintering of oxide solid electrolytes
abstract: Abstract Oxide-based solid electrolytes promise safe, high energy density all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs), but require high sintering temperature, which impairs cathode-electrolyte compatibility and manufacturability. Incorporating Ag nanoparticles enables low-temperature densification of a γ-Li3PO4-type LISICON (Li3.5Ge0.4Si0.1V0.4O4) via a ‘silver-zipping’ mechanism that transiently hosts Li, reduces local coulomb repulsion between solid electrolyte particles, and accelerates neck growth. The resulting microstructure yields higher ionic conductivity without a measurable rise in electronic conductivity, serves as both separator and catholyte, and co-processes with layered oxides at ≤ 750°C without parasitic phases. The strategy provides a practical route to low-temperature processing of oxide-based ASSBs with improved interfacial compatibility and manufacturability.

abstract: Protein-based functional hydrogels have attracted wide attention due to their biocompatibility, tunable structures, and functional diversity. We developed a novel spirulina peptide–functionalized hydrogel (SPP), integrating the intrinsic fluorescence of natural peptides with a highly hydrated, mechanically flexible polymer network. Spirulina peptides were embedded into a dual-network hydrogel, preserving fluorescence while maintaining high hydration and mechanical performance. Acting as both Hg²⁺-selective fluorescent probes and structural components, the SPP exhibits pronounced fluorescence quenching upon Hg²⁺ exposure, enabling sensitive detection with a linear range of 50–150 μg/L and a detection limit of 4.3 μg/L. Engineered into microneedle arrays, the developed hydrogel showed enhanced adhesion and interfacial adaptability on soft, curved, and moist surfaces. Meanwhile, fluorescence signals can be rapidly digitized via smartphone and analyzed with convolutional neural networks, achieving up to 97.73% quantification accuracy under complex interfaces. This study presents a versatile strategy for efficiently incorporating natural protein functionalities into hydrogel networks, offering a promising platform for biointerface materials and intelligent protein-based functional systems.

Optimizing aromatics yield-selectivity trade-off in zeolite-catalyzed biomass fast pyrolysis using machine learning
abstract: Catalytic fast pyrolysis of biomass to aromatic hydrocarbons is an attractive valorization technology to produce high-value chemicals and biofuels. However, process optimization to produce desired products remains challenging due to reaction complexity. Herein, we present a data-driven approach to address this issue. A literature dataset of ZSM-5-based catalysts, including promoted and unpromoted systems is compiled, resulting in 254 datapoints and subjected to data-mining. A random forest model with uncertainty quantification is devised to predict the aromatic hydrocarbon yield, and benzene, toluene, and xylene (BTX) selectivity. The models achieved comparable performance ( R 2 > 0.80) and feature-importance analysis identified feedstock composition, catalyst total acidity, catalyst-to-biomass ratio, and space velocity as key drivers of performance metrics. Given the inherent trade-off between aromatic yield and BTX selectivities, an optimization framework was devised to screen over 20,000 promoted-zeolite and reaction condition combinations, uncovering Cu, Ga, Sn, and Zr promoted-ZSM-5 as Pareto-optimal catalysts. Lastly, motivated by challenges encountered during data collection and model limitations in out-of-box predictions, we urge the community to report biomass fast pyrolysis protocols in standardized manner, and provide effective guidelines for the cause. Our study provides a predictive toolkit to identify promising catalytic systems and optimize biomass fast pyrolysis performance while improving machine readability.

abstract: Surface Sr segregation and CO2 poisoning are the primary hurdles for the long-term stability of La0.6Sr0.4Co0.2Fe0.8O3-δ (LSCF) oxygen electrodes. This study demonstrates a strain-engineered heterointerface strategy that synergistically enhances the catalytic activity and durability of LSCF by infiltrating Sm0.2Ce0.8O1.9 (SDC) nanoparticles. The lattice mismatch between the LSCF and SDC phases induced a localized tensile strain within the LSCF surface. This interfacial strain significantly lowers the formation energy of oxygen vacancies, increasing the surface oxygen vacancy concentration from 41.3% to 51.6%, thereby accelerating the kinetics of the oxygen reduction and evolution reactions (ORR/OER). Consequently, the optimized 5 wt.% SDC-infiltrated electrode achieved a superior polarization resistance (Rp) of 0.142 Ω cm2 at 800 °C. Furthermore, SDC decoration functions as a protective barrier and anchor for surface cations, suppressing Sr segregation and enhancing the CO2 tolerance. After 5 vol.% CO2 exposure for 200 h, the Rp increase was limited to 86% for LSCF@SDC, compared to 143% for pristine LSCF. Single-cell evaluations demonstrated a peak power density of 1411 mW cm-2 and exceptional stability with minimal voltage degradation of 0.229% over approximately 300 h. These results underscore that interface-induced strain engineering is a powerful strategy for modulating defect chemistry and surface reactivity, providing a promising pathway for the design of robust, high-performance SOC oxygen electrodes.

Molecularly functionalized high-Q THz metasurface via q-BIC for selective HbA1c detection
abstract: High-Q resonance enhanced metasurfaces provide a powerful platform for label-free biosensing and early disease diagnosis. Here, we report a dynamically tunable terahertz (THz) metasurface sensor in which high-Q quasi-bound states in the continuum (q-BIC) are generated by structural symmetry breaking in asymmetric split-ring resonators, leading to strong electromagnetic field confinement and enhanced sensing capability. To enable dynamic control of the resonance characteristics, the phase-change material vanadium dioxide (VO2) is integrated into the asymmetric region of the resonator, where its temperature-induced phase transition modified the electrical conductivity and consequently tunes the structural asymmetry and radiative loss of the q-BIC mode. By functionalizing the metasurface with a phosphonic acid self-assembled monolayer (SAM), selective recognition of glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) is achieved while suppressing nonspecific adsorption and enhancing the interaction between the captured biomolecules and the THz near field. Through the combined effects of high-Q resonance, dynamically regulated structural asymmetry, and molecular-specific recognition, the sensor achieves a detection limit at the picomolar (pM) level. This work demonstrates a reconfigurable THz biosensing platform for high sensitivity and label-free detection of the diabetes biomarker HbA1c, providing a practical approach for developing chip-scale THz biosensors.

abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) offer substantial potential for electrocatalysis due to lattice distortion, entropy stabilization, and the ‘cocktail effect,’ which create numerous catalytic centres. However, a significant challenge remains in developing reliable and scalable fabrication methods capable of producing nanometer-level HEA coatings to minimize the loading of critical raw materials (CRMs) without compromising performance. Addressing this gap, we report a laser-directed approach f or the synthesis of FeCoNiZnMn (FCNZM) HEA thin films onto nickel fibre (NFb) substrates. Beyond reducing the time and expense, this method offers strong HEA-substrate interactions, making it more active and durable in a harsh alkaline environment. As a result, the optimized FCNZM_2td_25p electrocatalyst demonstrates exceptional kinetics with an overpotential of 235.5 mV at 10 mA cm −2 and a favourable Tafel slope of 48 mV dec −1 . This initial activity is matched by extraordinary stability, maintaining performance for over 100 h at a high current density of 500 mA cm −2 and exceeding 160 h in a single-cell configuration against an Ir/NFb benchmark. Post-mortem characterization via TEM, XPS, and XAS reveals that the superior durability originates from a dynamic restructuring process involving the leaching of an unstable Zn-rich surface layer. These results demonstrate that our laser-directed approach provides a scalable pathway for low-loading, highly efficient transition-metal-based HEA anode, offering a viable PGM-free alternative for industrial alkaline water electrolysis.

title: Kinetic-driven separation of ethylene from ternary mixtures by engineering the crystal size of a novel 2D metal-organic framework
abstract: The purification of ethylene (C2H4) from ternary C2H2/CO2/C2H4 mixtures remains a critical yet challenging process in the petrochemical industry. Traditional physisorption methods integrating even advanced metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) often suffer from insufficient selectivity and/or impractical regeneration. Herein, we report a kinetic separation strategy using ZNU-16, a MOF with tunable crystal sizes, to selectively exclude C2H4 by leveraging its slower kinetics in larger crystals (ZNU-16-L). While conventional approaches minimize crystal size to enhance adsorption kinetics, ZNU-16-L intentionally retards C2H4 diffusion, achieving near-zero C2H4 uptake (2.9 cm3/g) while retaining high capacities for C2H2 (61.7 cm3/g) and CO2 (30.8 cm3/g) at 298 K and 1 bar. Breakthrough experiments demonstrate one-step production of ≥99.999% pure C2H4 with a productivity of 42.6-80.0 L/kg. Density functional theory calculations revealed the preferential interactions of C2H2 and CO2 via fluorine-mediated interactions, implying relatively moderate energies that enable mild regeneration. Notably, ZNU-16-L maintains separation performance under humid conditions and across multiple cycles, highlighting its industrial viability. This work demonstrates that crystal-size modulation in tandem with pore engineering, offers a sustainable pathway to address the growing global demand for high-purity ethylene.

Radial diffusion–reaction model for microperforation-assisted delamination
abstract: Multilayer flexible packaging (MFP) recycling is hindered by structural complexity. Chemical delamination via alkaline (NaOH) dissolution of the internal aluminum foil enables recovery, but impermeable polymer layers create transport bottlenecks, causing long processing times. To overcome this, this work develops a mechanistic diffusion–reaction model to quantify microperforation-assisted delamination kinetics. Moving beyond empirical fitting, a series-resistance formulation evaluates four independent regimes: external mass transfer, axial pore diffusion, radial interfacial diffusion, and surface chemical reaction. A dimensionless formulation (Biot and Damköhler numbers) and Monte Carlo simulations reveal the process dynamically transitions between radial transport and surface reaction limits. Parametric analysis demonstrates pore density (n) is the critical variable, reducing complete delamination time proportionally to 1/n under radial-diffusion control, whereas pore radius exerts only a secondary effect. Experimental validation on metalized PET/PE laminates confirmed these predictions: compared to 300 min for non-perforated edge-fed transport, a minimal pore density of 6 μP/cm 2 reduced delamination time to 130 min, and 61 μP/cm 2 achieved total separation in just 25 min. To quantify this intensification, a finite-size geometric correction ( n min = 1 / L s 2 ) was derived to decouple intrinsic kinetic improvements from macroscopic edge-fed transport. Ultimately, this framework provides a robust predictive tool for optimizing microperforation patterns in large-format industrial packaging recycling.
