A sulfonate-rich gel electrolyte enables coupled polyiodide confinement and Zn2+ transport regulation for durable aqueous ZnI2 batteries
abstract: Aqueous zinc–iodine batteries (AZIBs) are promising candidates for safe and cost-effective large-scale energy storage, yet their practical viability is hindered by the coupled challenges of soluble polyiodide shuttling and unstable Zn metal deposition. Herein, a sulfonate-rich quasi-solid-state gel electrolyte, denoted SP-1, is developed through the free-radical copolymerization of acrylamide and 2-acrylamido-2-methylpropanesulfonic acid to simultaneously regulate iodine cathode chemistry and Zn anode interfacial behavior. The crosslinked polymer framework spatially restricts polyiodide migration, while the abundant sulfonate groups promote selective Zn2+ transport, homogenize interfacial ion flux, and participate in constructing a stable organic–inorganic interphase on the Zn surface. In addition, the reconstructed hydrogen-bonding environment reduces free-water activity, thereby suppressing parasitic hydrogen evolution and corrosion reactions. Benefiting from this multifunctional electrolyte design, the SP-1-based AZIBs deliver a high initial capacity of 206.6 mAh g-1, and retains 95.83% of its capacity after 10000 cycles. In situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy combined with distribution of relaxation time analysis further reveals stable charge-transfer kinetics during cycling, confirming the robust interfacial regulation enabled by SP-1. This work demonstrates a sulfonate-engineered gel electrolyte strategy for coupling cathode-side polyiodide confinement with anode-side Zn2+ transport regulation, providing new insights into the design of durable aqueous conversion batteries.

Water electrolysis across the pH-universal catalyzed by Mo-doping NiO@NiCo heterojunction coupled with carbon
abstract: Energy efficiency of water electrolysis catalysts across the entire pH range under ambient conditions is restricted by the kinetic bottleneck and stability of the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Here, Mo-doping NiO@NiCo heterojunction, coupled with the lignin-derived gradient monolithic carbon catalyst (Mo-NiO@NiCo/LDC), was designed through synergistic electronic-strain engineering. Physical property and theoretical calculation results prove that the synergistic interplay between Mo-doping and heterojunction interfaces (NiO, NiCo alloy, and lignin-derived carbon) induces lattice strain and modulates the electronic structure, optimizing the H* adsorption/desorption (∆GH* = 0.026 eV) balance and boosting H–OH cleavage, and thereby accelerating the Volmer-Heyrovsky step. Thus, Mo-NiO@NiCo/LDC exhibits excellent HER activity with low potentials of 21/346 (acidic), 41/496 (neutral), and 29/421 mV (alkaline) at 10/1000 mA cm2. Furthermore, lignin-derived carbon with a gradient monolithic structure increases the number of active sites to enhance HER activity, boosts gas-liquid transport efficiency to improve mechanical stability, and confers superior corrosion resistance to ensure robust chemical stability, demonstrating 120 hours of stability under all electrolysis conditions. This work obtains a very promising HER catalyst and proposes a viable design strategy for the design of catalysts in pH-universal hydrogen

abstract: Inert atmospheres suppress oxidation in high-performance Cu(In,Ga)(S,Se)2, Cu2ZnSn(S,Se)4 and Sb2(S,Se)3 solar-cell fabrication, however, they substantially increase processing costs and severely limit the scalability of these technologies. Although ambient annealing has been achieved for Cu(In,Ga)S2 and Cu2ZnSnS4 as-prepared films, the selenization process still needs an inert atmosphere. The low melting point of Sb2S3 makes open-air annealing feasible, yet the annealing temperature of approximately 360 °C inevitably induces severe surface oxidation. Beyond this processing challenge, the performance of Sb2S3 solar cells remains limited by low fill factors (< 64.0%). Here we report an open-air annealing strategy coupled with hydrothermal sulfuration for efficient Sb2S3 solar cells with a record fill factor. A cracked Sb2O3 layer is formed on the Sb2S3 surface during open-air annealing. Subsequent hydrothermal sulfuration, conducted under an air atmosphere, converts Sb2O3 into Sb2S3 and induces nanorod-like protrusion reconstruction at the absorber surface, which reduces the hole-transport barrier and enhances hole extraction. As a result, we achieve a record efficiency of 7.25% for open-air-fabricated Sb2S3 solar cells, with the fill factor exceeding 66.0% for the first time. This work offers a low-cost route for scalable high-performance Sb2S3 solar cells and establishes robust Sb2O3-mediated surface reconstruction to overcome fill-factor losses.

Synergistic ion-flux homogenization and localized electronic modulation via a mesoporous-quantum hybrid architecture to mitigate cathode–anode cross-talk in aqueous zinc-ion batteries
abstract: Aqueous zinc-ion batteries (AZIBs) are highly attractive for large-scale energy storage, yet their practical deployment is severely hindered by system-dependent failures of zinc anodes. During cycling, diverse cathode chemistries continuously reconstruct electrolyte compositions and interfacial microenvironments, inducing dendritic growth, corrosion, and hydrogen evolution, making anodes highly sensitive to the specific cathode chemistry utilized. Here, we report an interfacial engineering strategy to decouple cathode–anode cross-talk by embedding CsPbI3 quantum dots (QDs) into an ordered SBA-15 mesoporous silica framework, forming a mesoporous-quantum hybrid coating (SBA+QDs). The ordered SBA-15 mesoporous framework provides low-tortuosity pathways for Zn2+ transport and buffers local electrolyte fluctuations, thereby homogenizing interfacial ion flux and alleviating concentration polarization. In parallel, the embedded CsPbI3 quantum dots primarily contribute to interfacial electronic modulation by regulating the local electronic structure and nucleation kinetics. As a result, the Zn nucleation barrier is reduced and parasitic reactions (e.g., corrosion and HER) are effectively suppressed. Consequently, the SBA+QDs-protected anodes exhibit highly consistent and stable cycling performance across diverse systems, including ZnI2, AlV6O13, PANI, and MnO2. Notably, the Zn//ZnI2 full battery achieves nearly 30,000 cycles at a high current density of 30 A g−1, showcasing exceptional low-temperature performance and long-term pouch-cell stability. This research solves the critical challenge of cathode-induced anode degradation from a holistic full-battery perspective, establishing a cathode-chemistry-agnostic decoupling of cathode–anode cross-talk interface design paradigm for high-power and long-life AZIBs

Compartmentalized hydrogel-based in situ fibrous bed bioreactor (isFBB) for spatially controlled multi-strain anaerobic human gut microbial growth
abstract: The scalable cultivation of anaerobic multi-strain probiotics remains a major challenge due to the requirement for controlled microenvironments, prevention of cross-contamination and maintenance of metabolic interactions within a single reactor system. Herein, we report a cellulose nanofiber (CNF)–alginate hydrogel-integrated radial in situ fibrous bed bioreactor ( is FBB) designed to enable process-intensified, compartmentalized multi-strain anaerobic fermentation. The hydrogel matrix functions as a multifunctional immobilization scaffold, facilitating simultaneous microbial growth, spatial confinement, and in situ encapsulation within a single vessel. The engineered fibrous architecture provides a porous and compartmentalized framework that supports nutrient and metabolite diffusion through semi-permeable interfaces while maintaining spatial separation of immobilized microbial populations. The system was validated using strict anaerobic gut microbial strains, demonstrating successful multi-strain cultivation with distinct growth kinetics and efficient substrate utilization. High encapsulation efficiencies (90–91%) were achieved across all strains, with stable microbial retention and preserved cell morphology confirmed by optical microscopy and SEM analysis. The compartmentalized reactor design enables diffusion-mediated metabolic exchange between adjacent compartments while preventing direct cell mixing and cross-contamination, thereby eliminating the need for multiple parallel bioreactors. Molecular docking analysis revealed strong interactions between hydrogel polysaccharides and microbial surface proteins (binding affinity up to −9.2 kcal·mol −1 ), providing mechanistic insight into hydrogel-mediated microbial adhesion and stabilization. By integrating functional hydrogel materials with reactor engineering, the is FBB platform enables simultaneous cultivation, immobilization, and encapsulation within a single bioprocessing system. These findings demonstrate a scalable strategy for multi-strain anaerobic bioprocessing and highlight the potential of hydrogel-enabled compartmentalized reactor architectures for advanced biomanufacturing applications.

Reactant-adsorption induced flexible hydrogen-bond networks on Co–O–Fe electronic bridges for enhanced electro-oxidation of methanol to formate
abstract: Regulating hydrogen-bond networks (HBNs) at electrode-electrolyte interface has been established as an effective strategy to boost electro-oxidation of organic molecules. However, the important role of adsorbed organic reactants on HBNs evolution are often overlooked. Herein, we construct a Co–O–Fe bridging motif on a Fe-doped CoOOH catalyst (Fe0.1Co0.9OOH), which achieves a 2.65-fold enhancement for methanol-to-formate conversion compared with pristine CoOOH (0.45 vs 0.17 mgformate cm-2 h-1 at 1.7 V vs RHE), as well as stable operation at 100 mA cm-2 for 100 hours. Quisa in situ/in situ spectroscopy and kinetic analyses provide insights into the reaction mechanism, identifying hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) from methanol to electro-generated Co4+ species as the rate-determining step. More importantly, are found to boost the kinetics of this step: the Co–O–Fe electronic bridges can modify the electronic structure and enhance methanol adsorption. The interfacial enrichment of hydrophobic methyl groups in methanol, in turn, disrupts the rigid interfacial HBNs, thereby facilitating the mass transfer of methanol and promoting HAT kinetics. This work provides novel insights into the dynamic evolution of interfacial HBNs for efficient electro-oxidation of organic molecules.

Decoupling dissolution and reaction for low-impurity synthesis of TDA through solvent-controlled activation and microreactor intensification
abstract: The nucleophilic substitution of 7-aminocephalosporanic acid (7-ACA) is a key step in the synthesis of cefazolin intermediate TDA, but its poor solubility often causes dissolution-reaction coupling, leading to heterogeneous reaction environments and impurity formation. Herein, methanesulfonic acid (MSA) was employed as a BF3-free Brønsted acid catalyst, and a solvent-controlled activation strategy was developed for the selective synthesis of TDA from 7-ACA. Pre-dissolution of 7-ACA in a trifluoroacetic acid/dimethyl carbonate (TFA/DMC) mixture transformed the conventional solid-liquid process into a liquid-liquid dispersion process, thereby decoupling substrate dissolution from substitution. Kinetic studies revealed a solvent-dependent transition from an SN2-like pathway under DMC-rich conditions to an SN1-like pathway under TFA-rich conditions. Molecular dynamics simulations showed that increasing TFA content reconstructed the local solvation environment around 7-ACA, while DFT calculations indicated that solvent polarity altered the relative preference of the two pathways. Based on this understanding, a membrane-dispersion microreactor was employed to rapidly establish a uniform liquid-liquid reaction environment. The relative impurity level was ultimately reduced from 4.86% to 1.47% (69.7% reduction), demonstrating the potential of this BF3-free strategy for selective continuous synthesis of β-lactam antibiotic intermediates.

abstract: Liquid metals represent an emerging class of reaction media that enables the unique use of metals in their liquid state for chemical processing. Despite their promise, their application in polymer and plastic recycling has remained largely unexplored. In this work, we demonstrate that a gallium–lithium alloy with a near room-temperature melting point can effectively decompose polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), a widely used but chemically inert fluoropolymer whose production continues to increase with ongoing industrial expansion and adoption in emerging technologies, posing significant recycling and sustainability challenges. The alloy provides a safe, on-demand route to harness the otherwise highly reactive lithium metal under mild conditions of temperature and pressure. Lithium dissolved in the gallium matrix diffuses to the PTFE surface, driving its reduction. Density functional theory calculations reveal that lithium atoms at the alloy surface act as chemically active sites, fundamentally reshaping the reaction energy landscape by stabilizing polymer adsorption and promoting C F bond cleavage through strong Li F interactions while comprehensive material characterization confirms the formation of amorphous carbon and lithium fluoride. Remarkably, the reacted alloy forms a gallium core with a self-assembled surface crust of reaction products, which can be directly employed as a binder-free nano-interface demonstrating excellent pseudocapacitive properties. This work highlights liquid metals as a powerful platform for sustainable recycling, offering a novel pathway to transform persistent polymers into functional energy storage materials.

abstract: This study addresses the challenge of removing the persistent mycotoxin deoxynivalenol (DON) by employing kaolin-group minerals - natural halloysite (HD), purified halloysite (HS), and synthetic kaolinite nanotubes (MNC) - as supports for TiO2, Fe2O3, and TiO2/Fe2O3 semiconductors. The nature of the mineral support strongly influenced the dispersion and size of the loaded semiconductors, leading to the formation of highly dispersed nanosized active particles, particularly on the MNC surface. In the presence of potassium peroxymonosulfate (PMS), TiO2-containing composites achieved up to 97.7% DON removal within 20 min under UV irradiation, while Fe2O3 showed higher activity under visible light. Among the composites, the MNC support loaded with TiO2/Fe2O3 exhibited the highest DON removal, correlating with more efficient charge transfer and lower charge-transfer resistance, indicating improved interfacial charge transport. Scavenger and EPR analyses suggested that PMS activation followed electron-transfer pathways, in which initially formed SO4•⁻ radicals underwent rapid reaction to yield •OH, identified as the dominant reactive species in aqueous solution, with an additional contribution from 1O2. UHPLC-ESI-MS/MS analysis indicated that DON degradation was initiated by oxidative transformation of key functional groups, including epoxide ring opening, followed by progressive fragmentation of the trichothecene structure, with pathways dependent on catalyst composition.

abstract: Achieving a physiological microenvironment in tissue engineering represents the ultimate objective. Current strategies for constructing osteochondral units focus primarily on biomimicking scaffold materials and often overlook the zonal distribution of seed cells. Studies indicate that chondrocytes, which are utilized as seed cells, are susceptible to reduced proliferation and dedifferentiation, which compromises regenerative outcomes. In this study, we biomimetically fabricated a three-layer hydrogel scaffold of zonal osteochondral units using gelatin methacryloyl and nanohydroxyapatite (GelMA/nHA), where the first and second layers were composed of superficial zone chondrocytes (SFZCs) and middle-deep zone chondrocytes (MDZCs), respectively. The lower layer contained a GelMA/nHA hydrogel loaded with bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) derived from a rat osteochondral defect model. The SFZCs and MDZCs were modified with histone deacetylase 4 (HDAC4) to increase their viability. The results showed that the simultaneous zonation of cells and the scaffold effectively enhanced osteochondral defect repair. Moreover, delivering HDAC4 to chondrocytes in each layer further improved the repair outcomes. Omics and validation data suggest that HDAC4 optimizes chondrocyte function across zones by upregulating oxidative phosphorylation. This study highlights the importance of zonal cell biomimicry in engineered osteochondral constructs and defect repair. In addition, this study reveals the molecular mechanism by which HDAC4 regulates chondrocytes, providing new insights for osteochondral regeneration.

abstract: Molecular solar thermal (MOST) energy storage systems utilize photoswitchable molecules to harvest, store, and release solar energy as heat on demand under ambient conditions. While much of the research to date has focused on molecular design, this work marks a significant advancement in the process engineering of MOST systems, moving beyond conventional batch-wise approaches. To this end, a milli-fluidic device was developed to enable operation under continuous-flow conditions and to screen a large operating window with small amount of the 1-cyano-2- p -methoxyphenyl-norbornadiene/1-cyano-3- p -methoxyphenyl-quadricyclane couple (NBD1/QC1). To ensure environmental sustainability, cyclopentyl methyl ether was employed for the first time as a green alternative solvent to toluene, and was found to achieve a higher quantum yield. The kinetics of the photochemical reaction was investigated in an LED-driven spiral-shaped reactor. A 1D model describing the reactive transport of NBD1 in the photoreactor was developed, which successfully predicted the NBD1 conversion over the whole set of operating conditions. The catalytic back-reaction was then performed using a heterogeneous platinum-on-alumina catalyst. Kinetic data obtained from a jacketed stirred batch reactor enabled the successful transposition of the reaction into a continuous-flow milli-fixed bed reactor. An isothermal plug flow model was considered for the latter, based on a first-order apparent reaction rate and including external mass transfer limitations. The model predictions satisfactorily reproduced the experimental conversion data of the photoisomer QC1. Finally, both steps were integrated in series with on-line UV spectroscopic monitoring, demonstrating efficient operation under continuous-flow conditions. This approach opens promising guidelines for the development of future closed-loop processes.

Viscosity-driven rapid photopolymerization of UHMW-PMMA/SBS: synergistic energy dissipation for high-temperature resistant ballistic adhesives
abstract: The inherent brittleness of poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) limits its application in high-velocity impact scenarios such as ballistic protection. Currently toughening methods often sacrifice stiffness or involve complex processes. To circumvent this fundamental stiffness-toughness trade-off, we report a highly scalable, viscosity-modulated in-situ photopolymerization strategy. By directly incorporating 20 wt% poly(styrene-block-butadiene-block-styrene) (SBS) into the methyl methacrylate (MMA) monomer, the precursor viscosity is strategically elevated to suppress bimolecular termination. This dramatically accelerates UV-induced kinetics, enabling the rapid (~40 min) synthesis of a phase-separated composite featuring an ultra-high molecular weight PMMA matrix (Mw ~1208 kg·mol-1) interwoven with uniformly dispersed, flexible SBS domains. The resulting UHMW-PMMA/SBS material exhibits a highly synergistic mechanical profile, preserving exceptional matrix stiffness (Young's modulus of ~2.2 GPa) while achieving profound impact toughness (notched impact strength of 32.4 kJ·m-2). Implementing this resin via in-situ polymerization with ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) fibers yields an exceptionally coherent interfacial network. The resulting ballistic composite achieves effective protection at a record-low areal density of 3.8-4.0 kg·m-2, representing a 20-35% weight reduction compared to mainstream commercial PMMA or SBS matrices, while maintaining robust structural integrity under high-temperature impact conditions. This facile, low-cost synthesis platform provides a highly translatable engineering framework for the continuous manufacturing of ultra-lightweight, extreme-environment protective materials.

Droplet-driven self-powered electronic skin for on-demand robotic hand disinfection
abstract: Surface contamination on robotic hands and electronic skin poses a growing biosafety concern in medical care, laboratory operation, food processing, and human-machine interaction. Conventional disinfection strategies, such as chemical disinfectants, ultraviolet irradiation, and antibacterial coatings, often require external energy input, cause chemical residues, or show limited compatibility with flexible robotic surfaces. Therefore, developing a self-powered, on-demand, and in situ disinfection strategy for robotic electronic skin is highly desirable. Here, a droplet-driven self-powered antibacterial electronic skin based on an Al-FEP-PPyNW-PM film is proposed. Water droplets naturally impact the multilayer film, converting droplet kinetic energy into electricity and triggering antibacterial reactions on robotic hands. The superhydrophobic FEP layer promotes rapid droplet contact–separation and enhances interfacial charge generation. The Al needle electrode supports charge collection and electron transfer. The PDMS@MXene substrate provides a flexible conductive network and piezoresistive sensing capability. The PPy nanowire tips amplify the localized electric field near bacteria. Droplet-induced electron transfer activates dissolved oxygen and produces reactive antibacterial species, including hydrogen peroxide, hydroxyl radicals, and superoxide radicals. These species synergize with localized electric-field-induced membrane disruption to achieve rapid bacterial inactivation. The system exhibits stable electrical output under repeated droplet impact and shows efficient antibacterial performance against both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. Meanwhile, the PDMS@MXene@PPy composite demonstrates reliable piezoresistive sensing, enabling the film to function as an integrated electronic skin. Overall, this work integrates droplet energy harvesting, ROS-mediated disinfection, localized electric-field enhancement, and pressure sensing into a multifunctional robotic interface, offering a promising strategy for self-disinfecting robotic hands without external power or chemical disinfectants.

title: Deciphering energy storage mechanism of oxygen-deficient mesoporous MnO2 for aqueous zinc-ion batteries: Operando and ex-situ analysis
Microorganism-dependent photocatalytic inactivation mechanisms in BiVO4-ZnO coatings enabling >7 log reduction
abstract: The transmission of pathogenic microorganisms represents a major environmental and public health challenge. In this context, the development of photocatalytic materials capable of inactivating a broad range of pathogens under mild conditions is of significant relevance for environmental disinfection and global health protection. Here, we report BiVO 4 -ZnO heterojunction coatings for light-activated antimicrobial performance. Structural, electrochemical and spectroscopic analyses support the formation of an electronically coupled heterojunction that diminishes recombination while enabling interfacial charge separation. In this heterostructure, interfacially enhanced charge transfer increases generation of hydroxyl and superoxide radicals compared to single-phase ZnO, resulting in rapid inactivation of structurally distinct pathogens (more than 7 and 3 log reduction for bacteria and virus respectively). Notably, broad-spectrum efficacy does not imply mechanistic uniformity. While both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, as well as enveloped and non-enveloped viruses, are efficiently inactivated, the kinetics and pathways differ fundamentally. Bacterial killing proceeds via membrane disruption and intracellular oxidative stress, whereas viral deactivation is governed by oxidative modification of envelope constituents and capsid proteins. These findings demonstrate that antimicrobial functionality emerges from pathogen-specific oxidative mechanisms that cannot be extrapolated across biological classes, underscoring the importance of mechanistic insights to ensure resilience against emerging threats while minimizing unnecessary environmental burden. Thus, interfacial electronic structure engineering enables ultrafast broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity by controlling charge separation and microorganism-specific inactivation pathways. Importantly, the coatings are stable and retain biocidal performance over repeated cycles, highlighting their durability as self-disinfecting materials.

Mg/Zn-coordinated solid–solid phase change material with intrinsic flame retardancy for battery thermal management
abstract: Phase change materials (PCMs) have attracted increasing attention as passive thermal management solutions for lithium-ion batteries due to their high latent heat and temperature regulation capability. However, conventional solid–liquid PCMs suffer from intrinsic limitations, including leakage during phase transition, low thermal conductivity, and high flammability. In this work, an intrinsically flame-retardant solid–solid composite PCM (CPCM) with high thermal conductivity is designed through hydroxide complexation of polyethylene glycol phosphate. Phosphorus pentoxide is esterified with polyethylene glycol to form polyethylene glycol phosphate, which subsequently reacts with magnesium and zinc hydroxides to construct a metal–organic framework–structured polymer complex. This molecularly integrated architecture converts the phase transition from solid–liquid to solid–solid, effectively eliminating leakage while imparting intrinsic flame retardancy. The resulting CPCM exhibits excellent shape stability with no leakage at 150 °C, a high thermal conductivity of up to 2.24 W m −1 K −1 , and outstanding fire safety performance, with a peak heat release rate reduced to 310.67 kW m −2 . The CPCM effectively suppresses temperature rise and the time of thermal runaway propagation is delayed to 298 s. This study provides a viable molecular design strategy for addressing leakage, flammability, and heat-transfer limitations of PCMs.

Wall topology optimization by additive manufacturing to harmonize porosity in packed beds of monodisperse beads
abstract: Monodisperse beads are used in selected packed-bed applications and provide a well-defined model system to investigate their performance. Flat walls induce an oscillatory porosity profile near the wall, leading to flow maldistribution, bypassing, and channeling. This study investigates the impact of optimized wall topologies on the porosity distribution and fluid flow in cylindrical packed beds. The proposed approach aims to achieve bulk-like porosity near the wall by wall patterns derived from the bulk structure. These patterns are implemented either additively or subtractively and scaled by factors between 1.00 and 2.00 to determine the most effective configuration for reducing porosity oscillations. To evaluate the transferability, packed beds with different ratios of packed bed diameter to bead diameter are examined. The complex wall geometries are fabricated using additive manufacturing. Three-dimensional structural information is obtained via micro-computed tomography, complemented by two-dimensional projections of bead center positions to analyze packing structure. Flow experiments are conducted to assess pressure drop and residence time distribution for the different configurations. Both wall modifications reduce the wall effect and homogenize the porosity profile. However, the additive topology proves more effectiveness in homogenizing porosity near the wall. The optimized designs are transferable across different packed bed diameter-to-bead diameter ratios and bead size-to-topology size ratios. Flow experiments reveal that additive wall modification leads to a narrower residence time distribution and shorter mean residence time, whereas subtractive modification results in broader distributions and longer residence times. At high Reynolds numbers, pressure losses are comparable to those of unmodified packed beds, while at low Reynolds numbers both modifications exhibit increased pressure losses due to dominant viscous effects.

A comparative life cycle assessment of Fe3+-polyaminocarboxylic acid-based catalysts for the degradation of phenol by photo-Fenton like process
abstract: Among the plethora of wastewater treatment processes, one of the most relevant Advanced Oxidation Processes (AOP) is the (photo) Fenton-like process in which Fe-complexes are employed as catalysts. Among the most investigated ligands belonging to the polyaminocarboxylic acids (APCAs) class are ethylenediaminetetraacetate (EDTA), ethylenediaminedisuccinate (EDDS) and iminodisuccinate (IDS). However, the environmental impacts associated with both the synthesis and application of Fe-APCAs is currently unknown thus limiting comparisons solely to catalytic performance. This study presents the first systematic comparison of the synthesis and application of these complexes, namely Fe-EDTA, Fe-EDDS and Fe-IDS, in (photo) Fenton-like catalytic processes for phenol degradation. The study integrates environmental sustainability assessment via life cycle assessment (LCA) with catalytic activities through the calculation of Turnover Frequencies (TOFs) to determine the optimum catalytic conditions. The study adopted a cradle to gate and cradle to grave approaches to evaluate the synthesis and application of the tested catalysts. Results show that Fe-IDS is the most environmentally sustainable option with respect to Fe-EDTA, achieving reductions of 4%–97% across twelve of the eighteen assessed impact categories during synthesis, including global warming potential, and reductions of 40%–50% across all impact categories for application although with a slightly lower TOF value than the highest value achieved with Fe-EDDS. Overall, these findings highlight the need to balance catalytic performance with environmental burdens when sustainability evaluations are carried out.

Simultaneous elimination of sulfonamides and antibiotic resistance genes via peroxymonosulfate activation by ligand-modulated iron sites on biochar: The critical role of interfacial EDTA complexation
abstract: Heterogeneous iron-based catalytic systems for peroxymonosulfate (PMS) activation typically suffer from iron active site passivation and severe metal leaching. In this study, a novel self-assembled tobacco straw biochar featuring interfacial EDTA-chelated iron centers (EDTA@FTBC) was synthesized with highly stable ligand-modulated active sites. The multi-dentate coordination structure stabilized the iron active sites, effectively reducing metal leaching and ensuring excellent reusability. The PMS/EDTA@FTBC system achieved 94.5% sulfamethoxazole degradation, exhibiting broad-spectrum efficiency and robust anti-interference capability in complex aqueous environments. Characterization and DFT calculations revealed that interfacial chelation optimized surface oxygen functional groups and iron center electron density, lowering the electron transfer energy barrier to sustain a continuous Fe(II)/Fe(III) cycle. Strong non-covalent interactions promoted the oriented adsorption of PMS onto the EDTA@FTBC surface, elongating the peroxide O O bond from 1.33 Å to 1.45 Å for highly efficient activation. Surface-bound non-radical pathways dominated, driven by 1 O 2 and direct electron transfer via a metastable surface complex. Beyond efficient elimination of sulfonamides, the system achieved 77.1% mortality of antibiotic-resistant bacteria within 120 min and effectively reduced the relative abundances of resistance genes. This study provided a novel ligand-modulated biochar technology for PMS activation, offering an efficient approach for the concurrent elimination of sulfonamides and resistance genes.

abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) metal oxide nanoplatelets with high aspect ratio and unique physicochemical features hold great potential for diverse functional applications. However, two challenges remain: (i) preparation of nanoplatelets from non-layered oxides needs improvement as it mostly involves organic solvents; and (ii) stacking and aggregation can be severe during polymer processing, e.g. melt-compounding. Bi₂O₃ herein was investigated as a representative model. 2D Bi₂O₃ nanoplatelets (BONs) with a lateral size of 0.74 ± 0.37 μm and a thickness of 15.46 ± 8.30 nm were successfully produced in deionized water through liquid-phase mechanical exfoliation. XRD showed anisotropic crystallite size reduction. For example, the size reduction of 13.37 nm along (120) plane was substantially greater than the other major planes. BON paste was added by melt compounding to prepare elastomer nanocomposites. BONs with a relatively uniform dispersion improved the mechanical properties. Simulations revealed that BONs could redistribute local stress fields effectively, leading to an enhancement in the overall tensile response. Through tensile-fractured surface analysis, the enhancement is due to (i) the well dispersed BONs (interparticle distance reduced from 24.96 ± 10.32 μm to 9.00 ± 2.94 μm), (ii) their 2D structural advantage and (iii) improved interfacial interaction. The nanocomposite at 3.3 vol% BONs exhibited a shielding efficiency of 68.01% against 80 kVp X-rays, a linear attenuation coefficient ( μ ) of 3.83 cm −1 , a mass attenuation coefficient (μₘ) of 3.14 cm 2 g −1 and a half-value layer (HVL) of 0.18 cm. This work establishes a sustainable route for producing metal oxide nanoplatelets and functional elastomer nanocomposites.

Synergistic multiscale structural engineering of hollow carbon spheres and 3D folded architectures for interfacial solar steam generation
abstract: Interfacial solar steam generation (ISSG) offers a sustainable route for solar-driven water purification, but its efficiency is often limited by insufficient light harvesting, excessive heat dissipation, and restricted evaporation interfaces in planar absorbers. Herein, we report a synergistic multiscale design strategy that integrates nanoscale hollow carbon spheres with macroscale three-dimensional (3D) folded architectures. Size-comparable hollow carbon spheres (h-CS, ~0.30 μm) and solid carbon spheres (s-CS, ~0.29 μm) were synthesized to elucidate the role of hollow morphology systematically. The h-CS exhibited strong broadband solar absorption of 95.3%, a large specific surface area of 352.8 m2 g-1, favorable wettability, and low thermal conductivity of 0.1 W m-1 K-1, enabling efficient light harvesting, water transport, and interfacial heat localization. Consequently, the flat h-CS absorber achieved an evaporation rate of 1.56 kg m-2 h-1 and a solar-to-vapor conversion efficiency of 76.3% under 1 sun illumination. Further integration with 3D folded geometries significantly expanded the effective evaporation interface, and the Miura-ori h-CS absorber delivered an evaporation rate of 2.15 kg m-2 h-1 with a projected-area-based efficiency of 110.9%, placing it among the highest-performing carbon-based evaporators reported to date. The absorber also maintained stable performance over 35 h and under acidic, alkaline, and saline conditions. This work demonstrates an effective multiscale structural strategy for high-performance carbon-based ISSG systems.

Why PdZn catalysts produce methanol under steady-state but not dynamic conditions: Insights from dual function material development
abstract: Developing dual function materials (DFM) for integrated carbon capture and utilization (ICCU) presents some unique catalyst design challenges such as matching the operating windows of CO 2 desorption and catalysis and controlling selectivity during a non-steady-state spillover-reaction sequence. Herein we show that while combining a methanation catalyst (Pd/SiO 2 ) with a suitable adsorbent component (CaO) leads to a DFM capable of directly methanating captured CO 2 , this is not the case when we incorporate the same adsorbent (CaO) into a methanol synthesis catalyst (Pd/ZnO). We find that the support (SiO 2 or ZnO) influences the CO 2 desorption temperature of CaO, with CO 2 being much more stable (and less reactive) on CaO/ZnO. At the same time, CaO also inhibits the methanol productivity of Pd/ZnO. In order to independently engineer the adsorbent and catalyst we adopted physical mixture and dual bed configurations using CaO/SiO 2 as adsorbent and Pd/ZnO as catalyst. However, these configurations yielded no hydrogenation products, suggesting that the surface spillover required for DFM operation is disrupted by the lack of adsorbent/catalyst interfaces. Moreover, under cyclic DFM tests (capture followed by hydrogenation) the active PdZn phase was not stable, deactivating irreversibly under oxidative capture conditions. These findings highlight the need to control adsorbent and catalyst site proximity with greater precision while protecting active alloy phases under dynamic (cyclic) operation when designing DFMs.

title: Dielectrically tuned core-shell microwave-responsive sorbents for high-efficiency direct air capture
abstract: Amine sorbent technology offers transformative low-energy potential for both direct air capture (DAC) and post-combustion carbon capture (PCC), its viability is severely undermined by the poor heat and mass transfer of conventional solid sorbents. Herein, we report a rationally designed core-shell microwave-responsive composite support that synergistically integrates a highly graphitized carbon nanotube (CNT) core and a mesoporous silica (MS) shell for ultra-low-energy carbon capture. The CNT core not only provides efficient microwave-to-thermal conversion but also constructs a loose fibrous skeleton that prevents silica agglomeration and creates hierarchical mass transfer pathways. The MS shell, synthesized via a dual-template method, enables uniform dispersion of polyethyleneimine (PEI) even at 70 wt% loading and enhances heat transfer from the CNT core to active amine sites. The optimized PEI70-MS/CNT06 adsorbent delivers exceptional CO2 adsorption capacities of 3.28 mmol·g-1 under PCC and 2.64 mmol·g-1 under DAC conditions. Importantly, it realizes ultra-fast regeneration under 20 W microwave irradiation for only 15 s, with regeneration energy consumptions of 1.64 MJ·kg-1 CO2 (PCC) and 3.28 MJ·kg-1 CO2 (DAC), which are 60–70% lower than conventional thermal swing adsorption (TSA). The adsorbent retains 75% of its initial capacity after 35 consecutive cycles, outperforming both PEI/CNT and TSA-regenerated counterparts. This work not only demonstrates the first application of microwave-assisted regeneration for high-performance DAC but also establishes a universal design principle for microwave-responsive solid amine adsorbents.

Methane assisted low temperature isothermal thermochemical water splitting over Pt/CeO2 nanorods
abstract: Thermochemical water splitting (TCWS) is a promising route to produce hydrogen using heat, but conventional redox cycles typically require large temperature swings at 800–1400 °C, which limits materials stability and process efficiency. Herein we demonstrate isothermal, methane assisted TCWS at 300 °C using Pt/CeO 2 nanorods as a redox active platform. Catalysts with 1 and 5 wt% Pt were characterised by XRD, HRTEM, H 2 -TPR, Raman spectroscopy, XPS and XAS to relate structure and reducibility to oxygen vacancy formation and redox performance. Under isothermal cycling, methane is used as a sacrificial chemical reductant to generate oxygen vacancies at Pt-ceria perimeter sites, while subsequent exposure to H 2 O produces H 2 exclusively from water in the oxidation step. At 300 °C, 1 wt% Pt/CeO 2 nanorods reach cumulative H 2 yields of 20 mLg −1 over four redox cycles and 5 wt% Pt/CeO 2 reaches 27.5 mLg −1 , with limited loss of nanorod morphology. D 2 O labelling experiments at 300 °C confirm that D 2 and HD form only in the oxidation window, whereas H 2 formed in the CH 4 reduction window originates from methane reforming. At 400 °C, the isotopic response shows additional D 2 formation during the CH 4 step and coincides with nanorod sintering and Pt agglomeration, indicating a change in the redox pathway. XPS and Raman analysis indicate that moderate Pt loading increases the accessible Ce 3+ fraction and defect level in the CeO 2 lattice while preserving a well-defined Pt-ceria perimeter. Although the absolute H 2 productivity is modest and methane is consumed sacrificially, the results establish a low temperature, isothermal TCWS process that exploits Pt-ceria perimeter chemistry at 300 °C and provide a mechanistic basis for designing chemically assisted looping redox cycles hydrogen production.

Mechanistic elucidation of CO₂ methanation kinetics on a novel LaNiO₃/CeO₂-derived catalyst
abstract: A comprehensive micro-macro kinetic study of CO 2 methanation was conducted over a highly active, selective and stable catalyst derived from a 10 wt% LaNiO 3 /CeO 2 precursor. A dataset of 184 experiments was collected in a fixed-bed reactor under conditions free of heat and mass transfer limitations by systematically varying temperature, pressure, gas hourly space velocity, and reactant and product partial pressures. Initial rate analysis yielded an apparent activation energy of 78.2 kJ mol −1 , while CO 2 and H 2 promoted the reaction and H 2 O acted as the main inhibitor. Guided by in situ NAP-XPS and FTIR spectroscopy, mechanistically derived Langmuir–Hinshelwood–Hougen–Watson (LHHW) models were formulated considering both formate- and H-assisted CO-mediated pathways, together with single-site and dual-site mechanisms. Model discrimination demonstrated that the formate pathway, in which hydrogenation of surface formate to formyl is the rate-determining step, consistently outperformed the CO-mediated alternative. Although the single-site model satisfactorily described the overall reaction behaviour, it underestimated the effects of reactant partial pressures and methane inhibition at low tempertures. A dual-site model, accounting for H 2 activation on metallic Ni sites, CO 2 activation at Ni–CeO 2 /Ni–La 2 O 3 interfacial sites and CH 4 adsorption, provided the best agreement with the experimental data, accurately reproducing CO 2 conversion from differential to near-equilibrium conditions with physically meaningful kinetic parameters. The developed model establishes a quantitative link between elementary surface processes and reactor-scale performance, providing a robust framework for mechanistic understanding, reactor design and process scale-up.

Local coordination order in high-entropy alloy nanowires for enhanced oxygen reduction catalysis in PEM fuel cells
abstract: The oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) demands electrocatalysts with both high activity and exceptional durability. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) catalyst offer a promising platform due to tunable composition and structural stability. However, the random coordination environments and undefined electron transport pathways limit performance. Herein, a tungsten (W) coordination strategy is proposed to construct two locally ordered coordination interfaces with distinct roles: W captures electrons from Mn and Co, and then acts as an electron medium to transfer to the noble metal. Beyond the direct electron transfer from base mental to noble metals, the mediating effect of W creates an extra efficient electron transport pathway, markedly boosts charge transfer efficiency and surface electronic activity. Meanwhile, the synergistic effect downshifts the overall orbital energy to lower levels and strengthens structural stability. The synthesized HEA nanowires exhibit the mass activity with 15.2 times of commercial Pt/C in a half cell and retains 95% after 10,000 cycles. In PEMFC tests, the HEA NWs delivers peak power densities of 2.38 W cm −2 (H₂–O₂) and 1.31 W cm −2 (H₂–air). This work successfully constructed a macroscopically disordered, but locally ordered coordination catalytic interface with high activity, opening up a new paradigm for the design of multi-component alloy electrocatalysts for proton exchange membrane fuel cells.

abstract: Lignin and tannin are valuable renewable aromatic compounds that can, for example, replace bisphenol-A, a fossil-based derivative, in the production of materials such as epoxy resins. These natural polymers, after functionalization to increase their carbonyl and carboxyl group content, have the potential to form dynamic bonds that allow the materials to be reprocessed. However, the kinetics and mechanism of functionalization are not yet fully understood. In this study, we investigated the controlled oxidation of model phenolic compounds (vanillin, acetovanillone, catechol and resorcinol) under mild alkaline conditions and without buffer solutions to better mimic realistic processing environments and developed pH-dependent kinetic models. Our results showed that vanillin remains stable at 50 °C across different pH values, with oxidation increasing at higher temperatures and especially at lower alkalinity. Acetovanillone was only minimally converted at 80 °C, but showed significant oxidation at 120 °C, with reactivity enhanced by increased alkalinity. In contrast, catechol was rapidly oxidized at pH 12 and 50 °C, while resorcinol, although more stable than catechol, achieved over 90% conversion over several hours at lower temperatures. A drop in the final pH value in all tests indicates the formation of carboxylic acids. These findings provide valuable guidelines for the optimization of oxygen-based, catalyst-free modifications of lignin and tannins and pave the way for the development of recyclable biomaterials from renewable sources.

3D-printed monolithic zeolite structures for terrestrial decarbonization and space life support systems
abstract: State-of-the-art packed-bed sorbent systems that rely on randomly distributed solid sorbent beads, pellets, or granules suffer from several constraints, including a limited packing density at about 64%, high pressure drop penalties, poor thermal management due to point-to-point contacts, and wall channeling leading to early breakthrough and uneven bed utilization. 3D-printed sorbent beds are envisioned to alleviate some of these challenges, particularly by addressing wall channeling and packing density limitations. However, existing 3D-printed sorbent beds are predominantly focused on small-scale structures, making it challenging to assess their system-level adsorption performance, including a conclusive determination of the presence or absence of the wall channeling effect. Moreover, prior 3D-printed sorbent structures exhibit limited packing densities, often substantially below those attainable with packed beds filled with beads. In this study, a large-scale 3D-printed zeolite-13X bed with a packing density exceeding the theoretical limit of conventional packed spherical-bead beds is developed to evaluate its system-level adsorption performance. Through detailed breakthrough sorption experiments comparing centerline and mixed outlet breakthrough curves, it is demonstrated, for the first time, that a 3D-printed sorbent bed can indeed eliminate the wall channeling effect. Also, the experimental results indicate that increasing the inlet air velocity shortens the breakthrough time due to enhanced adsorption rates; however, it elongates the axial dispersion length of the mass transfer zone, leading to reduced bed utilization at a target breakthrough percentage, as revealed by time derivatives of the centerline breakthrough curves in the spatial domain. Additionally, elevating the inlet CO 2 concentration decreases the breakthrough time owing to the greater CO 2 partial pressure potential and simultaneously shortens the axial dispersion length of the mass transfer zone, thereby improving bed utilization. Furthermore, at a similar packing density, the 3D-printed sorbent bed exhibits a lower pressure drop penalty compared to a conventional packed bed. Insights gained from this study advance the development of next-generation 3D-printed sorbent systems for selective gas separation, with potential impacts spanning from industrial decarbonization to extraterrestrial life support systems.

Configuration-dependent host–guest h-bonding enables high-efficiency ultra-long afterglow in boric acid RTP
abstract: Room-temperature phosphorescent (RTP) materials generally suffer from a trade-off between quantum efficiency and emission lifetime, a challenge that is particularly acute in purely organic systems. In this work, a series of host–guest phosphorescent composites are fabricated via a solvent-free solid-state thermal treatment, using three isomeric phthalic acids (ortho, meta, para) as guests and boric acid as the host. The different carboxyl positions modulate hydrogen-bonding construction modes and microscopic morphologies: The ortho-phthalic acid composite (L-BA) forms ribbon-like crystals with in-situ generated oxygen defects, achieving a high phosphorescence quantum efficiency of 92.77% (absolute PLQY, integrating sphere) and a lifetime of 1.089 s. The meta-phthalic acid composite (J-BA) exhibits a uniform nanoconfined microstructure, giving an ultra-long lifetime of 1.499 s along with 50.02% quantum efficiency. The para-phthalic acid composite (D-BA) relies on an ordered hydrogen-bond network to form dense nanoparticle packing. Spectral analyses reveal that the fluorescence and phosphorescence emission peaks of all three materials are highly overlapping, and variable-temperature spectra show no thermally activated delayed fluorescence signals, confirming pure RTP. Combined characterization by XRD, FTIR, XPS, and EPR demonstrates that the rigid confinement of intermolecular hydrogen bonds synergizes with exciton trapping by oxygen defects to enhance intersystem crossing efficiency, with no covalent bond formation between host and guest. Leveraging their deep-blue RTP properties, these materials are successfully applied in deep-blue OLEDs (achieving a maximum EQE of 6.807%), high-fidelity latent fingerprint imaging, and multi-wavelength time-resolved multi-level anti-counterfeiting. This work establishes a structure–property relationship linking molecular configuration, hydrogen-bond network, microscopic morphology, and RTP performance, providing new insights for the rational design of high-efficiency or ultra-long-lifetime purely organic RTP materials.

A mechanistic study on the concentration-dependent pyrolysis behavior of 3D cross-linked epoxy/TPP networks via ReaxFF-MD
abstract: The local flame-retardant (FR) chemistry of polymer composites involves complex atomic-level synergistic effects that are difficult to characterize experimentally. Here, we combined reactive force field molecular dynamics (ReaxFF-MD) simulations with thermogravimetry-Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy-gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (TG-FTIR-GCMS) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) experiments to elucidate the concentration-dependent FR mechanism of triphenyl phosphate (TPP) in a cross-linked epoxy resin (EP) network. The ReaxFF-MD simulations quantitatively reproduced the experimental activation energies (Ea) within 5% error across TPP loadings of 0–50% and captured the non-monotonic Ea trend, which peaks at 10% TPP (243 kJ/mol experimentally; 233 kJ/mol simulated). Atomic-level reaction pathway analysis revealed that TPP decomposes via O P bond scission to release C₆H₅O• radicals; these radicals abstract hydrogen to form phenol—the primary gas-phase dilution agent—while the phosphorus-containing fragments form P-O-C linkages that bridge carbon fragments into a protective char layer in the condensed phase. These findings indicate that an optimal FR loading exists beyond which thermal stability degrades, and the identified pathways provide molecular-level targets for rational FR design. The validated ReaxFF-MD framework offers a predictive simulation platform that can serve future machine learning (ML)-accelerated FR discovery.

title: Operational stabilization of high-rate partial denitrification-anammox using intermittent low-speed stirring in an expanded granular sludge bed reactor
abstract: Sludge flotation is a critical bottleneck hindering the stable application of one-stage partial denitrification–anammox (PD/A) processes in continuous-flow reactors. This study employed an expanded granular sludge bed (EGSB) reactor with intermittent low-speed stirring to evaluate the effectiveness in enhancing nitrogen removal and mitigating sludge flotation under gradually increasing nitrogen loading rates (NLRs). The reactor achieved long-term stable operation, with an average nitrogen removal rate of 2.40 g N/L/d and removal efficiency of 88.9%, even at a low influent COD/NO3−-N ratio of 2.0. By combining low-speed stirring with a reduced HRT, functional microorganisms such as Thauera (30.9%) and anammox bacteria (Candidatus Kuenenia, 13.5%) were enriched, while complete denitrification was suppressed, thereby maintaining an anammox contribution close to 100%. Notably, granular sludge exhibited distinct stratification and selective washout: poorly settling microgranules, which favored complete denitrification, were progressively removed, whereas well-settling large granules enriched with anammox bacteria were retained. This selective pressure optimized COD utilization, reinforced nitrite accumulation–consumption coupling, and enhanced reactor stability under high NLRs. The findings reveal the mechanistic role of stirring in shaping granule population dynamics, offering new insights into sludge fate and performance enhancement. Overall, intermittent low-speed stirring provides a simple and energy-efficient strategy to overcome flotation, promote functional enrichment, and improve the feasibility of continuous-flow one-stage PD/A systems for nitrogen removal.

title: Functional porous structures with CO2 adsorption capacity from an upcycling strategy for iron ore mining overburden recovery
abstract: The upcycling of mining residues into high-value-added materials is a sustainable strategy for the valorization of secondary raw material, with significant potential to support decarbonization and reduce the carbon footprint. In this context, the present study aimed to develop MIL-88A(Fe) structures, known for their excellent properties, versatility, and capacity for CO 2 capture, using iron-based precursors recovered from iron ore mining overburden. An optimized route for the acid leaching of Fe from previously characterized residues was established using experimental design and response surface methodology (RSM). The Fe 3+ rich leachate was subsequently used for the synthesis of the target Fe-MOF structure. The synthesized product was characterized by XRD, SEM, PSD, FTIR, TGA-DSC, textural analysis, and CO 2 adsorption measurements. The experimental results demonstrated that iron from the mineral residue can be more effectively solubilized at temperatures ≥85 °C and HCl concentrations ≥25 wt%; however, a pre-treatment step is required prior to leaching. Crystallochemical analysis of the synthesized product revealed the efficient crystallization of the MIL-88A(Fe) structure using metallic precursors derived from iron mining overburden, further demonstrating its “breathing” behavior through XRD measurements. The obtained crystals exhibited hexagonal morphology and FTIR spectra confirmed the formation of the structure through the presence of characteristic vibrational bands associated with (-COOH) groups, as well as Fe oxides and hydroxides. S BET values (21.98 m 2 /g) and pore volume (0.043 cm 3 /g) were consistent with those typically reported for this structure. The CO 2 adsorption capacity (>1.1 mmol g −1 ) indicates that the material obtained via metallic recovery from iron ore waste shows promising potential for application in CO 2 capture systems, contributing to carbon footprint reduction.

title: Nanoconfined cerium oxide in a gel-type anion exchanger for efficient fluoride removal from acidic water
Synergistic electronic regulation induces electron spin polarization to facilitate homogeneous Li+ flux for dendrite-free lithium metal anodes
abstract: Lithium metal anodes are regarded as the "holy grail" of anode materials, yet uncontrolled lithium dendrite growth and unstable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) remain the two major bottlenecks hindering their practical application. To address these critical challenges, we design and fabricate a cobalt-doped SnS2/SnO2 heterostructure grown on flexible carbon cloth via a facile hydrothermal method. Combining experimental characterizations and density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we reveal a novel synergistic electronic regulation mechanism: the SnS2/SnO2 heterointerface generates a spontaneous built-in electric field (BEF) through intrinsic charge redistribution, while Co-induced spin-polarized electronic redistribution around S sites creates more favorable Li-affinitive regions, which contributes to more homogeneous Li adsorption and deposition. This dual electronic regulation not only guides ordered lithium nucleation and uniform deposition but also modulates the formation of a stable SEI layer enriched with inorganic components. Electrochemical tests demonstrate exceptional performance: symmetric cells exhibit stable long-term cycling at low voltage, and full cells show excellent capacity retention and significantly enhanced Li+ diffusion kinetics. This work unravels the critical role of electron spin polarization in Li+ flux homogenization and demonstrates an effective synergistic electronic engineering strategy for high-performance dendrite-free lithium metal anodes.

A bioinspired flavin-based catalytic construct enabling intracellular NAD+/NADH redox regulation for mitigating skin aging
abstract: Regulation of intracellular redox homeostasis is fundamentally governed by the NAD + /NADH couple, yet catalytic strategies for directly promoting NADH oxidation in biological systems remain challenging. In particular, synthetic enzyme-like catalytic microenvironments often lack structural stability and fail to maintain well-defined organization under complex intracellular conditions. Here, we address these challenges by establishing a structurally defined enzyme-mimetic catalytic platform for redox reprogramming. We report a conjugated peptide-flavin enzyme mimic (CPFzyme) that functionally mimics bacterial NADH oxidase. Covalent integration of flavin within a lysine-rich peptide scaffold generates a locally organized microenvironment that local enrichment of NADH around the flavin center and facilitates electron transfer, thereby significantly enhancing catalytic NADH oxidation efficiency compared to free or noncovalent systems. Unlike precursor-based approaches, CPFzyme enables elevation of the NAD + /NADH ratio through catalytic turnover, leading to sustained redox rebalancing. In cellular systems, CPFzyme is efficiently internalized and partially localized to mitochondria, where it restores redox homeostasis, suppresses oxidative stress and DNA damage, and activates NAD + -dependent SIRT1/SIRT3 signaling pathways. In vivo, CPFzyme mitigates degenerative phenotypes in a UV-induced photoaging mouse model, representing an oxidative stress-driven pathological condition, accompanied by restoration of mitochondrial function, as supported by proteomic, functional, and molecular analyses. Notably, CPFzyme enables sustained efficacy after a single administration, compared to the short-lived effects of NAD + supplementation. These findings highlight a generalizable catalytic platform for intracellular redox regulation and underscore the potential of structurally defined organocatalysts for ameliorative applications in redox-associated diseases.

Hydrogen production via direct core-shell conjugation of functionalized fullerenes and ZnO QDs with accelerated optical catalytic properties
abstract: Efficient charge separation and operational stability remain central challenges in photoelectrochemical (PEC) hydrogen production. Here, we engineer a series of ZnO–fullerene (C 60 , C 70 , and C 84 ) core–shell quantum dot (QD) nanocomposites designed to regulate interfacial charge transfer and suppress recombination. Oxygen-functionalized fullerenes form direct conjugates with ZnO QDs, yielding uniform and robust core–shell architectures. The nanocomposites exhibit highly efficient nonradiative pathways associated with interfacial electron transfer, with photoluminescence quenched by up to 98.4%, consistent with efficient interfacial charge separation. Across the series, photoelectrochemical performance increases with fullerene size, reflecting improved interfacial energetics and charge-transfer kinetics. ZnO–C 84 demonstrates the most favorable energetic alignment with the FTO substrate and delivers the best performance, with a 3.5-fold enhancement in hydrogen evolution relative to pristine ZnO. Furthermore, the ZnO–C 84 PEC cell exhibits strong operational durability, retaining 85.3% of its photocurrent after 24 h of continuous operation. These findings establish fullerene-shell engineering as an effective strategy to simultaneously enhance charge separation and mitigate photocorrosion in oxide photoelectrodes, providing a rational framework for the interface engineering of oxide quantum-dot photoelectrodes.

Accelerating CO2-to-carbonate conversion for electrochemical water softening via a carbonic anhydrase-inspired gas diffusion electrode
abstract: Electrochemical water softening relies on alkalinity-driven precipitation of Mg(OH)2 and CaCO3, yet its effectiveness is fundamentally constrained by limited carbonate availability in most waters. Utilizing CO2 as an in-situ carbonate source offers a promising route, but is restricted by the intrinsically slow kinetics of CO2 hydration under aqueous conditions. Here, we address this limitation by developing a biomimetic catalytic gas diffusion electrode that couples CO2 transport and hydration. The hydrophobic carbon-felt substrate enables efficient gas-liquid contact, facilitating continuous CO2 delivery to the catalyst layer, where the enzyme mimic accelerates CO2 hydration and promotes rapid formation of CO32- within the cathodic boundary layer. The synergistic generation of local alkalinity and carbonate species drives efficient precipitation of Mg2+ and Ca2+ without external chemical addition. The system achieves >82% hardness removal in low-alkalinity water, with a corresponding CO2 utilization capacity of 0.15 kg m-3 via mineralization. These results show that coupling enzyme-inspired catalytic sites with engineered multiphase interfaces effectively regulates CO2 hydration kinetics, providing a basis for catalyst design in aqueous CO2 conversion with direct relevance to water softening applications.

Scalable core-sheath braided yarn-based textile triboelectric nanogenerator for energy harvesting and human motion sensing
abstract: Wearable electronics require flexible and sustainable power sources, while conventional batteries suffer from limited lifespan, rigidity, and environmental concerns. Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) offer a promising alternative by harvesting mechanical energy from human motion and enabling self-powered sensing through stimulus-induced electrical signals. To address the requirements of wearable applications, textile-based TENGs (T-TENGs) have emerged by integrating triboelectric functionality with flexible textile structures; however, conventional fabrication strategies involving chemical treatments, polymer coatings, or adhesive electrodes often compromise flexibility and durability. In this work, a high-performance T-TENG is developed using a flexible and scalable core-sheath braided yarn (CSBY), consisting of commercial multifilament nylon as the dielectric sheath and silver-plated nylon as the conductive core. This approach, which utilizes commercially available yarns without any additional coating or chemical post-treatment, enhances the mechanical robustness and electrical stability of the device. The optimized 2 × 2 Rib T-TENG exhibits superior performance, generating an output voltage and current of ~65 V and ~ 6.5 μA, respectively, under an applied force of 16 N at 8 Hz, with a maximum power density of 26 mW/m 2 at 7 MΩ. In addition, the T-TENG successfully charges capacitors and powers a series of 40 LEDs and is integrated into a wearable knee sleeve for self-powered motion monitoring. Combined with a custom-designed wireless readout system, the device enables detection of knee joint angles, cycling speeds, and daily activities such as walking and squatting. These results highlight the dual functionality of the CSBY-based T-TENG as an efficient mechanical energy harvester and versatile self-powered sensing platform, demonstrating its potential for next-generation wearable electronics and smart textile applications.

Unveiling the structural basis of Adeno-associated virus CNS tropism via geometric protein language modeling
abstract: Adeno-associated virus (AAV) capsid engineering enables tissue-selective gene delivery; however, identifying variants with enhanced central nervous system (CNS) tropism remains challenging. Notwithstanding the success of directed evolution approaches, it often faces practical limitations, including the substantial loss of library diversity during cloning and packaging, production biases that confound functional selection, and difficulties in assessing production fitness independently of tissue tropism. Moreover, this process requires extensive animal experimentation and iterative selection cycles, making it resource-intensive and time-consuming. Here, we developed a machine learning framework that simultaneously predicts both capsid production fitness and tissue-specific enrichment, providing capsid-residue-level biological interpretation that could be used rationally to identify CNS-targeting AAV variants. We performed in vivo directed evolution of AAV9 by replacing residues at the surface-exposed loops of VR-IV and VR-VIII, subjecting libraries to two rounds of systemic selection in mice, and quantifying tissue-specific enrichment across multiple CNS and peripheral tissues. Meanwhile, by integrating protein-language model embeddings and AlphaFold-derived structural features into attention-based neural networks, our framework achieved high predictive accuracy while providing residue-level biological interpretation. Structural validation confirmed a significant correlation between the predicted binding affinity and CNS enrichment. Moreover, this study demonstrates that high-performing tissue-targeting variants possess residues enriched in glycine, serine, and arginine, exhibiting broader charged surfaces, larger hydrophobic patches, and greater solvent accessibility. This computational framework enables capsid residue-level biological interpretation based on experimental data, which could potentially improve variant selection accuracy and reduce experimental time and animal use, establishing a foundation for rational identification of CNS-targeting variants in future studies.

The enhanced CO2 capture performance and cyclic stability via oxygen doping of three-dimensionally ordered micro-mesoporous carbon
abstract: Oxygen functionalisation is widely used to enhance the surface polarity of carbon adsorbents and improve CO 2 affinity. However, excessive oxidation may reduce porosity and limit adsorption performance, and this requires investigation. Three-dimensionally ordered micro-mesoporous (3DOm) carbons have shown promising CO 2 capture, but the interplay between surface chemistry and pore architecture across different pressure regimes remains unclear. To address this, the present work systematically investigates the effect of controlled oxidation on hard-templated 3DOm carbons for CO 2 capture. Oxygen-functionalised carbons with oxygen contents of ∼5–18 at% were prepared using nitric acid, sulfuric acid, and their mixtures, with maximum oxidation at a nitric/sulfuric ratio of 1:3. Nitrogen adsorption analysis revealed that increasing oxidation reduced the BET surface area from 2215 to 1028 m 2 g −1 and the total pore volume from 3.70 to 0.89 cm 3 g −1 , hile preserving the graphitic framework and the characteristic three-dimensionally ordered micro-mesoporous architecture. Despite these changes, oxygen functionalisation enhanced low-pressure CO 2 uptake via additional electrostatic and weak hydrogen-bonding interactions with surface oxygen groups, complementing ultramicropore filling. As a result, the most strongly oxidised 3DOm achieved the highest CO 2 uptake (3.1–3.2 mmol g −1 at 100 kPa and 273 K) and CO 2 /N 2 selectivity (83.2 for a 15/85 vol% mixture at 298 K). At elevated pressures, uptake was dominated by surface area and mesopore volume, with the undoped 3DOm showing the highest capacity (16.2 mmol g −1 at 2 MPa and 273 K). All samples exhibited excellent regenerability under pressure-swing conditions, consistent with reversible physisorption. These findings demonstrate that controlled oxidation allows rational tuning of 3DOm carbons for either selective low-pressure CO 2 separation or high-capacity high-pressure capture, providing clear design guidelines for process-specific carbon capture applications.

Dual-scenario photocatalytic degradation of polystyrene nanoplastics: Microstructure-dependent performance of rutile TiO2 in aqueous and solid-state laboratory systems
abstract: Nanoplastics are emerging contaminants of increasing environmental concern, and yet effective remediation strategies remain limited, particularly under non-aqueous conditions. In this work, rutile TiO 2 photocatalysts with tailored microstructures were synthesized via a controlled acid-hydrothermal route and evaluated for the degradation of polystyrene nanoplastics (PS-NPs) in both aqueous and solid-phase laboratory systems. By tuning the synthesis conditions, distinct microstructures were obtained, and their structural, optical, and surface properties were systematically characterized. Among the synthesized materials, a raspberry-like structured sample with enhanced surface hydroxylation exhibited the highest degradation efficiency in aqueous medium (~13% within 12 h under UV irradiation). In such condition, the photocatalytic degradation was primarily monitored by turbidimetry and supported by total organic carbon and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry analyses, which supported polymer transformation through the formation of soluble and volatile degradation products. Furthermore, to simulate the photocatalytic removal of airborne PS-NPs deposited on urban photocatalytic surfaces (e.g., walls, cement, and building facades), a solid-phase configuration was developed in which PS-NPs were directly deposited onto TiO 2 -coated substrates, enabling continuous interfacial contact during irradiation. Under these conditions, a degradation efficiency of 68% was achieved after 18 h of irradiation, as confirmed by FT-IR analysis, contact angle measurements, and morphological observations. The high degradation efficiency observed in the solid-phase configuration was attributed to interfacial oxidation processes driven by surface-bound reactive oxygen species and catalyst-polymer contact. These findings demonstrate that microstructural engineering of TiO 2 represents an effective strategy for PS-NPs degradation and highlight solid-phase photocatalysis as a promising approach for the remediation of surface-deposited airborne nanoplastics.

title: Enhanced transformation of sulfonamide antibiotics via chloride-enhanced catalytic polymerization in a NH2/MWCNT/PMS system
abstract: Catalytic activation of peroxymonosulfate (PMS) and PMS-based advanced oxidation processes have been widely employed for degradation of persistent organic pollutants. However, information has been very limited on the roles of chloride (Cl − ), which are ubiquitous in both fresh and saline waters. In this work, we tested the effects of Cl − in a heterogenous catalyst system consisting of aminated multiwall carbon nanotubes (NH 2 /MWCNT) and PMS for degradation of a suite of sulfonamide antibiotics (SAs). The system was able to nearly completely remove eight SAs in water within 20 min. The presence of 1 mM Cl − boosted the reaction rate by 278%. Based on degradation data, material characterization, and density functional theory calculations, we found that in addition to the conventional reaction pathways involving hydroxyl radicals (•OH) and singlet oxygen ( 1 O 2 ), a distinct non-radical pathway was enabled by in-situ generated HClO in the presence of Cl − . Unlike in homogeneous systems where HClO acts as a direct oxidant, HClO in the NH₂/MWCNT/PMS system preferentially complexed with nitrogen vacancies on the catalyst surface, thereby accelerating interfacial electron transfer and transformation/polymerization of SAs. Further mechanistic studies revealed that HClO promotes generation of aniline radicals, which undergo intramolecular hydrogen transfer and radical coupling reactions to form polymeric products. The polymers can be removed by methanol, which also regenerates the catalyst. This study provides new insights into chloride-enhanced catalytic polymerization and presents an effective strategy for enhanced removal of SAs while enabling recovery of sulfonamide-derived polymeric products. These findings have important implications for treatment of SAs in saline waters.

Upcycled polymer waste-derived N-doped carbon supports enabling durable PtCo catalysts for PEM fuel cells
abstract: Upcycling plastic waste into functional electrocatalyst supports enables a sustainable pathway for advancing fuel cell technologies. Herein, we develop nitrogen-doped carbon supports via a one-pot Friedel-Crafts reaction between waste polystyrene and pyrrole, enabling simultaneous hyper-crosslinking and nitrogen (N) incorporation without post-treatment. Upon carbonization, the resulting framework exhibits tunable N content and hierarchical porosity, providing a robust platform for proton exchange membrane fuel cell catalysts. N doping regulates ionomer distribution and strengthens Co N coordination, promoting the formation of uniformly dispersed intermetallic PtCo nanoparticles with enhanced structural stability. Density functional theory calculations reveal that subsurface Co induces a downshift of the Pt d-band center, weakening *O adsorption and accelerating oxygen reduction reaction kinetics. As a result, the catalysts deliver a mass activity of 0.84 A mg Pt −1 at 0.9 V, approaching twice the U.S. DOE 2025 target. In full-cell tests, a peak power density of 1180 mW cm −2 is achieved and retained at 1024 mW cm −2 after 30,000 potential cycles, demonstrating excellent durability. This work presents a scalable and cost-effective strategy that integrates plastic waste upcycling with rational catalyst design, offering a viable route toward high-performance PEMFC systems.

abstract: The achievement of periodontal bone regeneration using a barrier membrane in guided bone regeneration (GBR) technology is often limited by either its inferior mechanical strength or bioactivity. To address this limitation, we developed a novel Janus bilayer membrane by sequentially electrospinning poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) mixed with proanthocyanidin (PCL-PA) and chitosan (CS) in acetic acid, then biomineralized it in simulated body fluid (SBF) to form hydroxyapatite particles (HAp) in situ on a CS nanofiber layer (CS-HAp): PCL-PA/CS-HAp. This bilayer membrane exhibited superior mechanical performance compared to single-layer membranes, with a peeling strength of 58 J/m 2 and tensile strength exceeding 5.0 MPa under hydrated conditions. In vitro antioxidant assays demonstrated the strong free-radical-scavenging ability of PCL-PA/CS-HAp. In addition, the PA-incorporated membranes exhibited greater than 95% bacterial inhibition against both Gram-negative E. coli and Gram-positive S. aureus , and 90% against P. gingivalis . The bilayer membrane also alleviated oxidative stress induced by hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ), thereby promoting the proliferation of MC3T3-E1 cells, as monitored by cytoskeletal staining. Flow cytometry analysis showed that the PA-incorporated membrane can stabilize immunomodulatory effects by about 10% in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated RAW264.7 cells. When used in a rat periodontal bone defect model, significant bone regeneration was observed in the PCL-PA/CS-HAp group, with a bone volume to total volume ratio of 36.2% and a significant reduction in bone defect size after 8 weeks, outperforming other treatment groups ( p < 0.001). The PCL-PA/CS-HAp bilayer membrane represents a promising strategy for guided bone regeneration, effectively combining mechanical stability and bioactive properties.
