Strategy for alleviating the capacity-kinetics trade-off in moisture-swing direct air capture via mass transport engineering
abstract: Moisture - swing adsorption is a promising approach for direct air capture (DAC) because CO 2 capture and release are driven by humidity changes at ambient temperatures. However, there is generally a trade-off between working capacity and mass transport kinetics under finite-time conditions. This study proposes a strategy to alleviate this trade-off by engineering mass transport through crosslinking-driven morphology control using polymerization-induced phase separation and binder-free immobilization of a styrene-divinylbenzene copolymer bearing trimethylammonium groups with carbonate counterions (strong-base anion-exchange resin) onto carbon felt. Increasing the crosslinker (divinylbenzene) content induced a systematic morphological transition from a smooth coating to a nodular morphology and ultimately to an interconnected particle network. The adsorption performance of these adsorbents was evaluated by breakthrough experiments under a constrained desorption time of 90 min. The sample with nodular morphology exhibited a high working capacity of 1.74 mmol/g and a short half-time of 3.3 min, significantly outperforming the benchmark IRA900 (0.12 mmol/g, 8.1 min), despite sharing a similar polymer framework. This superior performance was attributed to improved mass transport, which enhanced adsorption kinetics and desorption efficiency, enabling near-complete desorption within the constrained time. Further transition to an interconnected particle network reduced the adsorption half-time to 2.4 min by creating macroporous diffusion pathways. These results demonstrate that rational pore structure design can simultaneously enhance working capacity and transport kinetics under finite-time operating conditions, highlighting the effectiveness of binder-free immobilization of porous adsorbents on permeable substrates. This study offers a promising route toward highly energy-efficient moisture-swing DAC systems with practical cycle times.

title: Microstructured flexible hydrogel sensors with synergistic conductive networks for intelligent handwriting interaction systems
Surface-access limitation in catalytic porous monoliths: Performance diagnosis using pore-resolved CFD
abstract: Porous monoliths are promising catalyst supports due to their high surface area, interconnected channels, thermal stability and mechanical robustness. However, their tunable topology complicates design: trade-offs between conversion and pressure drop are not reliably captured by macroscopic descriptors, such as porosity, specific surface area, or tortuosity. Pore-resolved computational fluid dynamics (PRCFD) addresses this gap by resolving pore-scale flow and transport, enabling diagnostics and discrimination between macroscopically similar structures. We investigate surface-access-boundedness: a case where conversion is limited by flow maldistribution and incomplete utilisation of the catalytic surface, even at low Damköhler numbers ( Da < 1 ). Using palladium-nanoparticle-coated silicone monoliths for p -nitrophenol reduction, we perform reactive PRCFD in microcomputed-tomography-based geometries, calibrate a pseudo-heterogeneous eggshell reaction model, and validate transferability across samples and flow rates. We then diagnose surface-access-boundedness via the limited influence of diffusivity and reaction kinetics on conversion. Furthermore, we compare synthesised random monoliths with triply periodic minimal surface structures under matched porosity and surface area. Significantly, the required pumping power can decrease by up to an order of magnitude for the same molar production rate, depending on topology. These results show that, in heterogeneous systems affected by surface-access limitations, reactor performance is governed by structure-dependent surface accessibility rather than intrinsic kinetics or molecular diffusion alone, and that validated reactive PRCFD provides a practical framework to diagnose and compare porous reactor geometries under realistic operating conditions.

abstract: Electrocatalytic oxygen reduction plays a central role in electrochemical energy technologies and in the production of hydrogen peroxide. Achieving selective control over the two-electron (2e − ) and four-electron (4e − ) oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) pathways within a single catalyst platform remains challenging. Here, we report a laser-driven synthesis of Fe C nanostructures that enables tunable ORR selectivity through controlled post-treatment. Air annealing at 300 °C yields high H 2 O 2 selectivity (~75% at 0.65 V vs RHE), attributed to oxygen-rich groups and well-developed mesoporosity. Notably, with an optimized 2-electron catalyst, 80 ppm of H 2 O 2 with 94% faradaic efficiency was achieved after 24 h of electrolysis. In contrast, an ammonia based (NH 3 /N 2 ) treatment at 900 °C promotes the formation of a microporous structure and the incorporation of nitrogen species, resulting in selective water production (~86% at 0.65 V vs RHE). The 4-electron catalyst delivers power and stability comparable to Pt/GC in a primary zinc–air battery. These findings demonstrate a practical approach for tuning ORR selectivity within a Fe-containing carbon-based platform, using scalable processing and trace Fe contents (<0.1 wt%) with Fe present as atomically dispersed sites, limiting leaching and Fenton-type reactions.

Cement-based ion-rectifying composite separator-Zn anode integrated architecture for durable batteries
abstract: Cement-based electrochemical devices are emerging as promising candidates for structural energy storage however, their intrinsically alkaline, humid, and multicomponent pore-solution environment accelerates Zn corrosion, hydrogen evolution, and nonuniform Zn deposition, thereby compromising long-term interfacial stability. Herein, a separator-Zn anode co-design strategy is proposed by constructing an anhydride-cured epoxy novolac resin (ER) adaptive interphase on Zn. The cement-based matrix provides interconnected ion-transport channels, whereas the oxygen-rich, highly cross-linked ER network functions as a compact barrier and ion-flux-regulating interphase to homogenize Zn2+ transport and stabilize Zn deposition. In situ pH monitoring and optical microscopy demonstrate that the ER interphase mitigates local alkalization, suppresses bubble generation, and inhibits dendritic growth. DFT calculations reveal stronger Zn2+ binding affinity of ER than H2O, indicating preferential Zn2+ coordination and facilitated interfacial desolvation. Moreover, the higher hydrogen adsorption free energies ΔGH∗ on ER hydroxyl sites compared with Zn suggest thermodynamically unfavorable H* adsorption and inhibited hydrogen evolution. COMSOL simulations and EIS–DRT analysis further confirm homogenized electric-field/Zn2+ flux distributions and stabilized interfacial kinetics. Consequently, ER-Zn enables Zn ‖ MnO2 cells to retain 256.74 mAh g-1 after 500 cycles at 0.1 A g-1 and Zn ‖ I2 cells to maintain 171.45 mAh g-1 after 700 cycles at 1 C, providing an effective interphase engineering strategy for durable cement-based energy storage systems.

Mg hydrogen generator based intelligent responsive stent for in situ therapy of reflux esophagitis
abstract: Reflux esophagitis (RE), primarily caused by gastric acid reflux, is closely associated with mucosa defect and inflammation of the esophagus. Acid-suppressive therapies are often ineffective, highlighting the need for alternative therapies. Herein, we fabricated a Mg Hydrogen Generator based Intelligent Responsive Stent (HiRS) using fused deposition modeling 3D printing technology by integrating Janus Mg particles for in situ treatment of RE. During acid reflux, the HiRS could be activated by acidic environment, and then neutralize gastric acid that is the key factor in RE pathogenesis. Besides, the Janus Mg particles coated with PLGA were used as hydrogen generator, which enabled controlled H2 release after acid neutralization to exert anti-inflammatory and ROS-scavenging effects. The PVA hydrogel matrix further regulate H2 release, extending the therapeutic effects up to 40 days. Moreover, HiRS also provides a protective barrier for the esophageal mucosa, exhibiting excellent mechanical stability in acidic conditions. The in vivo experiments showed that the HiRS could reduce pro-inflammatory markers, alleviate oxidative stress, and accelerate mucosal repair. This intelligent responsive stent can not only broaden the biomedical applications of emerged active hydrogen intelligent stents, but also offer an appealing strategy for esophageal diseases therapy represented by reflux esophagitis.

Heat transfer modelling in adsorption-based direct air capture - Validation of a 1D model and simulation of an embedded heat exchanger using geometric heat transfer distribution
abstract: Despite the importance of accurate heat transfer modelling in the simulation of adsorption-based direct air capture (DAC), it has gained very little focus in the literature. This study addresses this gap by focusing on the role of heat transfer in dynamic 1D DAC modelling, and by introducing a method to simulate DAC heat transfer in 1D in the case of an embedded fin-tube heat exchanger. The 1D column model produced a satisfactory match with experimental temperature profiles in inert experiments and in DAC-relevant conditions. The 1D geometric distribution model introduced in this study clearly improved the match of 1D axial temperatures versus 3D steady-state and transient simulations, when compared to a conventional 1D modelling approach. The main difference between 1D and 3D models was an early CO 2 breakthrough due to axially non-uniform velocity caused by the tube, which the 1D models could not replicate. Based on the results of this work, different heat transfer mechanisms play an important role especially in humid DAC and should be separately considered in 1D in most cases. The 1D geometric distribution model is expected to be useful in cases where axial temperature distribution is important, such as contactor optimization. However, while the results suggested predictiveness with condition variance, the need for heat transfer coefficient re-calibration should be assessed for example in staggered tube configurations. Additionally, the method does not yet cover variable velocity due to structural axial non-uniformity, which affects adsorption breakthrough profiles.

Light-coloured solar-thermal textiles for personal thermal management enabled by bio-derived flavonoid-based photothermal polymer
abstract: In this study, natural-derived photothermal polymer is synthesized for the first time from the plant-derived flavonol quercetin (Q). The resulting photothermal polymer is integrated onto a cotton-based textile as a coating, enabling the development of a solar-driven thermoregulatory textile for personal thermal management (PTM) applications. The systematic synthesis and characterization of the Q-based photothermal polymer (PQ) are presented in detail. Integrating PQ onto textile substrates enables the fabrication of a solar-active textile (PQ-TEX), whose solar-heating performance is evaluated under controlled conditions using a solar simulator. The outdoor solar-heating performance of PQ-TEX is further evaluated under real sunlight in both summer and winter conditions across different locations, including Ireland and Türkiye. The results demonstrate strong solar-to-thermal energy conversion, with the PQ-TEX surface temperature reaching 29.1 °C at an ambient temperature of 7.1 °C. Furthermore, the rapid drying behaviour of PQ-TEX (evaporation rate of 1.22 kg m −2 h −1 and a solar evaporation efficiency of 82.8%) is also tested and reported, together with comprehensive investigations into its durability under harsh environmental conditions, phytotoxicity, washability, and applicability to textiles of different colours. These results collectively highlight the robustness and multifunctionality of the developed photothermal textile platform.

cRGD-modified liposomes with enhanced blood-tumor barrier penetration enabling NO-mediated modulation of chemoresistance in orthotopic glioblastoma
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the most lethal brain malignancies, largely due to the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and the pathologically heterogeneous blood-tumor barrier (BTB), which severely restrict drug delivery. To achieve targeted BBB/BTB traversal, we developed cRGD-modified ICG/TMZ@Lips nanoparticles (ITC NPs). The nanoplatform actively targets αvβ3 integrin overexpressed on tumor endothelial cells and GBM cells, thereby promoting receptor-mediated transport and tumor penetration. Under near-infrared (NIR) irradiation, ITC NPs trigger temozolomide (TMZ) release and photo-responsive NO-associated effects. These effects are accompanied by heat shock protein 70 (HSP70) downregulation and modulation of resistance-related pathways, which may contribute to enhanced chemosensitivity. Furthermore, we integrated near-infrared II (NIR-II) fluorescence imaging with laser speckle contrast imaging (LSCI) for real-time GBM diagnosis and perfusion monitoring. To the best of our knowledge, among existing BBB/BTB traversal strategies, this is the first study to apply cRGD peptide for specific and efficient BBB/BTB penetration in GBM therapy. This strategy directly addresses the fundamental limitations imposed by the heterogeneous and efflux‐active BTB, offering a precise nanomedicine approach for improved therapeutic outcomes.

Oxophilic Nb incorporation induces reaction pathway transition in hollow RuO2 toward durable acidic oxygen evolution
abstract: Developing active and durable Ru-based electrocatalysts to reduce the dependence on expensive iridium for the acidic OER remains a significant challenge due to lattice oxygen participation and Ru leaching. Herein, we report a hollow RuO2 architecture with atomically dispersed oxyphilic Nb dopants that modulate the local Ru–O coordination environment, thereby enabling enhanced activity and durability for acidic OER. Combined experimental and theoretical investigations reveal that oxyphilic Nb incorporation weakens Ru–O covalency, suppressing lattice oxygen activation, while simultaneously tuning the electronic structure of Ru to optimize *OOH adsorption. Additional isotopic labeling tests confirm that the Nb–O–Ru configurations switch the reaction mechanism from the lattice oxygen mechanism toward the more energetically favorable adsorbate evolution mechanism, thereby decoupling catalytic activity from lattice instability in Ru-based acidic OER catalysts. As a result, Nb0.2-RuO2 delivers a low overpotential of 193 mV at 10 mA cm-2 and exhibits outstanding durability of 500 h at 1 A cm-2 in a proton exchange membrane water electrolyzer, outperforming commercial RuO2. This work demonstrates that atomic-scale electronic regulation can beneficially redirect OER pathways to decouple activity from lattice instability.

Sensor-guided self-optimizing photocatalytic–biological treatment of wastewater under fluctuating toxicity and turbidity
abstract: An integrated photocatalytic–biological wastewater treatment reactor was developed and operated under dynamic feedback control to achieve cost-effective treatment of streams with fluctuating turbidity and biotoxicity. The Bio-Photocatalytic Reactor (BPR) combines a Gd-doped TiO₂ -coated monolith irradiated by UV LEDs with encapsulated working bacteria (Rhodococcus zopfii) confined in Small Bioreactor Platforms (SBPs) that protect the biomass from UV light and short-lived reactive oxygen species. Humic acid and ciprofloxacin were used as model turbidity-causing and toxic contaminants, respectively. Photocatalyst formulations were optimized, and the effect of turbidity and UV photon flux on ciprofloxacin degradation was quantified, revealing a strong light-screening effect above ~100 NTU. Parallel biological studies showed that R. zopfii combines high ciprofloxacin tolerance and low degradation capacity with significant humic acid removal, and that encapsulation does not impair its activity.,A resazurin-based online toxicity sensor and a commercial turbidity probe were integrated into the reactor to provide in-situ measurements of biotoxicity (expressed as ciprofloxacin-equivalent concentration) and turbidity. These state variables were fed into a control algorithm that adjusted photon flux and retention time based on an experimentally-derived operational cost function. The system was evaluated under step changes in inlet toxicity at low turbidity and, separately, under step changes in turbidity at constant high toxicity. In both cases, the BPR maintained effluent biotoxicity below a pre-set threshold (~6.5 ppm ciprofloxacin-equivalent) while converging toward cost-optimal combinations of UV power and retention time. The approach is generic and can be extended to other photo-activated AOP–biological configurations.

Local electrochemical signatures and SEI formation pathways in silicon-graphite composite negative electrodes
abstract: The spatial heterogeneity of composite electrodes is a key factor governing their electrochemical performance and stability, yet local electrochemical behavior is difficult to resolve using conventional bulk techniques. This challenge is particularly critical in lithium-ion batteries, especially for composite negative electrodes, where complex distributions of active materials lead to poorly understood interfacial processes such as solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) formation. Here, we employ scanning electrochemical cell microscopy (SECCM) to visualize nanoscale electrochemical activity in silicon-graphite composite electrodes. Localized cyclic voltammetry (CV) enables high-resolution mapping of electrochemical responses, allowing clear classification of graphite-dominant, silicon-dominant, and mixed domains within a single electrode. Furthermore, we demonstrate that SEI formation strongly depends on the local composition. Silicon-rich regions exhibit pronounced irreversible reactions associated with alloying, whereas graphite-dominant regions show more stable behavior. Mixed domains display intermediate characteristics, suggesting their role in mediating interfacial processes. These findings provide direct insight into spatially heterogeneous electrochemical behavior and offer new guidelines for the design of high-performance composite electrodes.

Orders-of-magnitude reactivity enhancement in persulfate activation by curvature-dependent oxygenated carbon nanotubes
abstract: Advanced oxidation processes based on peroxymonosulfate (PMS) have attracted increasing attention for the removal of refractory organic contaminants. Yet, the structure-activity relationship governing PMS activation over carbon-based catalysts remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate an orders-of-magnitude enhancement in PMS activation driven by curvature-dependent reactivity of carbonyl (C=O) active sites on carbon nanotubes (CNTs). Six CNT catalysts with diameters ranging from 1 to 60 nm and comparable surface oxygen functionalization were systematically investigated to decouple curvature effects. Using 2,4-dichlorophenol as a target contaminant, 1 nm single-walled CNTs achieve pseudo-first-order reaction rate constants up to 0.67 min −1 , which are 1–2 orders of magnitude higher than those of large-diameter multi-walled CNTs. Turnover-frequency analysis, normalized to the abundance and surface density of C O groups, reveals that this enhancement originated from the substantially higher intrinsic reactivity of individual C O sites rather than from differences in active-site density or edge localization. Mechanistic investigations show that highly curved CNTs preferentially activate PMS via non-radical pathways dominated by singlet oxygen ( 1 O 2 ) generation and electron-transfer processes, which account for 90.1–94.6% of contaminant removal. Density functional theory calculations further demonstrated that increased curvature strengthens interfacial charge transfer and PMS adsorption, stabilizes key reaction intermediates, and lowers the energy barriers for 1 O 2 formation. Furthermore, integration of CNTs into a membrane filtration device enables contaminant removal efficiencies exceeding 90% during continuous operation for over 45 h in real water matrices. This work identifies curvature as a key design parameter for engineering high-performance metal-free CNT catalysts and provides new insights into the development of efficient PMS-based oxidation technologies.

title: Constructing hollow tubular nanoreactors with nanoconfined Co sites for ultrafast water purification in Fenton-like reactions
abstract: Rational design of nanoconfined Co-based catalysts for peroxymonosulfate (PMS) activation remains challenging, particularly in suppressing toxic Co leaching while maintaining high catalytic activity. Herein, we engineered a hollow tubular nanoreactor featuring nanoconfined Co active sites. This unique structural configuration not only forms a spatially restricted reaction environment, but also significantly promotes the exposure of active Co sites, accelerating the Co2+/Co3+ redox cycling to enable ultrafast PMS activation for sulfamethoxazole (SMX) degradation. The as-prepared hollow tubular nanoreactor/PMS system achieves pollutant degradation within seconds, yielding an outstanding reaction rate constant of 3.71 min-1, which substantially outperforms previously reported Co-based catalysts. Furthermore, the nanoconfined structure effectively suppresses Co leaching from 0.98 mg/L to undetectable levels. Mechanistic investigations revealed that both radical (SO4•–) and non‐radical pathways (1O2) concurrently drive the SMX degradation. Crucially, this hollow tubular nanoreactor demonstrates robust adaptability and interference resistance, maintaining over 90% SMX degradation efficiency across consecutive cycles. This work highlights the power of nanoconfinement and nanoreactor engineering to tune metal stability and redox kinetics, offering a promising strategy for the rational design of green and highly efficient Fenton-like catalytic systems.

Ascorbic acid enhanced performance of trace Cu(II)-Peroxydisulfate in oxidation of PPCPs: Mechanism and application
abstract: The Cu(II)/peroxydisulfate (PDS) system has been investigated for organic pollutants degradation, yet its application to a broad range of pharmaceuticals and personal care products (PPCPs) is severely limited by the sluggish conversion of Cu(II) to Cu(I) and the consequent low PDS activation efficiency. In this study, ascorbic acid (AA), an eco-friendly antioxidant, was employed to accelerate the Cu(II)/Cu(I) redox cycle and enhance trace Cu(II)-mediated PDS activation. The Cu(II)/PDS/AA system achieved 98% removal of naproxen (NPX) within 1 min at neutral pH, whereas NPX remained recalcitrant in the binary Cu(II)/PDS, Cu(II)/AA and AA/PDS systems. Scavenger tests, probe experiments, and electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy collectively confirmed the simultaneous generation of hydroxyl radical (HO•), sulfate radical (SO4•-), and singlet oxygen (1O2). Kinetic analysis revealed that SO4•- and 1O2 were the primary contributors to NPX degradation, accounting for 60.0% and 34.1% of the total removal, respectively. The efficient generation of these reactive species was driven by the AA-mediated in-situ reduction of Cu(II) to Cu(I), which possesses superior reactivity toward PDS activation. NPX degradation was negligibly affected by Cl- but was inhibited by alkalinity and humic acid. Fourteen transformation intermediates were identified, and cytotoxicity assays with Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) cells confirmed a significant reduction in toxicity after treatment. The Cu(II)/PDS/AA system also achieved efficient degradation of structurally diverse PPCPs including metronidazole, carbamazepine, and primidone. This study demonstrates that naturally occurring trace Cu(II) combined with eco-friendly AA provides an efficient and sustainable strategy for PDS-based PPCP removal.

title: Electrically and redox-responsive PEDOT/waterborne polyurethane membranes for controlled delivery of a tumor-homing peptide
abstract: Stimuli-responsive biomaterials that integrate endogenous and externally addressable triggers offer advanced opportunities for controlled and localized delivery of therapeutic biomolecules. In this study, we present the fabrication and characterization of hierarchical conductive membranes based on poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) (PEDOT) and a redox-responsive waterborne polyurethane (WPU), functionalized with the tumor-homing peptide CREKA. A stepwise electropolymerization strategy was employed to generate a compact PEDOT base layer followed by a PEDOT/CREKA composite layer, while a glutathione-responsive WPU topcoat provided mechanical compliance and an additional peptide reservoir. The resulting membranes exhibited high water uptake (approximately 1.85 X) and long-term hydrolytic stability up to 90 days. Atomic force microscopy revealed mechanically heterogeneous surfaces, with compliant WPU domains overlaying rigid, conductive PEDOT layers. Electrochemical analysis demonstrated preserved PEDOT redox activity and enhanced cycling stability (≈3% loss of electroactive charge after 200 cyclic voltammetry cycles), while the formation of an additional capacitive interface upon peptide incorporation resulted in tunable interfacial charge storage and polymer-peptide interactions. Moreover, the integration of an electroactive PEDOT phase with a redox-responsive WPU matrix enabled the precise modulation of peptide release through complementary electrical and biochemical triggers. Overall, this membrane-based architecture enables the controlled peptide delivery at soft biointerfaces, being especially relevant for localized cancer-related applications and electrically addressable biomaterial systems.

Electrostatic modulation on Ni-gallate enables control over gate-opening transitions for low-pressure CO2 capture
abstract: Flexible metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) exhibiting gate-opening transitions are promising for gas separations, yet their performance at low partial pressures is fundamentally constrained by the intrinsic energy barrier governing the structural transition. Here, we suggest that heterometal incorporation can tune the local pore-wall environment and thereby affect gate-opening adsorption. By incorporating In3+ into Ni-gallate framework to construct heterometallic Ni-O···In motifs, we induce localized charge redistribution and enhance the electrostatic potential gradient within the pore environment without significantly altering pore size or volume. As a result, the gate-opening pressure for CO2 is shifted from 0.10 to 0.07 bar, accompanied by a marked enhancement in low-pressure uptake and IAST selectivity (13287). In situ DRIFTS and kinetic analyses further show a faster establishment of CO2 adsorption features and a quicker approach to steady state. XAS and PALS reveal strengthened local polarization, while DFT calculations show a substantial reduction in the free-energy barrier for CO2 migration between adjacent cavities. These results are consistent with a contribution from modified pore-wall polarization and gating energetics. This work identifies electrostatic control as a promising approach for tuning gate-opening transitions in flexible porous materials, providing new design principles for low-pressure gas capture.

Nitrogen valorization via autotrophic nitrous oxide production in a partial nitritation sequencing batch biofilm reactor
abstract: Autotrophic nitrous oxide (N₂O) production was intentionally enhanced in a partial nitritation sequencing batch biofilm reactor (PN-SBBR) treating high-strength ammonium wastewater (1000 mg N–NH₄ + L −1 ). Reactor performance was evaluated under three pH conditions (6.8, 7.3, and 7.8), which strongly influenced N₂O production rates (97, 230, and 132 mg N–N₂O L −1 d −1 , respectively) while maintaining similar ammonia oxidation rates (0.79–0.86 g N–NH₄ + L −1 d −1 ). Combined analysis of N₂O production, emission factor, and hydroxylamine accumulation identified pH 7.3 as the most favorable among the tested range for promoting N₂O formation under specific redox conditions. Operation with real reject water (from dewatering of digested sludge) further validated process robustness, increasing N₂O production by 38% and achieving a maximum conversion of 0.36 g N–N₂O g −1 N–NH₄ + oxidized. Mass and energy balance analysis demonstrated that integrating the PN-SBBR as a dedicated autotrophic N₂O production stage enables energy-efficient nitrogen valorization. Among the configurations evaluated, coupling PN-SBBR with Anammox provided the highest energy efficiency. Furthermore, incorporation of the autotrophic stage into Coupled Aerobic-anoxic Nitrous Decomposition Operation (CANDO)-based systems substantially improves their overall energy balance. These results demonstrate a viable route for energy recovery from ammonium-rich waste streams through controlled autotrophic N₂O production.

Reduced order CFD framework for kinetic parameter estimation in reactive flow applications
abstract: For most reactors designed for understanding catalytic kinetics, often the kinetics part is strongly coupled with the transport. Conventional approaches try to alienate effect of the transport phenomena by making simple assumptions about the reactor flow. This could lead to false understanding of kinetics. Since accounting for this transport requires full scale computational fluid dynamics (CFD) analysis consuming several hours of computation for one simulation, a kinetic parameter estimation (KPE) problem formulation was far from feasible. We tackle this issue by employing our recently developed two specialized CFD based reduced order models (ROMs) designed for heterogeneous catalytic systems. The first ROM called Asymptotic Approach(AA) assumes a constant reactivity over the surface of the catalyst whereas the second model Reduced Basis Strategy (RBS) resolves the catalyst surface completely. The accuracy and performance of these two models for KPE is demonstrated on a trivial mass action kinetics system as well as a realistic methanol formation reaction system. Both models demonstrate superior performance compared to conventional PFR based KPE. Among the two models AA and RBS, a trade off exists between accuracy and computational speed. The choice is left to practitioners according to their application needs.

Engineered bacteria as ultrasound-responsive carbon monoxide vehicles for Cancer gas therapy and synergistic immunotherapy
abstract: Carbon monoxide (CO) gas therapy is emerging as a highly promising strategy in cancer treatment. However, the tumor-targeted delivery and on-demand release of CO remain formidable challenges, and monotherapeutic efficacy is inherently limited. To address these issues, we report a self-guided “CO-releasing bomb” constructed by armoring Escherichia coli ( E. coli ) with 3-hydroxyflavone-D-alanine (HF-D-Ala) and calcium peroxide (CaO 2 ) nanoparticles (EHC). Upon reaching the acidic, hypoxic tumor microenvironment (TME), CaO 2 instantly generates Ca 2+ and H 2 O 2 ; the bacterium then self-catalyzes H 2 O 2 to produce a local O 2 burst. Subsequent ultrasound irradiation triggers HF-D-Ala to liberate a high concentration of CO owing to the O 2 -rich environment, selectively damaging tumor-cell mitochondria and inducing apoptotic death. Moreover, the O 2 generation alleviates tumor hypoxia and reverses the immunosuppressive TME. Concurrently, E. coli antigens promote dendritic cell maturation and enhance T-lymphocyte recruitment and infiltration. In vivo studies demonstrate that the EHC under US irradiation significantly suppresses tumor growth and potently activates antitumor immunity. These findings provide compelling evidence to support the potential application of combined CO gas therapy and immunotherapy for in vivo tumor treatment.

abstract: Fossil-resource constraints drive renewable materials for advanced energy-storage devices. A room-temperature dual-crosslinked chitosan/Pluronic F127 composite gel polymer electrolyte (GPE) is developed for supercapacitors (SCs). Biomass-derived levulinic acid forms dynamic Schiff-base linkages with chitosan, while sodium borate introduces reversible borate crosslinks to build a tough, self-adaptive network. Pluronic F127 is incorporated as a soft-templating additive that regulates multi-scale pore architecture and creates continuous ion-transport pathways. The GPE delivers high mechanical performance (12 MPa tensile strength, 120% elongation), effective cryoprotection, and high ionic conductivity (33.74 mS cm-1 at 25 °C). SCs assembled with the GPE achieve an energy density of 15.55 Wh kg–1 and stable operation over 10 000 cycles. Spent gels are upcycled into KOH-activated porous carbon (1975.28 m2 g-1) with a capacitance of 332 F g-1 at 1 A g-1, enabling electrolyte-to-electrode reuse. A self-derived electrode–electrolyte SC retains capacitance over 50 000 cycles with stable coulombic efficiency. Life-cycle assessment (LCA) indicates a low global warming potential (GWP) of 6.135 CO2 eq kg–1 GPE. This work demonstrates a biomass-derived, recyclable electrode–electrolyte supercapacitor platform for wearable and portable electronics and provides a generalizable, biodegradable materials strategy for developing diverse sustainable energy-storage components.

Evaluation of turbulence models for transitional-regime flows in a stirred tank equipped with a wide-blade hydrofoil
abstract: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) prediction of stirred-tank flows in the transitional regime remains challenging due to the coexistence of coherent impeller-driven structures, weak turbulence and strong sensitivity to operating conditions. This study evaluates turbulence-modelling strategies for Newtonian flow in a baffled stirred tank equipped with a wide-blade hydrofoil impeller. Simulations spanning laminar, transitional and fully turbulent regimes are performed using a laminar model, the generalised k - ω (GEKO) Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) model, Stress-Blended Eddy Simulation (SBES) and a modified SBES formulation with a fixed RANS–LES blending distance (SBES-FBD). Predictions are validated against time-resolved Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) data using mean velocity fields, turbulence kinetic energy and Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD). For the impeller-tank combination considered here, the laminar model is valid only at low Reynolds number ( Re < 50), while GEKO systematically underpredicts turbulence in the transitional regime (simulated for 150 < Re <700). Default SBES performs well only at higher transitional and turbulent Reynolds numbers ( Re ~35,000), whereas SBES-FBD provides consistent agreement across transitional and turbulent conditions by maintaining sufficient LES activation (150 < Re < 35,000). The results offer clear guidance for CFD model selection in transitional stirred-tank applications.

abstract: This study reports the engineering design of boron-modified bismuth oxide catalysts decorated with platinum, targeting thermo-photocatalytic methanol reforming for H 2 production. The catalytic process was investigated using a novel gas-phase thermo-photoreactor featuring strict control over both photon absorption and thermal heating profiles, thereby ensuring a reliable and quantitative evaluation of the catalytic properties. Catalytic evaluation identifies an optimal boron loading of 3 wt%, leading to a significant enhancement in H 2 production compared to the pristine oxide. Although the Pt/B-Bi catalyst exhibits a lower initial activity than Pt/Ti, it shows improved resistance to deactivation during prolonged operation, resulting in enhanced long-term stability. The highest performance is achieved under combined UV365 LED irradiation at 300–400 °C, evidencing a strong synergistic effect within the ternary architecture. Pt/B-Bi achieves a remarkable H 2 evolution rate of 19.3 mmol g −1 h −1 under UV + 300 °C. Furthermore, the real/intrinsic quantum efficiency of the system is quantitatively evaluated for the first time in this reactor by solving the Radiative Transfer Equation for the determination of the absorption photon rate, yielding highly relevant values of 0.13% (UV + 300 °C) and 9.0% (VIS +300 °C). The catalytic results are coherently correlated with a comprehensive set of characterization techniques, while stability and repeatability tests demonstrate excellent structural and operational robustness under both continuous and cyclic operation.

Multilevel optimization for integrated CO2 capture systems under techno-policy transitions
abstract: Membrane CO 2 capture processes are an environmentally benign and low-carbon option removing CO 2 from major point sources. However, the subambient pressure of CO 2 product typically requires energy intensive liquefaction for transportation, utilization, or storage. Consequently, the optimal CO 2 purity and recovery from the membrane process cannot be determined without considering the downstream liquefaction process, highlighting the need for integrated optimization. This study proposes a two-level nested optimization framework for an integrated CO 2 membrane separation and liquefaction process treating approximately 40,000 Nm 3 /h of flue gas originating from natural gas combined cycle. At the upper level, the optimized CO 2 purity and recovery from the membrane process were determined. At the lower level, a deterministic global solver optimizes the membrane superstructure and a Bayesian optimization algorithm optimizes the liquefaction process. The framework optimizes the integrated process under six current and future scenarios involving advanced membrane properties and carbon emission penalties. This optimization simultaneously determines scenario dependent CO 2 recovery and purity by evaluating technoeconomic tradeoffs between membrane specific selectivity and permeability and liquefaction process cost. The results show that the economically optimal membrane purity and recovery points shift with carbon emission penalties and membrane properties. With the optimum futuristic membrane scenario at a carbon emission penalty of 160 USD/t-CO2, the membrane process achieves 93.0% CO2 purity and 77.7% CO2 recovery. The integrated process recovers 72.3% of the CO2 in the flue gas. This represents a significant shift toward higher CO 2 recovery compared to the current baseline of 93.2% purity and 20.0% recovery in the membrane process under near-term membranes. Futuristic membranes reduce the total annualized cost by 4.5–8.6% compared to near-term benchmark scenario. This proposed two-level nested optimization framework provides essential insights for designing integrated capture processes as technology and policy evolve.

title: FeSO4 combined with intermittent aeration promotes humification during rapeseed straw composting by sustaining Fe-ROS activity
Techno-economic assessment of single-cell protein production at industrial scale from a wide range of carbon sources
abstract: Using aerobic fermentation, single-cell protein (SCP) can be produced from a wide range of carbon sources (C-sources), including glucose, glycerol, methanol, ethanol, and organic acids. The technical and economic performance of large-scale SCP production varies significantly with C-source, driven by differences in biomass yield, O 2 demand, and productivity, for example. To determine the preferred C-source, a techno-economic assessment for continuous SCP production in an industrial bubble column was performed for nine non-gaseous C-sources. This was based on a process model that included microbial kinetics, gas-liquid mass transfer kinetics, downstream operations, and a detailed cost analysis. Per C-source, dilution rate and aeration conditions were optimized to minimize the minimum selling price (MSP) of SCP. The results highlight C-source costs as the dominant MSP driver, with O₂ transfer rates strongly affecting capital and utility costs. At their current prices, glucose, glycerol, methanol and ethanol emerge as the most economically favorable C-sources, achieving MSPs of about 2.5 $/kgₓ due to high biomass yields and low C-source prices. Acetic acid exhibits an MSP of 3.2 $/kgₓ but, lactic, formic, glycolic and oxalic acids exhibit MSPs in the range of 7–20 $/kgₓ due to low biomass yields, high O 2 demand, and high C-source prices. Sensitivity analyses confirm that C-source price and biomass yield exert the strongest economic influence, while the electricity price and fixed costs have a more marginal effect. This work identifies promising candidates for further environmental and scale-up assessments, providing a framework to guide C-source selection and process optimization for SCP production.

Dynamic wet-adhesive and anti-adhesive bilayer hydrogel system for preventing post-ESD esophageal stricture
abstract: Preventing esophageal stricture after endoscopic resection requires biomaterials that maintain robust adhesion under wet, dynamic conditions. Conventional hydrogels face a conflict: water absorption enhances initial attachment but weakens mechanical cohesion. Here, the authors introduce a triamcinolone acetonide (Tr)-enabled strategy in which the tissue-adhesive ST layer, prepared from silk fibroin and tannic acid, rapidly absorbs moisture to enable instant bonding. Crucially, sustained release of Tr from F127 micelles progressively elevates β-sheet content within the silk network, counteracting hydration-induced softening and ensuring durable interfacial integrity. Paired with a lubricious SO anti-adhesive top layer, the sequentially assembled ST-SO Janus bilayer hydrogel effectively prevents stricture in a porcine model by modulating inflammation and fibrosis. This work presents a mechano-adaptive drug-delivery approach to resolve the hydration-weakening paradox in wet tissue adhesion, offering a promising therapeutic platform for luminal repair.

Scalable continuous-flow photocatalytic system based on a TiO2-coated sand composite for microplastic mineralization
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) represent a persistent environmental threat, with polyethylene terephthalate MPs (PET) from textiles and domestic washing posing particular challenges due to their widespread use in bottles, cleaning products, and clothing fibers. While most reported photocatalysis strategies for PET degradation rely on TiO 2 suspensions, often requiring pH adjustment or chemical additives, we present here the first continuous-flow systems to achieve effective mineralization of PET directly in untreated domestic washing wastewater generated without detergent addition. Accordingly, an optimized TiO 2 layer was immobilized onto commercial sand and SiO 2 microspheres, and the resulting materials were integrated to yield a structurally robust photocatalytic system (sand@TiO 2 -SiO 2 @TiO 2 ) that synergistically combines the intrinsic mechanical filtration capacity of sand with the enhanced specific surface area provided by the TiO 2 -functionalized SiO 2 microspheres. This material was thoroughly characterized using FESEM, Raman, XRD, UV–Vis diffuse reflectance, and XPS. Its implementation in a lab-scale tubular photoreactor equipped with LED lamps (λ max = 362 nm) demonstrated complete removal of PET microplastics from wastewater generated from domestic textile washing with tap water at a flow rate of 0.05 L h −1 , as confirmed by COD, TOC, gravimetry, turbidimetry, FTIR, and microscopy. Mechanistic elucidation of PET photodegradation was achieved using EPR and LC-MS. The results of this study indicate that the sand@TiO 2 -SiO 2 @TiO 2 photocatalyst is effective for the mineralization of microplastics in continuous-flow systems. This scalable strategy advances microplastic remediation by linking traditional laboratory-scale suspension photocatalysis research with real-world wastewater treatment applications. Moreover, this approach paves the way for the design of new advanced materials to improve microplastic removal.

Performance of UVA/periodate and UVA/performic acid advanced oxidation processes for Enterococcus faecalis disinfection and tetracycline removal in aquaculture water
abstract: Aquaculture wastewater frequently contains residual antibiotics (i.e., tetracycline, TC) and microbiological pathogens (i.e., Enterococcus faecalis ), posing environmental and health risks. While UVA-based advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) using emerging oxidants such as performic acid (PFA) and periodate (PI) remain unexplored for aquaculture water treatment despite promising performance. This study evaluated UVA/PFA and UVA/PI for simultaneous E. faecalis and TC removal across simulated (SW) and real aquaculture water (RW), assessing temperature and pH effects, reactive species, phytotoxicity, and bacterial regrowth. Optimal performance occurred at pH 8, matching aquaculture conditions, at operationally optimal doses (0.02 mM PFA vs. 2.50 mM PI; 125-fold molar difference). UVA/PFA reached 81% TC removal under low COD conditions, and 4.52 ± 0.21-log E. faecalis reduction in 5 min under high COD conditions. Meanwhile, UVA/PI achieved complete removal of both TC and E. faecalis : 100% TC removal and 4.40 ± 0.16-log E. faecalis reduction (15 and 60 min under low and high COD conditions, respectively). However, TOC-based mineralization remained limited (9–20%). Scavenger studies indicated predominance of oxidant-derived reactive species for UVA/PI (IO 4 • /IO 3 • ) and non-HO • radical species for UVA/PFA. UVA/PI showed toxicity toward Solanum lycopersicum L. and high turbidity in RW (401 NTU), not observed with UVA/PFA. No E. faecalis regrowth occurred over 2 weeks with UVA/PI, whereas UVA/PFA exhibited matrix-dependent variability and oxidant instability. UVA/PFA offers dose-efficient disinfection for low-organic load aquaculture systems, while UVA/PI provides robust performance across variable conditions. These results are proof-of-concept and require further validation, particularly ecotoxicity assessment, before scale-up in aquaculture systems can be considered.

title: Engineering compartmentalized utilization of acetate with glucose for high-level squalene and C30 carotenoids production in Yarrowia lipolytica
abstract: Acetate is increasingly recognized as a promising feedstock for biorefineries, serving as an alternative carbon source for microbial cell factories. Nevertheless, high concentrations of acetate can inhibit microbial growth and metabolism. In this study, the acetate assimilation capability of Yarrowia lipolytica was progressively enhanced through metabolic network reprogramming, leading to the accumulation of 968.01 mg/L (196.41 mg/g DCW) of squalene. Subsequently, the construction of an orthogonal squalene biosynthetic pathway within subcellular compartments boosted production to 1815.46 mg/L (354.61 mg/g DCW). By engineering a parallel glucose-acetate metabolic pathway to enable compartmentalized squalene synthesis, titers were further elevated to 2957.25 mg/L (371.84 mg/g DCW) in engineered strain YAS13. Upon introducing the engineered MspCrtN variant, the YAS13 was employed as a squalene-producing platform for the biosynthesis of downstream C30 carotenoids, achieving a titer of 150.99 mg/L (18.37 mg/g DCW). Finally, fed-batch fermentation in a 1.5 L bioreactor using a glucose-acetate co-substrate strategy with the engineered strain yielded a maximum C30 carotenoid production of 3028.76 mg/L (59.26 mg/g DCW). Collectively, this work presents an effective metabolic reprogramming approach that coordinates carbon co-utilization to improve bioproduction efficiency, thereby establishing a versatile platform for the synthesis of various high-value terpenoid compounds.

Synergistic modulation of electron transport layer and perovskite via CrB MBene interfacial engineering in hole transport layer-free carbon-based CsPbI2Br perovskite solar cells
abstract: To break through the bottlenecks of carbon-based perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs), involving sluggish charge transfer, mismatched energy level alignment, as well as pervasive defect-mediated recombination, we report a multifunctional engineering strategy employing two-dimensional (2D) layered CrB MBene to modify the TiO2 electron transport layer (ETL) and the CsPbI2Br perovskite layer simultaneously. The strong interaction between CrB and TiO2 effectively modulates the electronic configuration of the TiO2 ETL, which elevates its conduction band minimum (CBM). The optimized interfacial energetics endows the CrB-modified TiO2 with improved electron conductivity, and constructs a favorable energy level alignment for efficient charge separation, extraction and transport. Importantly, the buried CrB induces the formation of enlarged perovskite grains with increased crystallinity and hydrophobicity, and alleviates residual stress. Such structural optimization further enables efficient defect passivation and suppresses ion migration of the perovskite film, considerably reducing non-radiative recombination. As a result, the synergistic effects of CrB on charge transport kinetics, energy level alignment, and defect passivation collectively boost the power conversion efficiency (PCE) of CsPbI2Br-based hole transport layer-free C-PSCs from 12.76% to 16.44% with excellent long-term stability.

Cross-linked torlon/P84 hollow fiber membranes for highly selective NH3 separation with enhanced stability
abstract: Efficient ammonia (NH 3 ) separation is essential for NH 3 synthesis, recovery, and utilization; however, the separation processes are often limited by NH 3 -induced swelling and plasticization. Herein, we report a cross-linked Torlon/P84 (X-T/P) polyimide hollow fiber (HF) membrane for selective and stable NH 3 permeation. The membrane was fabricated by dry-jet wet spinning of a Torlon/P84 (T/P) blend, followed by cross-linking with p -xylylenediamine ( p -XDA) to form a rigid covalent network that preserved the asymmetric HF morphology. Structural, thermal, and mechanical analyses confirmed successful cross-linking, enhanced thermal resistance, and restricted polymer-chain mobility. Gas-transport analysis revealed that cross-linking increased NH 3 solubility through polar amide/amine-containing interaction sites while suppressing N 2 diffusion through the rigidified polymer network. Consequently, the X-T/P membrane exhibited improved NH 3 /N 2 and NH 3 /H 2 ideal selectivities compared to the uncross-linked membrane. In mixed-gas permeation tests, the X-T/P HF membrane demonstrated an NH 3 purity above 99.5% for NH 3 /N 2 mixtures, with NH 3 recovery reaching 75% at elevated feed pressures. For the NH 3 /H 2 mixtures, the membrane preferentially permeated NH 3 , achieving NH 3 purities of approximately 73–88% and a maximum recovery of 40%. These findings highlight the potential of cross-linked polyimide HF membranes for high-purity NH 3 recovery from NH 3 -containing gas streams.

abstract: Efficient uranium extraction from uranium-containing wastewater is considered to be vital for the sustainable development of nuclear energy. The extraction efficiency for uranium greatly depends on the availability of uranium and active adsorption sites on the adsorbents. Therefore, it is critical to maximize the utilization rate of adsorption sites. Herein, a polyamidoxime (PAO)-based adsorbent of high porosity and light/magnetically-driven motion is designed for the enhanced uranium adsorption from uranium-containing wastewater. The adsorbent is engineered with micro and nanopores that enhance uranium diffusion, and increase the exposure of adsorption sites for capacity improvement. The near-infrared (NIR) light-driven effects including the photothermal conversion and the motion further improve the adsorption capacity under light and produce antibacterial effect for anti-biofouling. An adsorption capacity of 585.5±22.8 mg g-1 is achieved under NIR irradiation (uranium 40 ppm). The magnetically-controlled locomotion enables the removal of uranium in confined and hard-to-reach sites. Meanwhile, the microreactor exhibits high selectivity for uranium over other groundwater cations, along with strong recyclability. This work presents a novel strategy for the uranium recovery from uranium-contaminated water.

A multicopper oxidase from Paenibacillus polyethylenelyticus JNU01 oxidizes polyethylene
abstract: ABSTRACT Polyethylene (PE) is a widely used plastic that persists in the environment and resists breakdown via microbial degradation. In this work, we discovered a new bacterium, Paenibacillus polyethylenelyticus JNU01, that grows on a PE-like wax (PELW, 4 kDa) as its sole carbon source, causing chemical modifications to the substrate and releasing small-molecule products. Genomic and transcriptomic analyses identified a multicopper oxidase ( Pp MmcO) as a key enzyme candidate for this observed activity. Pp MmcO caused surface oxidation, increased hydrophilicity, and the release of oxygenated products such as ketones, alkanes, and alkenoic acids. Scanning electron microscopy confirmed surface damage on both PELW and post-use greenhouse PE films. Weight loss analysis showed mass losses of 5.2% for the PELW powder and 1.6% for the greenhouse PE film after treatment with wild-type Pp MmcO. We propose a radical-mediated pathway catalyzed by Pp MmcO. These findings identify a new bacterium and enzyme capable of initiating PE oxidation and provide insight into biological processes that may act on polyethylene.

title: Selective electrochemical recovery of rare-earth element europium with amine functionalized electrodes in capacitive deionization
abstract: This work investigates selective europium (Eu3+) recovery from zinc mine tailings that uniquely contain Eu3+ as the sole rare earth element co-existing with transition metals. Building on our previous work on selective Eu3+ recovery with amine-based metal–organic frameworks (Cr-MIL-PMIDA), we report for the first time the development of a functional amine ligand, PEI-PMIDA, featuring a simple and scalable synthesis route. PEI-PMIDA–functionalized electrodes integrated into capacitive deionization system exhibited enhanced Eu3+ selectivity, outperforming Cr-MIL-PMIDA electrode. The superior performance is attributed to the strong amine functionality of PEI-PMIDA, its homogeneous dispersion within the carbon electrode, high specific electro-capacitance, and low contact resistance (688 Ω), collectively enabling preferential Eu3+ complexation and rapid electro-kinetic transport. Eu3+ selectivity was influenced by functional material loading, operational timing, and solution pH. By exploiting the faster electro-kinetic transport of Eu3+ relative to competing trivalent metals, selectivity was maximized. Under optimized conditions (420 s operation time, 1.2 V, 2:1 carbon: PEI-PMIDA electrode mass ratio), high Eu3+ selectivity was achieved (ρ_Al^Eu = 4.3, ρ_Fe^Eu = 5.9, and ρ_Zn^Eu = 8.5) from zinc mine tailing. Desorption studies confirmed effective regeneration, with 70% Eu3+ recovery. Overall, PEI-PMIDA–functionalized electrodes represent a promising electrochemical strategy for selective Eu3+ recovery while creating value to mining waste by-product.

Defect - dispersion synergy and single-atom stabilization in Ru/TiO2 catalysts for CO2 hydrogenation
abstract: Carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) hydrogenation represents a central route for sustainable fuel production and carbon recycling, yet its efficiency is critically dependent on the structural and electronic properties of the catalyst. In practical heterogeneous systems prepared by conventional wet-chemical methods, a distribution of active sites, ranging from atomically dispersed species to subnanometric clusters and nanoparticles, typically coexist in the final catalyst. Here, we investigate how support defect engineering governs this distribution in Ru/TiO 2 catalysts with varying metal loadings and oxidative pre-treatments. Comprehensive spectroscopic and imaging analyses, including XPS, HR-STEM, and XAS established a clear correlation between Ru structure and catalytic behavior. Critically low Ru loadings (0.2 wt%) induced a transition from metallic nanoparticles to highly dispersed and single atom species, while oxidative pretreatment generated RuO 2 like domains. A fraction of isolated Ru atoms persisted, particularly on defect-rich TiO 2 , where oxygen vacancies act as anchoring sites, improving stability under redox conditions. Catalytic testing revealed that Ru dispersion and oxidation state jointly determine activity and selectivity: extended metallic Ru or oxidized Ru nanoparticles favor complete hydrogenation to CH 4 , whereas isolated Ru species promote CO formation via the reverse water–gas shift pathway. The coexistence of these Ru configurations is associated with enhanced low temperature activity, while defect engineered supports improve stability against deactivation. Defect engineering of TiO 2 provides an effective strategy to stabilize atomically dispersed Ru and to balance nanoparticles and atomic species, offering a versatile strategy to tune CO 2 hydrogenation performance and advance the design of Ru based catalysts for sustainable hydrogenation processes.

abstract: All-inorganic halide perovskites have attracted significant attention for photodetection applications owing to their excellent optical and electrical properties, together with superior stability against chemical and radiation-induced degradation. Here, we report a facile solution-processing strategy for synthesizing large-area (up to 8.5 × 8 cm2) single-crystal-like CsPbBr3 films. Compared with bulk single crystals, these films offer advantages including large-area scalability, controllable thickness, and improved device integration while maintaining comparable optoelectronic properties. The as-prepared films exhibit a low trap density of 9.4 × 1010 cm-3, enabling a high carrier mobility of 66 cm2 V-1 s-1 and an outstanding mobility–lifetime product of up to 1.02 × 10-3 cm2 V-1. Photodiodes based on these films demonstrate excellent performance, including a high responsivity of 432 mA W-1, a detectivity of 2.4 × 1011 Jones, and a fast response time of 44 ms. Importantly, the large-area devices exhibit excellent uniformity in responsivity and detectivity across different regions. Moreover, the devices retain over 90% of their initial responsivity after one month of storage under N2 conditions and remain operational after 5 days in air. Stable photocurrent responses under varying laser intensities for up to 20 min further confirm their excellent operational stability.

title: Corrosion-induced bulk halide doping enables chloride-resistant cobalt oxides for oxygen evolution
Phosphorus leaching and recovery via alternating electrode function in an electrochemical sludge treatment system
abstract: Phosphorus (P) recovery from anaerobically digested sludge (ADS) is attractive but conventional methods often require extensive chemical addition and complex operation. Herein, a single-unit electrochemical sludge treatment (EST) system was developed that integrates P leaching, recovery, and sludge pH neutralization by alternately operating a shared electrode as an anode in Step 1 and as a cathode in Step 2. In Step 1, anodic acidification (pH ~ 2.0) doubled the liquid-phase PO 4 3− -P concentration to 178.3 ± 11.2 mg L −1 under 50 A m −2 for 2 h, primarily via dissolution of Ca- and Mg-bearing minerals. In Step 2, the applied electric field drove phosphate electromigration across an anion exchange membrane while neutralizing the ADS pH by cathodic alkalinization, achieving 71.0 ± 8.5% P recovery at 5 A m −2 for 4 h; the P loss was mainly associated with Ca-induced precipitation at pH > 6. Extended 15-cycle operation concentrated PO 4 3− -P and NH 4 + -N to 874.5 and 3084.3 mg L −1 , respectively, enabling high-purity struvite production (>95% P precipitation). Meanwhile, the EST system improved sludge dewaterability with a 35.8% decrease in sCST, reduced both TSS and VSS by >35%, and decreased the liquid-phase TOC from 1.55 ± 0.01 to 0.29 ± 0.01 g L −1 . Compared with previously reported two-cell systems with similar functions, the EST simplifies the system, avoids inter-cell sludge transfer, lowers electricity demand for P recovery, and eliminates chemical dosing for ADS pH adjustment. These benefits enhance its technical and economic feasibility for integrated nutrient recovery and sludge management.

Kinetics of pure and industrial hematite powder reduction with hydrogen and carbon monoxide mixtures
abstract: The steel industry plays a key role in society and the global economy, but it also has a significant environmental impact. The fossil-based process utilizes blast furnaces, in which coke acts as a reducing agent and energy source, which is why it accounts for about two gigatons of CO2 emissions on an annual basis. Reducing iron oxides with hydrogen instead of carbon monoxide provides an elegant carbon-free alternative with water as the byproduct. However, the rapid advancement of this technology on the market would require extremely large investments in entirely new reactors and reactor systems. Moreover, the current and foreseeable hydrogen capacity and infrastructure are insufficient to meet the demand, and the price of non-fossil hydrogen is still high. An alternative to reducing emissions would be to adapt current reactor infrastructure to flexibly utilize mixtures of carbon monoxide and hydrogen, depending on hydrogen availability and price. This dynamic approach requires a rigorous understanding of the reduction kinetics of iron oxides with varying gas composition and reaction conditions. The present work studies the kinetics of pure and industrial hematite powders using H2 and CO mixtures in small scale in the laboratory. The reduction process was followed by analyzing the off-gases online, and the physical-chemical behavior of the solid phase during reduction was studied through detailed analysis of partially reduced material obtained at different stages of the reduction process. The experimental data revealed critical factors influencing the reduction of kinetics, both qualitatively and quantitatively, which support understanding of the complex overall process. Moreover, the study revealed significant differences between pure hematite and industrial feedstock.

Structural engineering of Cu/SiO2 catalysts via controlled hydrothermal treatment: Unveiling the role of silanol evolution and Cu dispersion for enhanced DMO hydrogenation to ethylene glycol
abstract: Rational engineering of the metal–support interface is essential for developing efficient and durable Cu/SiO 2 catalysts. Herein, we report a facile and controllable hydrothermal-assisted ion-exchange method to tailor the surface structure of Cu/SiO 2 catalysts for the selective hydrogenation of dimethyl oxalate (DMO) to ethylene glycol (EG). By integrating ion exchange with hydrothermal treatment and systematically tuning the hydrothermal conditions, we reveal that the evolution of surface silanol (Si–OH) groups and the formation of copper phyllosilicate critically governs Cu dispersion, particle size, and metal–support interactions. Comprehensive characterization—including BET, XRD, TEM, H 2 -TPR, FTIR, and XPS—demonstrates that moderate hydrothermal treatment fosters the formation of highly dispersed metallic copper (Cu 0 ) species and strengthens interfacial contact via enhanced Si–O–Cu linkage density. The optimized catalyst exhibits superior activity (DMO conversion >99%) and remarkable stability over 300 h of continuous operation. Mechanistic studies indicate that surface Si–O–Cu moieties suppress Cu sintering and stabilize active Cu 0 sites by reinforcing metal–support interactions, thereby maintaining an optimal Cu + /Cu 0 ratio that enables synergistic catalysis in DMO hydrogenation. This work provides valuable insights into ion-exchange-coupled hydrothermal interfacial engineering and offers a practical approach for maximizing copper utilization and enhancing catalyst durability in selective DMO hydrogenation.

abstract: Carbon dioxide hydrogenation provides a route for converting CO 2 into methane (CH 4 ), but the large compositional space of high-entropy alloy (HEA)-based catalysts complicates empirical catalyst selection. In this study a literature-derived dataset of 251 observations was analysed using machine learning to evaluate composition-derived atomic and electronic descriptors together with surface, synthesis, and reaction variables. XGBR achieved random-split test R 2 values of 0.95 for CO 2 conversion and 0.91 for CH 4 selectivity, whereas intrinsic-descriptor-only models achieved R 2 values of 0.37 and 0.69, respectively, showing that full-model performance arises from combined catalyst and process information. SHAP and partial-dependence analyses identified reaction temperature and composition-derived descriptors including weighted Pauling electronegativity (EN), weighted atomic radius (R), and ΔR as influential model features. Weighted Pauling EN above approximately 1.2, smaller weighted atomic radii (R), and low ΔR were associated with favourable model predictions within the present dataset. These relationships are interpreted as empirical screening trends rather than direct mechanistic thresholds. NSGA-II and fuzzy logic analysis defined descriptor space screening regions, and more than 205 million five-element compositions were enumerated, of which 4,811,467, or 2.35%, satisfied the property window criteria. Experimental assessment showed lower apparent activation energies than Ni/Al 2 O 3 for several HEA-based formulations, with AlCdMgCoNi achieving 45 kJ mol −1 compared with 75 kJ mol −1 for the reference. However, the synthesized catalysts were multiphase, CH 4 selectivity remained below 60% at atmospheric pressure, and selectivity predictions transferred poorly to the experimental systems. These limitations indicate that surface-sensitive descriptors and descriptors capturing the local chemical environment are required for selectivity-focused catalyst design. Therefore, the framework is supported primarily as an activity-oriented screening and property-space narrowing approach.

Sloughing events in biofilm modeling – how model structure and biofilm geometry impact predictions
abstract: One-dimensional (1d) biofilm models are designed for macroscopic simulations of biofilm reactors. However, accurately describing reactor responses to dynamic conditions such as sloughing events remains challenging for several reasons. For instance, the complex interactions contributing to biofilm detachment are not fully understood. Moreover, detachment appears to be a microscopic process characterized by strong spatial heterogeneity throughout the reactor, which contradicts the longitudinal homogeneity inherent to the 1d biofilm model structure. Consequently, detachment functions in such models are restricted to a generalized, macroscopic description of the actual physical processes. Despite these limitations, 1d biofilm reactor models remain indispensable in practice. Therefore, this study conceptually assesses how the choice of detachment function impacts reactor performance and biofilm dynamics when simulating sloughing events within 1d frameworks. Two different detachment functions were compared, differing in their focus on maintaining either a predefined biofilm thickness or predefined detachment forces. The simulated scenarios also investigated the additional effect of co- vs. counter-diffusion biofilm geometry and level of detail of the biokinetic model. For the latter, a traditional approach with a single heterotrophic microbial group was compared against an approach with different functional groups. Overall, the simulated scenarios demonstrated that while the influence of the detachment function can be significant, it is not generalizable, as it depends heavily on the biofilm geometry and the biokinetic model. Particularly for strongly stratified biofilms, such as frequently encountered in counter-diffusion biofilm geometries, sloughing events may significantly alter reactor performance when the detachment function does not enforce a prescribed biofilm thickness. Consequently, the structure of the detachment function, including its representation of sloughing events, should be considered during model calibration to operational data of biofilm reactors.

title: Engineered transition metal pseudocapacitive electrodes from 0D to 3D structures: Emerging trend for high performance supercapacitors
abstract: Supercapacitors (SCs) store significantly more energy than conventional capacitors and the charge-discharge rates are far superior to those of batteries. However, their practical large-scale adoption remains constrained by inherently low capacitance and energy density. To address these challenges, transition metal (TM) based composites have emerged as promising SC electrode materials, exploiting their exceptional physical, mechanical, and electrochemical properties. Various TM nanostructures, ranging from 0D to 3D, have been developed highlighting their potential in energy storage applications. Notably, pseudocapacitive materials with diverse structures have demonstrated remarkable improvements in electrochemical performance when employed as SC electrodes. This review is dedicated to overviewing recent progress and key achievements in TM nanostructures and their application in SCs. Emphasis is placed on how structural dimensionality influences the synthesis, physicochemical properties, and electrochemical behavior of cathode materials. The review concludes by recognizing outstanding challenges and proposing to address them in the future direction, aiming to provide clear guidance toward the design and development of next-generation, high-performance SCs.

abstract: Production of high-purity nitrogen by a combination of a pressure-swing adsorption system and a thermo-chemical air separation redox cycle using the perovskite SrFeO 3 is investigated. In this way, low remaining oxygen impurities in ppm-range required for ammonia production by the Haber-Bosch process can be reached. Using the Finite Volume method a transient 1D-simulation of a complete reactor cycle, consisting of oxidation, reduction and non-isothermal heating and cooling steps in between, is set up to predict the oxygen non-stoichometry, δ , the oxygen concentration in the gas phase, x O 2 , and the gas and perovskite temperature, T F and T S , respectively. Whenever necessary, oxidation and reduction are modeled in a coupled way in order to be able to represent the transition between them. With the goal of understanding the reaction better different oxidation and reduction temperatures are compared in terms of specific energy demand per mole of nitrogen produced and strategies to further decrease the energy demand per cycle are developed. With T ox = 723 K and T red = 1173 K , as optimal reaction temperatures, a specific energy demand of 25.2 kJ/mol N 2 can be reached making this process competitive with cryogenic air separation and very promising for an industrial use.

title: Microwave-assisted synthesis: Crystallinity-driven donor-acceptor covalent organic frameworks for high-performance room-temperature HCl vapor sensing
Model-guided targeted synthesis and structural regulation of polyethylene via α-diimine nickel/MAO-catalyzed ethylene homopolymerization in a microflow system
abstract: Ethylene homopolymerization catalyzed by an α-diimine nickel/MAO system was investigated in toluene using a microflow platform. The effects of catalyst concentration and Al/Ni ratio on polymerization behavior and polymer structure were systematically examined. Increasing catalyst concentration enhanced the overall polymerization capability but also intensified chain-transfer effects, while the Al/Ni ratio exhibited an optimal window governed by the balance between catalyst activation and activity suppression at excessive MAO levels. Based on the chain-walking mechanism, polymer structure formation was interpreted as a dynamic competition among chain propagation, chain walking, and chain transfer, which mainly determined conversion, branching degree, and molecular weight. A mechanism-inspired apparent model was established by combining variable transformations, a third-order polynomial response surface, and Ridge regularization, enabling simultaneous prediction of key polymer properties. Furthermore, an inverse design model was developed for identifying feasible reaction conditions toward target-oriented polyethylene synthesis.

title: Self-compensatory dual-functional patch integrating passive cooling and humidity-triggered antimicrobial release for postharvest preservation
abstract: Postharvest fruits and vegetables are highly susceptible to quality deterioration caused by heat accumulation and microbial contamination, especially under ambient storage or insufficient cold-chain conditions. To address this issue, a dual-functional antimicrobial sustained release patch, termed the DAS-Patch, was developed by integrating a thermo-responsive poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAm) hydrogel incorporated with TiO2@polydopamine (TiO2@PDA) as the upper layer, and a sodium chlorite (NaClO2)-loaded gelatin/sodium alginate (Gel/SA) aerogel as the lower layer. In this design, the upper hydrogel layer enables passive radiative and evaporative cooling, achieving average and maximum temperature reductions of 6.1℃ and 9.9℃ below ambient conditions, respectively. The lower aerogel layer provides humidity-responsive ClO2 release for antimicrobial protection. Importantly, the two layers function as a coordinated dual-protection system rather than independent modules. Under elevated thermal conditions, hydrogel dehydration enhances local moisture availability at the aerogel interface, thereby triggering increased ClO2 release and providing a self-compensatory antimicrobial backup when passive cooling became less effective. Consequently, the DAS-Patch exhibits broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity (up to 99.9% inactivation), significantly reduced sunscald damage, and prolonged strawberry shelf life to 8 days at room temperature, with residual ClO2 (0.75 mg/kg) below the regulatory limits. Overall, this work provides self-compensatory dual-protection synergistic strategy for low-energy ambient postharvest storage.

abstract: Interfacial instability and energy-intensive synthesis remain fundamental bottlenecks in heterostructure engineering for high-rate alkaline energy storage, often arising from weak interfacial coupling and suboptimal adsorption energetics. Here, we report a chemical-locking and electric-driving interfacial strategy realized through a surface-confined phase regulation route. A mild, pressure-free, and scalable solution process enables the construction of a Ni3S2@NiSe (NiSSe) heterostructure, featuring a surface-confined NiSe layer interfacially coupled to a conductive Ni3S2 scaffold. Spectroscopic analyses reveal a chemically reconstructed Ni-S/Ni-Se coordination environment, while multiscale electronic descriptors identify intensive interfacial coordination interactions that chemically lock the heterointerface and enable efficient charge communication. Concurrently, work-function mismatch induces a built-in electric field, driving interfacial charge redistribution. Density functional theory further uncovers an optimized adsorption-electron-transfer synergy, where NiSSe achieves balanced OH − adsorption relative to its individual components. Consequently, the NiSSe electrode delivers an exceptional areal capacitance of 7641.6 mF cm −2 at 2 mA cm −2 with superior rate capability. The assembled NiSSe//AC device achieves an energy density of 62.5 Wh kg −1 at 703.5 W kg −1 and retains 87.2% capacitance over 10,000 cycles. This work provides a transferable blueprint for integrating chemical locking with electric driving to engineer high-performance heterointerfaces for alkaline energy storage.

abstract: Selecting for high quality carbon nanotube (CNT) growth during the floating catalyst vapour deposition (FC-CVD) synthesis process remains a challenge due to the coupling of physical and chemical phenomena inside the reactor. While there is evidence implicating C2 species as the precursors to CNT formation in FC-CVD reactors, the heterogeneous chemistry remains poorly resolved both as it pertains to CNT growth as well as potential parasitic reactions. This work utilises a specialised Temporal Analysis of Products (TAP) reactor to isolate the kinetics for heterogeneous C2 decomposition over previously grown multi-walled CNT samples, single-walled CNT samples, supported Fe nanoparticles, and graphite. Our results indicate that the catalysed decomposition of acetylene primarily occurs over the Fe catalyst seed, whereas the catalysed decomposition of ethylene primarily occurs over the CNTs. Further, we find that as the crystallinity of a CNT sample decreases, a decreased barrier to ethylene decomposition is observed. Interestingly, both pristine and defective graphite did not catalyse ethylene decomposition, indicating that curvature or morphology may play a role. Under all conditions tested, the decomposition of C2 species lowered the CNT sample crystallinity, as measured by Raman spectroscopy. Thus, we conclude that the secondary decomposition of ethylene over defective carbon and the secondary decomposition of acetylene over Fe catalyst seeds are both drivers of decreased crystallinity of CNT samples. We also emphasise the importance of including surface catalysed decomposition alongside pyrolysis in FC-CVD reactor models, as our results demonstrate that surface processes are fundamentally distinct from previously reported gas-phase dominated pyrolysis behaviour. More broadly, this work establishes TAP as a methodology for isolating heterogeneous gas-surface chemistry from coupled physical phenomena in complex reaction systems.
