Hybrids of spacer-stabilized antimicrobial peptides and graphene oxide exhibit unusual antibacterial potency
abstract: In the wake of escalating antibiotic resistance, graphene oxide (GO) has emerged as a promising antibacterial nanocarbon with multimodal mechanisms of action, including membrane damage and oxidative stress. However, even when its morphology and surface functionalities are tuned, pristine GO often displays limited and inconsistent activity. Here, we conjugated GO with a moderately potent antimicrobial peptide (AMP) employing a facile spacer-assisted chemical strategy originally intended to enable on-site peptide release for targeted delivery. Unexpectedly, although our GO-Spacer-AMP construct contained an enzymatically cleavable linker in principle, we observed no AMP release. However, the designed nanohybrids still exhibited unusually high antibacterial activity against both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. Spectroscopic evidence further indicated that the GO conjugation helped preserve the structural integrity of AMP, resulting in pronounced synergistic antibacterial activity. We propose that our unconventional design will open new avenues for chemically designing ultrapotent nanohybrids for antimicrobial nanomedicine.

abstract: The electrochemical reduction of CO 2 to CO represents a pivotal step towards electrification of industries and Power-to-X strategies, however, industrial implementation remains limited by electrode flooding, salt accumulation, and unstable operation at high current densities. Herein, we demonstrate the use of oxygen depolarised cathodes (ODC), that are established and well-proven in chlor-alkali electrolysis, as a robust alternative electrode for CO 2 electroreduction under industrially relevant conditions. Notably, ODC exhibits superior mechanical durability, electrical conductivity, and flooding resistance enabling stable operation in membrane electrode assembly configuration over a wide current density range. By conducting a systematic tuning of both reactor temperature and CO 2 humidification, we identify that a delicate balance of water management and cation transport is critical for sustained performance. Stable operation was achieved at 100 mA/cm 2 and 200 mA/cm 2 with CO Faradaic efficiencies of 97% and 95% respectively over 24 h using a 0.1 M KHCO 3 anolyte. At 300 mA/cm 2 , an intermittent electrolysis strategy with periodic current relaxation extended operation to 100 h maintaining 70% CO selectivity. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of using ODC as scalable and durable cathode for CO 2 electrolysis to CO and adapting operational conditions to achieve the industrially relevant deployment.

abstract: Lignocellulosic biomass is a sustainable feedstock for carbon-neutral aviation fuels. However, its structural complexity causes rapid catalyst deactivation through carbonaceous deposition during upgrading. This study presents a three-step continuous-flow process for the production of petroleum-replacing hydrocarbons from lignocellulose fast pyrolysis oil. The catalyst bed contained carbon-supported palladium, La-Ti-Ce-Ni mixed oxide, and tungstate-zirconia-supported ruthenium. Cracking of high‑carbon-number reactants over the La-Ti-Ce-Ni mixed oxide suppressed deactivation in the continuous flow process. Lewis acid sites generated by mismatched metal‑oxygen coordination in the La-Ti-Ce-Ni mixed oxides are responsible for the catalytic activity. The optimized continuous flow process operates stably with La 2 Ti 0.5 Ce 0.5 NiO x for more than 100 h and yielded 34.0% deoxygenated oil with an oxygen-to‑carbon ratio of 0.0072 mol/mol. Bench-scale operation remained stable for 132 h and achieved an oil-phase yield of 42.1%. Techno-economic analysis indicates that this optimized catalyst system reduces production costs by 33%, while life-cycle assessment identifies a 30% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. These results demonstrate a viable pathway for the commercial production of hydrocarbons from lignocellulose fast pyrolysis oil.

Mechanism-matched design of nitrogen-functionalized and Cu(I) active-site carbon aerogels for CO2/CO adsorption
abstract: A multifunctional carbon aerogel adsorbent for fire-smoke purification is developed by integrating structural regulation and active-site engineering. Urea is employed as a nitrogen precursor to modify carbon aerogels. Its dual roles in nitrogen doping and structural regulation enable the modulation of framework evolution and pore development during gel formation and high-temperature treatment, yielding N-doped porous carbon aerogels with synergistically optimized microporous structures and surface chemistry. Characterization results indicate that urea incorporation significantly promotes micropore development and introduces abundant nitrogen-containing functional groups, thereby enhancing CO2 adsorption performance. The CO2 adsorption behavior exhibits pronounced temperature dependence, being dominated by micropore confinement at low temperature and by surface Lewis acid–base interactions at ambient temperature, highlighting the critical role of synergistic regulation of pore structure and surface chemistry. Based on this optimized support, CuCl is further introduced to construct Cu(I)-functionalized carbon aerogels. The results demonstrate that CuCl is uniformly dispersed and structurally stable within the carbon framework, significantly enhancing CO adsorption capacity. Cyclic adsorption tests further confirm excellent stability and reusability. Overall, this study presents a hierarchical functionalization strategy for selective and sequential CO2 and CO adsorption, providing a viable design strategy for multicomponent fire-smoke purification materials.

title: Enhancing oil removal and mitigating thermal runaway limitations in microwave treatment of petroleum hydrocarbon contaminated soils
abstract: Total Petroleum Hydrocarbons (TPH) released through oil spills and leaks during oil production, transport, and processing are a primary pollutant that destroys vegetation and poses health risks. Microwave processing has been identified as a promising technology for removing petroleum hydrocarbons from contaminated soils. However, successful remediation must take a site-specific approach. This study examines the impact of contaminant and soil characteristics on three different microwave-based treatment strategies. Four petroleum-contaminated materials were collected and analysed for dielectric properties, oil and moisture contents, before undergoing microwave treatment under varying conditions. Oil removals up to 94% (filter cake), 42% (planings), 44% (Bodo soil), and 30% (K-Dere soil) were achieved. Filter cake's texture and hydrated clay layers contributed significantly to the high oil yields, with steam stripping proposed as a dominant contributing mechanism. Pre-wetting the samples with 5% ethylene glycol (EG) enhanced the removal of oil to 87% (planings), but its impact on the remaining contaminated samples was minimal. Thermal runaway posed a major technical barrier during material processing, resulting in equipment damage and degraded treated samples during the EG-wet and dry microwave remediation. To address this, contaminated materials were remediated using inert liquid microwave heating. This approach demonstrated that inert liquid microwave heating reduces thermal runaway risks and showed potential for enhancing oil removal under the investigated conditions. It reduced hydrocarbon levels in K-Dere and Bodo soils, meeting Environmental Guidelines and Standards. However, high specific energy was required compared with dry processing. The three microwave treatment approaches were compared with conventional heating (thermal desorption), and suitable remediation approaches were recommended.

abstract: Efficient utilization of CO 2 as a sustainable carbon feedstock is crucial for controlling climate change and producing value-added chemicals. Herein, we report starpolymer catalysts incorporating a porphyrin core and quaternary ammonium halide groups for CO 2 cycloaddition under ambient conditions. By tuning the density of nucleophilic units around the porphyrin core, we achieved enhanced catalytic activity and reduced activation energy compared to conventional catalysts. The inclusion of thermoresponsive P(DEGMA) segments enables simple catalyst recovery via temperature-induced precipitation, allowing for multiple recycling cycles while maintaining their catalytic activity. Substrate scope studies revealed that steric accessibility significantly influences catalytic performance. These findings demonstrate the potential of rationally designed starpolymer catalysts for sustainable CO 2 conversion and demonstrates a versatile platform for polymer-based catalysis with tunable activity and recyclability.

Circular economy approaches for carbon fiber-reinforced polymers: recent advances in recycling, life cycle assessment, and high-value reuse
abstract: Carbon fiber-reinforced polymers (CFRPs) are essential for lightweighting in aerospace, automotive, and renewable energy applications, yet their projected growth beyond 280,000 t per year by 2030 generates a mounting end-of-life waste challenge. This review evaluates sustainable CFRP recycling and closed-loop reuse based on peer-reviewed literature and publicly available technical, industrial, and project information available through 30 June 2026. Mild-chemical solvolysis, hybrid thermal-chemical processes, and emerging biological routes are assessed with respect to fiber recovery, mechanical-property retention, environmental performance, economic viability, and technology maturity. Optimized processes can recover fibers retaining high tensile properties while substantially reducing the environmental burdens of virgin carbon-fiber production. The review examines interfacial modification, fiber alignment, recyclable and cleavable matrix systems, and their roles in enabling higher-value reuse across aerospace, automotive, renewable-energy, marine, and multifunctional applications. Particular attention is given to differences in feedstock characteristics, fiber grade, process conditions, system boundaries, economic assumptions, and technology-readiness assessments, which can strongly influence reported performance. Persistent barriers associated with heterogeneous waste streams, large-tow fibers, collection logistics, process scale-up, standardization, certification, and environmental trade-offs are identified. Laboratory evidence, pilot-scale demonstrations, commercial deployment, announced capacity, and forward-looking projections are explicitly distinguished. Future reclaimed-fiber adoption is discussed through scenario-based projections rather than a single deterministic forecast. An operational decision framework is proposed that links waste characteristics, matrix chemistry, recycling-route selection, recovered-fiber quality, reprocessing strategy, application requirements, and lifecycle and economic considerations, thereby supporting the transition toward more circular CFRP systems.

Tunable redox–basic interfaces for super-dry reforming of methane over leaching-assisted MgO/Ni–Ce–Al catalysts
abstract: Super-dry reforming of methane (SDRM) couples dry reforming of methane (DRM) with the in situ reverse water–gas shift reaction (RWGS) to enhance CO2 utilization under a CO2-rich feed. Herein, leaching-assisted MgO/Ni–Ce–Al catalysts were designed by combining accessible Ni–Ce redox domains with MgO-derived basic sites. Ni–Ce–Al oxide microspheres prepared by spray pyrolysis were selectively leached and subsequently loaded with 1–5 wt.% MgO. MgO loading produced a nonmonotonic structural and functional response. Low MgO loading preserved the pore structure and increased the estimated Ni active-site amount, while also yielding a smaller reduced Ni crystallite size and dispersed Mg-containing environments. In contrast, excessive loading reduced pore accessibility and promoted crystalline MgO formation. Accordingly, 1MgO/NCA(L) exhibited the highest Ce3+ fraction and oxygen storage capacity. In situ DRIFTS showed that low MgO loading diversified CO2 adsorption and promoted the temperature-dependent evolution of carbonate- and formate-related intermediates, whereas excessive loading favored persistent carbonate species. Low MgO loading enhanced conventional DRM activity, primarily because 1MgO/NCA(L) exhibited the highest estimated Ni active-site amount and smallest Ni crystallite size while preserving pore accessibility. Under SDRM conditions, these advantages were further coupled with MgO-derived CO2 adsorption and Ce-containing redox functionality within the DRM–RWGS network. At 750 °C, 1MgO/NCA(L) achieved CH4 and CO2 conversions of 87.0% and 44.7%, respectively, and retained conversions of 75.1% and 40.2% after 12 h. These results identify the balanced integration of accessible Ni sites, MgO-derived basicity, and Ce-containing redox functionality as a key design principle for CO2-rich methane reforming.

abstract: Formaldehyde (HCHO), a hazardous volatile organic compound, poses serious threats to human health in daily life and industrial environments. Herein, a pulse airflow-driven triboelectric nanogenerator (ZZP-TENG) with a ZIF-8/ZIF-67/copper foam composite microstructure was fabricated for high-sensitivity HCHO detection. Benefiting from micro/nano structural modification, the ZZP-TENG efficiently harvested ambient mechanical energy, yielding a short-circuit current of 3.62 μA and a maximum output power of 45.63 μW. Its stable energy output could drive 54 LEDs and charge various capacitors, demonstrating reliable energy-harvesting capacity. The sensor delivered superior HCHO response of 80% at 40 ppm, with a 22 s response time and 80 s recovery time, To verify practical indoor application feasibility, a simulated post-renovation HCHO release scenario was constructed with HCHO-containing wood blocks, supporting accurate indoor air quality assessment and environmental safety evaluation. In this study, an improved extreme learning machine (ELM) algorithm was employed to classify HCHO signals from the ZZP-TENG sensor. The ELM model realized 100% HCHO concentration recognition accuracy and constructed a three-level safety early warning system, achieving real-time intelligent indoor HCHO monitoring. This work realizes simultaneous airflow energy harvesting and HCHO detection, providing a novel route for integrated gas sensors and broadening the application of TENGs in self-powered indoor environmental monitoring.

Ageing and CEI formation mechanisms in porous carbon positive electrode in sodium-ion capacitors
abstract: This work reports on the ageing and cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI) formation mechanism of porous carbons (PCs) positive electrode in sodium ion capacitors (SICs) operating in 1 M NaPF 6 in EC:DMC(1:1) electrolyte. Three salt-templated PCs with different textures and graphitization degree were used and compared to commercial activated carbon (Kynol). The PCs electrodes were subjected to voltage hold at 4.5 V and analyzed via various complementary postmortem techniques. The ageing study revealed that the performance loss is due to a combined textural, structural and surface chemistry changes. The synthesized salt-templated carbon materials showed discharge capacity between 96 and 149 mAh g −1 , exceeding commercial Kynol (77 mAh g −1 ). The highest capacity retention during floating (~18 h) was observed for LiNaCl-T and Kynol, attributed to a combination of high graphitization degree and low surface chemistry. Operando electrochemical dilatometry revealed that capacity retention of aged electrodes is more strongly affected by Na + solvation in the voltage range of 1.5–2.8 V, than by desolvated PF 6 − ion operating at 2.8–4.5 V. Postmortem analysis showed that aged electrodes suffer from porosity blockage, structural changes, and increase in oxygen functionalities, resulting in capacity and electronic conductivity loss. In-situ XPS revealed that the CEI layer stabilizes within few electrochemical cycles, while prolonged floating leads to CEI layer dissolution of the organic component and fracture of the inorganic component, which significantly increases the resistance of the PCs electrode. A mechanism of degradation of electrode is proposed along with some solutions to extend the PCs electrode's cycle life.

Green-solvent-processable and mechanically tough poly(p-phenylene) proton exchange membranes enabled by backbone conformation control
abstract: Growing regulatory pressure on per - and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) is accelerating the transition from perfluorosulfonic acid to fluorine-free hydrocarbon proton exchange membranes. However, most hydrocarbon ionomers require highly polar aprotic solvents for membrane casting and membrane−electrode assembly (MEA) fabrication, limiting their sustainability and compatibility with scalable processing. Here, we report a poly( p -phenylene) ionomer that is processable in alcohol-based green solvents through polymer backbone conformation control induced by meta -linkage incorporation. Systematic modulation of the backbone conformation reduces the persistence length, disrupts aromatic packing, and thereby enables alcohol solubility while enhancing mechanical toughness by a factor of 4.7 relative to the fully para -linked polymer. The resulting green-solvent processability allows the fabrication of all-hydrocarbon MEAs using hydrocarbon binders. In proton exchange membrane water electrolysis, the meta -linked membranes exhibit stable operation under pressurized conditions up to 3.1 MPa with suppressed hydrogen crossover, while the green-solvent-processed MEA containing 16 mol% meta -linkages delivers a current density of 3.0 A cm −2 at 1.8 V, comparable to the US DOE 2026 technical target, and maintains continuous operation for 300 h at 2.0 A cm −2 . Overall, polymer backbone conformation control offers a practical strategy for developing PFAS-free membranes that combine green processability, mechanical robustness, and high electrochemical performance.

The impact of morphology on the catalytic glycolysis kinetics of post-consumer poly(ethylene terephthalate)
abstract: The catalytic glycolysis of poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) is a promising strategy for enabling a closed-loop PET economy. To realise the recycling of varied real-world wastes it is important to understand how the recycling process operates with different forms of feedstock. This study examines how PET particle size, geometry, polymer crystallinity, and additives impact depolymerisation under Zn(OAc)₂ catalysis. Under identical reaction conditions, the depolymerisation rate was highly dependent on the effective radius of the substrate. A linear relationship between apparent rate constant and specific surface area (SSA) enabled rate prediction across morphologies utilising shrinking core kinetics. Morphology evolution was investigated throughout the depolymerisation. DSC analysis of the PET showed early-stage annealing and lamellar thickening, followed by lamellar breakdown during depolymerisation. Microscopy revealed surface roughening and cracking that increased reactive area exponentially. Uniaxial compression testing indicated >95% loss of compressive strength by 20% conversion, consistent with mechanochemical weakening. End-group analysis showed a drop in number-average molar mass from 35 to 3 kDa, correlating with embrittlement and fragmentation. Together, these observations support a mechanistic sequence of chain scission, annealing, surface cracking, and auto-acceleration via rising surface area. Applying grinding or attrition after early-stage weakening increased the apparent rate constant by two orders of magnitude, providing scope to minimise reactor time and therefore develop a more efficient chemical recycling pathway.

Bio-mineral engineering of aliphatic-enriched humic-like substances through biological precursor-MnO2 coupling: Toward tunable architectures with enhanced pollutant adsorption
abstract: Humic substances are essential for soil fertility and environmental remediation, yet their natural formation requires decades to centuries. Here, we develop a microbial–mineral catalytic strategy enabling rapid formation of structurally tunable humic-like substances (HLS) within 15 days, where the aliphatic–aromatic carbon balance is precisely controlled through coupled microbial fermentation and MnO₂ catalysis. Four microbial systems (Lactobacillus acidophilus, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, vitamin C-enriched yeast, and rennet), tested with and without MnO₂, were characterized by UV–Vis, FTIR, XRD, SEM, XPS, ¹³C NMR, and DFT, showing a dual-pathway mechanism: MnO₂ drives aromatic condensation (30–45% carbon) via surface-mediated radical coupling, while microbial metabolism stabilizes aliphatic domains (50–60% carbon). The resulting dual-domain architectures exhibit ~48% interlayer expansion (4.0 → 5.9 Å), enhanced porosity, and moderate E₄/E₆ ratios (3–4), confirming structural maturity resembling natural humic acids — optimally balanced in the S. cerevisiae–MnO₂ system (~55% aliphatic, ~35% aromatic). DFT calculations confirm MnO₂-mediated electronic activation through an 82% reduction in the HOMO–LUMO gap and nine-fold increase in binding energy (111.13 kcal mol⁻¹), reflecting thermodynamic stabilization of the ternary complex and selective C–C coupling during polymerization. Functional validation via aflatoxin B1 adsorption demonstrates a maximum equilibrium capacity of 127.43 mg g⁻¹ for the HQ–Rennet-MnO₂ system, approximately 2-fold higher than uncatalyzed HQ oxidation, with Elovich kinetics (R² ≥ 0.985) confirming chemisorption on energetically heterogeneous surfaces. By integrating biological and mineral catalysis under ambient conditions, this work provides a rational design framework for engineering functional HLS with tunable properties for environmental remediation applications.

Bioinspired multifunctional composite for impact attenuation, pressure sensing, and fatigue resistant functional retention
abstract: Flexible protective materials are important for plantar protection and wearable devices, but achieving impact attenuation, fatigue resistant performance retention, and real time pressure sensing in one soft material remains challenging. Here, inspired by the porous ring and spoke skeleton and gel like flesh of mature loofah, we developed a bioinspired energy dissipation layer, RSCS-FSGC, by filling a foam ring and spoke coupled skeleton with a silicone gel composite. A CNT/PDMS flexible sensing layer was further designed on its surface for real-time pressure monitoring. The ring and spoke coupled skeleton supported stable load transfer and uniform stress distribution, while the silicone gel composite improved viscoelastic energy dissipation. Compared with conventional flexible materials, RSCS-FSGC showed reduced peak impact force, lower pressure time integral, longer impact duration, lower average impact load, and higher specific energy absorption. After repeated cyclic compression, RSCS-FSGC retained higher mechanical stability, height retention, and post fatigue impact attenuation performance, indicating good fatigue resistant functional retention. The CNT/PDMS flexible sensor layer showed stable pressure response, frequency recognition, and long-term cycling stability. Walking, running, and egg drop tests further verified its potential for smart insoles and impact protection.

Direct crystallization of nickel- and lithium-sulfate for lithium-ion battery recycling
abstract: The rapid growth of electric-vehicle and portable-electronics markets has intensified the need for efficient recycling of spent lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). A major bottleneck in conventional hydrometallurgical routes is the selective separation of nickel and lithium from the mixed sulfate leachate that results after removal of cobalt, manganese, aluminum, iron and copper. This work demonstrates a novel, precipitation-free separation strategy that couples eutectic freeze crystallization (EFC) with subsequent heating crystallization (HC) to recover high-purity nickel- and lithium-sulfates directly from the Ni-Li-sulfate aqueous stream. Solubility measurements were used to validate the OLI Stream Analyzer thermodynamic model. Multi-stage EFC on a synthetic leachate (24.5 g.L −1 Ni, 6.1 g.L −1 Li, 82.3 g.L −1 SO 4 2− , pH 4.5) yielded NiSO 4 ·7H 2 O and NiSO 4 ·6H 2 O crystals with a Ni recovery of 89%. The Ni-rich filtrate (≈ 41 g.L −1 Ni, 17 g.L −1 Li) was then subjected to HC, producing Li 2 SO 4 ·H 2 O crystals and delivering an overall Li recovery of 88%. A flowsheet integrating reverse osmosis water-recovery and heat integration between the refrigeration and heating sections was developed in Aspen Plus. The integrated process recovers ~90% of the water, and reduces the total heating, cooling water and electrical duties to 9.2, 25.1 and 17 kW per m 3 .h −1 of feed (5.4%, 11.9% and 35.5% of a baseline without heat integration). The combined EFC/HC route therefore offers an energy-efficient, high-purity alternative to conventional precipitation-based hydrometallurgy for LIB recycling, providing Ni- and Li-sulfates that can be reused as cathode-precursor salts.

Performance enhancement strategies in transition metal dichalcogenides (MX2) gas sensors: Structure, morphology, mechanism, performance, and real-world applications
abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenides (MX 2 ) have emerged as promising materials for gas sensors, due to their abundant active sites, layered structures, inimitable semiconducting properties, high surface area, and tunable electronic properties. Recent studies revealed that intrinsic MX 2 sensors could not simultaneously achieve high sensitivity, selectivity, speed, and stability without further modification. However, incorporating various strategies could significantly modulate the structural and chemical properties, thereby improving gas-sensing performance through synergistic effects. This review presents a comprehensive, performance-oriented overview based on four sensing parameters: sensitivity, selectivity, response/recovery times, and stability (4S). The influence of charge transport, defect states, phase-dependent properties, and charge-transfer mechanisms is highlighted. Recent advances in performance enhancement through a multidimensional approach, such as morphology design, light-assisted activation, noble metal decoration, heterostructure engineering, plasma modification, and organic compound functionalization, are systematically examined. The influence of these strategies on active sites, adsorption behavior, electronic properties, and interfacial interaction is critically highlighted. Furthermore, the review explores the practical application of these sensors in environmental monitoring, indoor air quality, clinical breath analysis, and food quality assessment. Finally, current challenges and insights into the prospects of MX 2 -based gas sensors are discussed.

An injectable GelMA-CMCS double-network cryogel for enhanced bone regeneration
abstract: Minimally invasive bone repair requires injectable scaffolds, yet conventional single-network hydrogels are too soft to provide adequate mechanical support or promote osteogenesis. Achieving both injectability and osteogenic stiffness therefore remains a major challenge. Here, we developed a gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA)–carboxymethyl chitosan (CMCS) double-network (DN) cryogel using a sequential crosslinking strategy: EDC/NHS-mediated amide coupling first established the CMCS network, followed by LAP-initiated UV photo-crosslinking of the GelMA network. The resulting DN cryogels showed increasing Young's modulus with higher CMCS incorporation while maintaining an interconnected macroporous architecture. Despite the increased stiffness, the cryogels remained injectable, rapidly recovered their original shape after needle passage, and protected encapsulated cells during injection. CMCS incorporation further imparted antibacterial and antioxidant activities. The optimized GC2D cryogel exhibited the highest Young's modulus and the lowest degradation rate. Importantly, the DN cryogels were cytocompatible and enhanced osteogenic differentiation of hBMSCs in vitro, with osteogenic gene expression increasing at higher CMCS content. Consistently, the cryogels promoted new bone formation in an in vivo mouse cranial defect model, with GC2D achieving the most substantial regeneration. The GelMA–CMCS DN cryogel thus provides an injectable system for minimally invasive bone tissue engineering.

abstract: Medium-nickel high-voltage cathode materials (0.6<Ni<0.8) have attracted extensive attention owing to their high energy density, superior thermal stability, and cost-effectiveness. Nevertheless, rapid capacity degradation and structural instability continue to pose significant challenges to the commercialization of high-voltage cathodes. In this study, high-valence elements such as W, Nb, and Sb were separately co-doped with Zr to synthesize high-voltage single-crystal LiNi0.70Co0.06Mn0.24O2 (Ni70) cathode materials through the solid-phase method. Powder X-ray diffractometer, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and electron probe micro-analyzer (EPMA) are applied to characterize the as-prepared samples. Characterization results reveal that the high-valence Nb element suppresses Li+/Ni2+ intermixing and facilitates the formation of a more uniformly distributed population of smaller primary monocrystalline particles, thereby effectively enhancing lithium-ion diffusion kinetics. Electrochemical tests indicate that when the cut-off voltage is raised to 4.45 V, the Zr/Nb-NCM cathode demonstrates outstanding performance compared to other co-doped counterparts, capacity retention of 88.8% after 100 cycles at the rate of 1C. The improved performance is attributed to the pinning effect of co-doping, which enhances the structural stability of the cathode material, suppresses planar gliding and microcracks, thereby optimizing the electrochemical behavior and decreasing the interfacial impedance. This work provides a general strategy and insights for inhibiting chemo-mechanical degradation during intercalation and paves the way for the next generation of high-energy-density and low-cost cathodes.

In-situ CO2 capture outperforms conventional bulk pH-swing electrolyzers
abstract: Electrochemical CO 2 capture via pH-swing electrolyzers offers a promising alternative to thermally driven amine scrubbing, yet mass transfer limitations at the gas-liquid interface remain a critical bottleneck limiting scalability. This work addresses this challenge through a novel reactor architecture integrating gas diffusion electrodes (GDE) to enable in-situ CO 2 capture at the electrode surface. We systematically evaluated two flow regimes: the flow-by (diffusion dominated) and flow-through (convective gas transport) and compared their performance against conventional ex-situ setups including bulk bubbling and countercurrent scrubbing . Using 0.1 M 2,7-anthraquinone disulfonic acid (AQDS) as a model active redox carrier, the in-situ setup achieved 213.0 mL captured CO 2 versus 152.2 mL for bulk one, representing a 39.9% volumetric gain. Energy consumption decreased from 86.1 kJ·mol −1 ( bulk ) to 66.7 kJ·mol −1 ( in-situ ), corresponding to 22.5% reduction. Finally, it demonstrated superior capture efficiency (43.7%), volumetric capacity (5.6 kgm −3 ) with minimum CO 2 concentrations of 6.4% from a 10% feed stream compared to the ex-situ setups. Continuous operation over 96 h confirmed reversible cycling without performance degradation. These findings establish reactor engineering as the primary design variable for electrochemical capture systems, enabling substantial performance improvements independent of electrolyte optimization. The demonstrated scalability pathway provides actionable design principles for industrial CO 2 capture applications across diverse source concentrations.

Redox-active coordination catalysts for selective thermochemical valorization of biowaste: Mechanistic insights and structure-performance relationships
abstract: The growing demand for renewable energy has intensified global efforts to transform biowastes into value-added fuels and chemicals rather than viewing them as disposal challenges. Derived mainly from lignocellulosic and other organic residues, these wastes are rich in carbon and reactive functional groups, making them promising feedstocks for thermochemical conversion via pyrolysis, gasification, and hydrothermal liquefaction. Yet, their compositional complexity, high oxygen content, and inorganic impurities remain major barriers to efficient transformation and catalyst durability. This review offers an integrated perspective on recent advances in the catalytic valorization of biowaste, with a particular emphasis on how coordination chemistry principles can enhance reaction selectivity and energy efficiency. Redox-active metal complexes, zeolites, and metal-organic frameworks are highlighted for their ability to mediate controlled bond activation and electron transfer during reforming and aromatization processes. By linking feedstock chemistry, pretreatment strategies, and catalytic mechanisms, this work establishes structure-activity-selectivity relationships that underpin syngas and aromatic production. Finally, emerging concepts such as AI-guided catalyst design, integration with circular bioeconomy frameworks, and dual-function redox systems, are discussed as promising pathways toward scalable, low-carbon, and sustainable energy technologies.

title: Support-induced growth of lumen-side ZIF-67 membrane on asymmetric hollow fibers for hydrogen separation
Polymorph engineering for organic detectors enabling high-sensitivity and high-resolution X-ray imaging
abstract: Organic semiconductor single crystals (OSSCs) hold great promise for direct X-ray detection owing to their low cost and tissue equivalence. However, their performance is often limited by inefficient charge transport. Herein, we develop a cooling-rate-modulated polymorphic growth strategy to simultaneously regulate intermolecular torsion angles and molecular packing, yielding two large-sized polymorphs of 9,10-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)anthracene (BMOPA-α and BMOPA-β). Comparative studies on polymorphs reveal that the deviation angle between the charge transport pathway and the intermolecular interaction axis leads to significant differences in carrier mobility. The BMOPA-β crystal shows a much smaller deviation angle, enabling more efficient carrier transport, with the hole mobility reaching 8.59 cm2 V-1 s-1. As a result, the BMOPA-β single-crystal detector achieves a high sensitivity of 584.4 μC Gyair-1 cm-2, and an ultralow detection limit of 37.8 nGyair s-1, enabling high spatial-resolution (3.47 lp mm-1) X-ray imaging. This work highlights molecular packing structure control via polymorph engineering as an effective strategy for improving carrier transport characteristics in organic X-ray detectors.

title: High-resolution near-infrared imaging by systematic engineering of electron transport layers in organic photodetectors
abstract: Organic photodetectors (OPDs) are promising candidates for next-generation imaging systems owing to their high absorption efficiency and tunable spectral response. Achieving high-performance OPDs, in terms of responsivity, noise current, and specific detectivity, is therefore essential for advanced optoelectronic systems integrated with modern Internet of Things technologies. Here, we present a high-resolution imaging system with reduced random noise under near-infrared (NIR) illumination, enabled by an optimized OPD incorporating a Zn 2+ -chelated polyethylenimine (PEI Zn) electron transport layer (ETL). Strong chelation between Zn 2+ ions and nitrogen atoms, together with the low surface roughness of the PEI-Zn layer, improves the interfacial properties with the photoactive layer. As a result, the PEI-Zn-based device exhibits enhanced responsivity and reduced noise current, leading to higher specific detectivity compared to devices employing polyethylenimine ethoxylated (PEIE) or zinc oxide (ZnO) ETLs. In NIR single-pixel imaging, the PEI-Zn-based OPD produces clear object contours and improved contrast, whereas PEIE- and ZnO-based devices show increased noise and image distortion. These findings provide insight into how ETL engineering influences device performance and image quality, serving as experimental evidence that may support future studies on OPD-based imaging.

title: Regenerable, molecularly engineered bio-based rosin gels for resilient underwater sensing and deep learning-augmented intelligent biometrics
Hydrogen-bond mediated phase regulation in deep eutectic solvents enables green fabrication of highly crystalline sub-nanoporous COFs membranes for efficient pharmaceutical desalination
Interdiffusion engineering driving defect network evolution toward high-power-factor n-type Bi2Te3 thermoelectric thin films
Fe3O4@quaternary chitosan accelerates microalgal-bacterial granular sludge formation through EPS enhancement and surface thermodynamic modulation
Carbon black and hydrogen production from upgraded fast pyrolysis bio-oils via high-temperature pyrolysis
abstract: The current manufacturing of carbon black (CB) has a high climate impact and must transition to a carbon-neutral process to meet sustainability goals. In this work, fast pyrolysis bio-oil (FPBO) from biomass and four different upgraded bio-oils (represented by synthetic mixtures made from model compounds) were used to produce renewable CB in an entrained flow reactor (EFR) at different temperatures (1100–1700 °C). The aim of this work was to investigate how the composition of bio-oils produced via the following upgrading technologies, catalytic fast pyrolysis (CFP), catalytic hydropyrolysis (CHP), slurry hydroprocessing (SHP), and slurry hydroprocessing followed by fixed bed hydroprocessing (SHP + FBHP) affects the yield and structural properties of CB. The experimental results demonstrated that CB yield from FPBO were 34–45 wt% on a carbon basis, whereas substantially higher yields (67–93 wt%) were obtained from the upgraded bio-oils depending on the specific upgrading technology and temperature of the EFR. Furthermore, the nanostructure of the CB produced at 1300–1500 °C showed similarities to that of conventional rubber-grade CB, whereas the CB produced at 1700 °C exhibited a higher degree of graphitization, with features more similar to those of conductive-grade CB. Considering the entire conversion pathway from raw biomass to CB, upgrading the FPBO prior to its use as feedstock in the CB reactor was found to increase the overall yield from ∼27 wt% for FPBO to ∼40 wt%. The highest CB yield of ∼44% was obtained for the combination of SHP + FBHP as upgrading technology and a process temperature of 1700 °C in the EFR. The results demonstrate that bio-oil upgrading could be a key strategy for maximizing biomass carbon utilization in renewable CB production.

title: Corrigendum to “Chiral CD@Ag2O nanoparticle-mediated highly efficient antibacterial activity based on synergistic multi-pathway interactions” [Chem. Eng. J. 532 (2026) 174280]
Machine learning-guided design of glycosaminoglycans composite fiber scaffolds for neuro-osteogenic regeneration
abstract: Repairing large bone defects caused by trauma or disease poses a significant clinical challenge. Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), major components of organic matrix, play a crucial role in osteogenesis. Here, we report a machine learning (ML)-guided strategy for enhancing the design of osteogenic multicomponent GAGs. First, we constructed a dataset of 169/173 data for cell differentiation and viability of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) cultured on different GAGs formulations to build an optimal formulation screening model through random forest (RF) and XGBoost (XGB) algorithms. We efficiently screened 59 good GAGs from 10,000 formulations generated in the whole space that own maximized cell differentiation and viability through the model. Based on cell mineralization activity, secondary screening identified 3 optimal formulations (GAG3–5). Based on these formulations, optimal formulation GAGs adsorbed into magnesium doped amino modified mesoporous bioactive glass (MBG) as the core, nerve growth factor (NGF) adsorbed into silk fibroin (SF) as the shell to form a composite fiber MBG/GAG@SF/NGF scaffold through coaxial electrospinning. Interestingly, we observed that MBG/GAG3,5@SF/NGF scaffolds promoted the osteogenesis process by activating the Bone morphogenetic protein 2 (Bmp2)/Smad and p-Erk1/2 signaling pathways in vitro . Furthermore, we found that MBG/GAG3,5@SF/NGF scaffolds enhanced the neurogenesis process in vitro . Intriguingly, we also observed that MBG/GAG5@SF/NGF scaffold effectively guided functional bone regeneration accompanied with enhanced neurogenesis and angiogenesis in mouse cranial defect model in vivo . This study not only provides an efficient MBG/GAG5@SF/NGF composite fiber multifunctional scaffold for bone defect repair but also establishes a scalable paradigm for ML-guided screening of bioactive formulations.

Nonflammable sulfonate deep eutectic electrolyte for lithium-metal dual-ion battery
abstract: Lithium-metal dual-ion batteries (LDIBs) are intriguing due to high working voltage and quick charge capability. However, the implementation of dual-ion batteries (DIBs) is hindered by the lack of compatible electrolytes that can simultaneously fulfill the requirements of a 5 V cathode and an active lithium metal anode. Herein, we propose a binary deep eutectic electrolyte (DEE), composing of lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) and prop-1-ene-1,3-sultone (PES), for LDIBs. The eutectic phenomenon of PES with LiFSI can be triggered in a wide ratio range of 1:1 to 2.75:1 at room temperature, endowing DEEs with non-flammability, a wide liquid range (−50–100 °C) and over 5 V electrochemical window. As a consequence, both Li plating-stripping and anion intercalation/deintercalation proceed reversibly in DEEs. The resultant graphite||Li cell shows an impressive cyclability with 98% capacity retained after 350 cycles at 5C. Even under an elevated temperature of 60 °C, the LDIBs performs stably without obvious capacity decay, while the LDIBs based on carbonate electrolytes cannot work at all. Our work underlines the electrolyte compatibility issue in DIBs and offers a promising electrolyte for safe and durable LDIBs.

title: Dual-functional PEGDA hydrogel electrolyte: Suppressing water activity and regulating Zn2+ flux for long-life aqueous zinc-ion batteries and Ah-level scalability
Unlocking rapid deprotonation in hierarchical NiCoFe-LDH cathodes via Fenton-like etching defects for hybrid supercapacitors
Unraveling the synergistic role of Pd and defective UiO-66 for ethanol Guerbet reaction
abstract: The catalytic upgrading of short-chain alcohols into higher-value products is a key step toward sustainable fuel synthesis, with the Guerbet reaction offering a direct pathway to long-chain alcohols. In this study, Pd-modified UiO-66 materials are examined to clarify how Pd species and framework functionalities cooperate to guide the catalytic activity and product selectivity whilst promoting the catalyst stability. Operando characterization and DFT calculations reveal that: (I) H 2 pretreatment generates finely dispersed Pd 0 nanoparticles (Pd 0 NPs). In parallel, (II) a secondary fraction of Pd remains in ionic form occupying the linker-defective positions near the zirconium oxo-clusters of the framework, and (III) that palladium ions undergo partial migration during the reaction. Catalytic evaluation reveals that low Pd loadings promote selective 1-butanol formation by suppressing ethanol dehydration, whereas higher Pd loadings induce nanoparticle growth, active-site agglomeration, and diminished catalytic efficiency. All in all, optimal Guerbet performance relies on the complementarity of Pd 0 sites, which enable hydrogen transfer, and framework μ-OH and Zr acid sites that drive acetaldehyde coupling. These findings establish that precisely balancing linker defectivity and Pd loading in UiO-66 is key to achieving efficient ethanol chain growth, outstanding Guerbet selectivity (>90%), and stable operation without external H 2 , underscoring the potential of MOF-based catalysts for sustainable fuel production.

title: Decoupling geometric effects in furfuryl alcohol hydrogenation by regulating the surface coordination of Pt nanoparticles
Regenerable ion-exchange resin beads for continuous PFAS capture and regeneration for improved aqueous zinc batteries
abstract: Newly innovated sorbents for removal of per - and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) reported to date are predominantly unstructured powders, constraining their integration into continuous-flow water treatment systems. Here we use surfactant-based suspension polymerization to produce regenerable ion-exchange resin beads with well-defined spherical morphology. The bead architecture reduces swelling and fragmentation relative to an irregular resin control, supports stable cartridge operation, and retains rapid sorption, high capacity, and multicycle regeneration. The beads remove a broad range of PFAS, including challenging short-chain species, from complex water matrices and delay breakthrough by more than 1000-fold relative to a commercial PFAS ion-exchange resin under matched column conditions. We further demonstrate functional use of the processed regeneration stream as a fluorinated additive in aqueous Zn batteries. The RF11-containing electrolyte promotes formation of a Zn-F-containing interphase and improves Zn plating/stripping stability and full-cell cycling. These results establish a capture-concentrate-utilize strategy that links flow-compatible PFAS separation with reuse of the regenerated stream. This capture-concentrate-utilize pathway reframes PFAS from persistent contaminants to functional resources, providing a strategy for circular PFAS management and sustainable water treatment.

title: Phosphine emissions for early warning of phosphorus pool vulnerability of estuarine wetlands
Local WO coordination regulates PtW electronic coupling for glycerol hydrogenolysis to 1,3-propanediol
abstract: Selective hydrogenolysis of biomass-derived glycerol to 1,3-propanediol (1,3-PDO) requires coordinated glycerol activation, hydrogen transfer, and C–O cleavage at the Pt–WO3-x interface. Although spillover-induced W–OH Brønsted acid sites are well recognized, how Pt–W electronic states and local W–O coordination govern glycerol anchoring and W–OH formation remains unclear. Here, Pt/WO3-x interfacial environments were tuned through air calcination and H2 reduction. Spectroscopic analyses show that Air-300 preserves terminal W=O and a coupled Ptδ⁺–W5+ interfacial state. DFT calculations further reveal that the W=O-retained structure strengthens Pt anchoring and induces net electron transfer from Pt to WO3-x, directly linking local W–O coordination to the stabilization of electron-deficient Ptδ⁺ species. The XPS-derived effective Pt–W coupled-state index (Ieff) tracks the 1,3-PDO yield, associating this coordination-regulated electronic state with catalytic performance. Functionally, the W=O-retained interface preferentially anchors glycerol on the WO3-x side rather than on Pt (-0.36 vs. -0.18 eV), leaving adjacent Pt sites available for H₂ dissociation and thereby enabling spatial cooperation between oxide-side glycerol adsorption and Pt-side H2 activation. Terminal W=O accepts spillover hydrogen from Pt–H more readily than framework W–O–W (0.34 vs. 0.84 eV), generating interfacial W–OH species consistent with the enhanced H2-induced Brønsted acidity of Air-300. These sites mediate β-OH dehydration, followed by Pt–H hydrogenation of the resulting C3 intermediate to 1,3-PDO. These findings demonstrate how local W–O coordination and Pt–W electronic coupling construct an active metal–acid interface for selective glycerol hydrogenolysis.

title: Boosting non-radiative decay in thiadiazolequinoxaline-based polymers via molecular engineering for solar-thermal conversion
Al3+ coordinated and Hofmeister-reinforced conductive chitosan/PEDOT:PSS hydrogels for highly fatigue-resistant wearable strain sensor
Functionalized graphene oxide-reinforced semi-interpenetrating liquid crystal elastomers for near-body-temperature actuation and high toughness
Asymmetric carbonized biomass frameworks for self-sustaining Ionohydrovoltaic energy generation
abstract: Harvesting electricity from water–solid interactions is a viable approach for sustainable and decentralized energy generation; yet traditional hydrovoltaic systems are constrained by environmental sensitivity, water loss, and inadequate power supply. This study presents a bio-derived ionohydrovoltaic energy generator (iHEG) that addresses these limitations by combining hydrovoltaic and ionovoltaic processes inside a semi-enclosed structure. The system features an internal circulation mechanism that utilizes photothermal effects to facilitate internal water recirculation, allowing for sustained electricity generation without the need for continuous external water supply, thereby significantly diminishing environmental reliance. The device comprises hierarchically porous carbonized red Reishi mushroom frameworks that are functionalized with oppositely charged polyelectrolytes, resulting in spatially segregated ionic domains. This asymmetric interfacial structure creates Janus-like wet–dry areas and a built-in electric field, facilitating rectified ion transit during hydration. The iHEG attains an open-circuit voltage of around 1.1 V, a short-circuit current of about 0.55 mA, and a power density of 16 μW cm −2 , while sustaining continuous operation for 170 h with little water input. The technology is inherently scalable, able to power multicolor LEDs and facilitate water electrolysis for green hydrogen generation. This research presents an innovative framework for sustainable energy harvesting via bio-derived ionic interfacial engineering, providing a viable and ecologically sound approach for resilient and scalable energy conversion.

title: Breaking the superexchange interlock for high-performance regeneration of degraded single-crystal cathodes
abstract: The accumulation of spent Li-ion batteries necessitates sustainable recycling. However, regenerating high-performance cathodes remains challenging due to severe surface rock-salt phase accumulation and poorly understood regeneration mechanisms. This study elucidates the superexchange interaction–driven failure mechanism of Li1-xNi0.6Co0.1Mn0.3O2 cathodes via magnetic atomic force microscopy and X-ray absorption spectroscopy and unveils the associated regeneration processes through in situ structural, morphological, and surface chemical characterizations. By introducing a medium-temperature preoxidation mechanism, the strongly electron-withdrawing NO3- ligand field extract electrons directly from the localized Ni–O network, effectively oxidizing Ni2+ to Ni3+. This charge depletion substantially downshifts unoccupied antibonding orbitals, decoupling the rigid Ni–O–Ni superexchange network and thermodynamically unlatches the magnetic pinning of the rock-salt phase. Consequently, the decoupled lattice structurally relaxes in situ to form a highly reactive layered NiOOH intermediate. This profound electronic reconfiguration drastically alleviates the electrostatic barrier for rapid Li+ insertion, enabling complete phase reconstruction while eliminating conventional reliance on high Li-salt concentration gradients. Moreover, the specific adsorption of free Cl- in the molten salt regulates isotropic crystal growth, thereby exposing abundant active facets that accelerate Li+ migration. The developed one-pot, dual-temperature-zone, bifunctional molten-salt strategy regenerates spent single-crystal Li1-xNi0.6Co0.1Mn0.3O2 into submicron, pillow-like single crystals. Benefiting from this unique architecture, the regenerated cathode delivers a high reversible capacity (177.7 mAh g-1) and exceptional rate capability (121.1 mAh g-1 at 10C, with 84.1% retention after 100 cycles), outperforming commercial counterparts. This study simultaneously achieves direct regeneration and morphological engineering of spent materials, providing a commercially viable, closed-loop recycling strategy for degraded single-crystal cathodes.

title: Corrigendum to “Heterogeneous catalytic ozonation of atrazine with oxygen vacancy-rich Cu-loaded and Ce-loaded attapulgite: Efficiency, mechanism and environmental application” [Chem. Eng. J. 486 (2024), 150079]
Secondary-metal regulation of K-promoted Ru/γ-Al2O3 catalysts for plasma-catalytic ammonia decomposition
Bio-denitrification under Cr(VI) stress: System responses, inhibitory mechanisms, and mitigation strategies
Fabrication of FeSiMn core-shell-like structure by HTMC: Tailoring Mn content to optimize microwave absorption properties
Topology-dependent cracking behaviors of bulky aromatics over BETA and mordenite zeolites derived from interzeolite transformation
Atmosphere-responsive Ru/CuCoFe-LDH dual-functional material for direct air CO2 capture and low-temperature in-situ hydrogenation conversion
DES-assisted isolation of Sargassum-derived nanocellulose for progesterone removal: Effects of citric acid modification on adsorption mechanisms and electrochemical quantification
abstract: The continuous release of endocrine-disrupting compounds, such as progesterone (P4), into aquatic environments requires sustainable, highly efficient remediation strategies. This study presents an integrated approach for the removal and trace-level monitoring of P4 using Sargassum -derived nanocellulose and a bimetallic PdCuO/C electrocatalyst. Nanocellulose (NC) was isolated using a green methodology based on deep eutectic solvents (DES) and modified with citric acid, primarily via noncovalent interactions. This green modification significantly enhanced structural stability, network density, and controlled swelling of the resulting matrix (X-NC). Adsorption assays revealed that X-NC exhibits a maximum adsorption capacity of 37.69 mg g −1 , as determined by the Liu isotherm model. Density Functional Theory calculations corroborate that the adsorption mechanism is thermodynamically favorable and primarily driven by hydrogen bonding and polar interactions between the progesterone carbonyl groups and the X-NC framework. Furthermore, to address the challenge of quantifying the endocrine-disrupting compounds at trace levels, an advanced electrochemical quantification methodology was implemented using a modified PdCuO/C electrode. Operating via a continuous surface-refreshing and site-blocking mechanism, the electrode demonstrated a broad linear range (0.026–23.44 μM) and a competitive limit of detection of 1.51 nM. The integration of Sargassum biomaterials modified with DES for water remediation, along with advanced electrochemical techniques for their evaluation at low concentrations, represents a remarkable approach in this field of research. This preliminary study lays the foundation for the design of sustainable materials that enable highly efficient progesterone removal and constitutes a starting point for the development of next-generation electrochemical sensors.

title: Tapping high photocatalytic activity in an S-scheme CuBi2O4-TiO2 heterojunction via robust interfacial electronic interactions for enhanced solar‑hydrogen production
abstract: Solar water splitting represents a sustainable strategy for the production of clean hydrogen fuel. Nevertheless, the photocatalytic efficiency of water splitting remains limited by rapid electron-hole recombination and insufficient redox capability in conventional photocatalysts. Constructing S-scheme heterojunction photocatalysts offers an effective strategy to promote charge-carrier separation while retaining strong redox capabilities for solar-to‑hydrogen conversion. Herein, we report a rationally designed S-scheme p-n heterojunction comprising p -type CuBi 2 O 4 and n -type TiO 2 for photocatalytic hydrogen evolution without a noble-metal cocatalyst. Under the employed reaction conditions, pristine CuBi 2 O 4 exhibits no detectable H 2 evolution, whereas the optimized 1 wt% CuBi 2 O 4 -TiO 2 heterostructure achieves a hydrogen evolution rate of 639.8 μmol.g −1 .h −1 , representing an approximately 5.0-fold enhancement compared with pristine TiO 2 . The enhanced photocatalytic performance is associated with favorable interfacial charge transfer and separation arising from the CuBi 2 O 4 -TiO 2 interface. Experimental results, supported by density functional theory (DFT) calculations, provide evidence for the proposed S-scheme charge-transfer mechanism, which promotes efficient utilization of photogenerated charge carriers. This work demonstrates the potential of low-loading CuBi 2 O 4 -TiO 2 heterostructures for noble-metal-free photocatalytic hydrogen production and highlights the importance of interfacial electronic interactions in designing efficient heterojunction photocatalysts.

Corrigendum to “Construction of high-performance glycoprotein molecularly imprinted polymers using boronic acid-containing imidazolium ionic liquid monomer and UiO-66@wood sponge composite carrier” [Chem. Eng. J. 506 (2025) 160283]
Corrigendum to “Achieving efficient photoreduction of CO2 by simultaneously facilitating the splitting of H2O and the conversion of *CO intermediates” [Chem. Eng. J. 505 (2025) 159308]
Impact of the impregnation method on the volumetric behaviour of vermiculite–CaCl2 composites under packed-bed cycling for thermochemical energy storage
abstract: Thermochemical energy storage (TCES) based on salt hydrates offers high energy density and negligible standby losses. However, repeated hydration–dehydration in packed beds can cause salt redistribution, pore restructuring, and substantial changes in settled packed volume, which may alter vapour transport and thermal output. This study compares atmospheric impregnation (AP), wet vacuum-assisted impregnation (WVac), and dry vacuum-assisted impregnation (DVac) for vermiculite–CaCl 2 composites over 20 hydration–dehydration cycles at 25 °C and 50 ± 2% relative humidity. The initial estimated volumetric salt contents were 0.073, 0.208, and 0.249 g cm −3 for AP, WVac, and DVac, respectively. At cycle 20, DVac retained the highest dynamic temperature response and showed a 43% increase in settled packed volume. After 20 cycles, the DVac composite retained a more open mercury-accessible pore structure than in the as-prepared state. The MIP, microscopy, and static-sorption measurements are consistent with improved vapour accessibility in the cycled DVac composite. Using the measured outlet-flow information, the estimated 3 h cumulative sensible heat carried by the air stream during hydration was approximately 480 kJ for DVac, 390 kJ for WVac, and 290 kJ for AP. The results show that impregnation-route screening should consider not only initial salt loading but also the evolution of pore accessibility and packed-bed volume during cycling.

title: Circular upcycling of end-of-life batteries into functional adsorbents: Process pathways, environmental applications, and emerging sodium and zinc-ion battery opportunities
abstract: The rapid expansion of electrochemical energy storage is generating growing volumes of end-of-life batteries, creating both environmental risks and opportunities for resource recovery. Upcycling these wastes into functional adsorbents offers a twofold environmental benefit: mitigating the risks associated with discarded batteries while producing value-added materials capable of removing hazardous contaminants from water, and air. This review critically examines the conversion of spent lithium-ion (LIB), zinc–manganese (Zn Mn), zinc–carbon (Zn/C), while prospectively assessing the opportunities of emerging sodium-ion (SIB), and zinc-ion (ZIB) batteries into adsorbents through direct-use, chemical, thermal, hydrothermal, mechanochemical, hybrid, and composite preparation routes. Particular emphasis is placed on how each preparation pathway governs key physicochemical properties, including surface chemistry, porosity, phase composition, morphology, oxidation state, and active-site accessibility, which ultimately determine adsorption performance. The review further compares reported adsorption metrics, including capacity, surface area, particle size, pH dependence, contact time, and initial concentration, across different battery chemistries and preparation strategies. By establishing explicit links between processing route, structural evolution, and adsorption behavior, this work provides a method-centred framework for the rational design of battery-derived adsorbents. This dual-purpose circular strategy connects hazardous battery-waste management with broader pollution mitigation, thereby transforming one environmental liability into a resource for addressing other contaminant challenges.

title: Tailoring the spatial arrangement of amino groups in aminosaccharides toward durable zinc anode interfaces
Nanodomains and highly polarizable ions enable outstanding energy storage performance in lead-free Bi0.5Na0.5TiO3-based ferroelectric ceramics
abstract: Lead-free ferroelectric materials based on Bi0.5Na0.5TiO3(BNT) are regarded as promising candidates to replace lead-based materials. However, the low breakdown electric field (Eb) and large remanent polarization (Pr) hinder the improvement of their energy storage performance (ESP). Herein, Sr0.7Bi0.2HfO3(SBH) was doped into 0.85Bi0.5Na0.5TiO3-0.15NaNbO3 (BNNT) relaxor ceramics through the introduction of highly polarized ions and multi-domains design, showing the ultra-high energy storage performance (Wtotal = 7.8 J/cm3, Wrec = 6.5 J/cm3, η = 84%) under a moderate electric field of 450 kV/cm and satisfactory charge-discharge performance (CD = 3108 A/cm2, PD = 419 MW/cm3, t0.9 = 41 ns). The coexistence of rhombohedral and tetragonal phases and highly dynamic polar nanoregions was achieved through the introduction of highly polarized ions, as evidenced by XRD Rietveld refinement and piezoresponse force microscopy. The reduction in freezing temperature broadens the relaxation temperature range in BNT-based relaxor ferroelectrics, while the increase in electrical resistivity contributes to enhancing insulation properties. This study presents an effective strategy that simultaneously boosts polarization and breakdown strength, offering an optimized material for the design of advanced capacitors.

title: Multi-dimensional systematic metabolic engineering and dual-pathway construction in Yarrowia lipolytica for development of a high-performance L-tyrosine platform strain
Structural-interfacial co-stabilization of high-nickel cathodes enabled by a multifunctional covalent binder network
Engineering f–p–d orbital hybridization for fast coupled electron–ion transport in aqueous zinc-ion batteries
Ru3Sn7 phase development on ZnO and its catalytic function in vapor-phase hydrogenation of biomass-derived butyric acid to n-butanol
abstract: Solvent-free vapor-phase hydrogenation of biomass-derived butyric acid (BA) to n-butanol (n-BuOH) was investigated over Ru-Sn/ZnO catalysts to establish structure, reaction-network, and kinetic descriptors for selective alcohol production. The Ru:Sn molar ratio governed Ru0/Ru3Sn7/SnOx speciation and the ZnO acid-base balance, thereby determining the distribution of hydrogenation and ester-forming functions. The optimized 1Ru-2Sn/ZnO catalyst achieved 99.9% BA conversion and 98.9% n-BuOH yield at 265 ℃ and 25 bar H2 after catalyst stabilization. Structural and surface analyses showed that Sn incorporation promotes Ru3Sn7 formation, whereas Ru assists SnOx reduction during alloy development. Direct reduction without calcination produced a Ru3Sn7-rich working phase before reaction and markedly shortened the induction period, demonstrating pretreatment as an engineering handle for active-phase control. Space-time-resolved product evolution revealed that the butyl butyrate branch is the most residence-time-sensitive part of the network and is kinetically coupled with n-BuOH formation, while butyraldehyde and 4-heptanone pathways remained secondary. Low-conversion temperature-response experiments validated the catalyst-mass-normalized BA disappearance coefficient (\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{BA}}^\mathrm{m}) as an apparent kinetic descriptor that gave an apparent activation energy of 102.9 kJ mol-1, consistent with alternative BA disappearance metrics. The stabilized Ru3Sn7-rich catalyst also retained alcohol productivity during H2O and acetic acid co-feeding, supporting its relevance to upgrading fermentation-derived carboxylic acid streams. This integrated descriptor framework links active-phase formation, acid-base properties, and network evolution to process-relevant selectivity under continuous fixed-bed operation without solvent addition.

Rational design of D-A type fully conjugated porous aromatic frameworks for multifunctional optimization of perovskite solar cells performance and stability

A macrophage membrane-biomimetic composite antibacterial nanoplatform co-loading vancomycin and silver nanoparticles for the treatment of infective endocarditis
Amyloid-like sodium caseinate/pectin assemblies as multi-interface building blocks for wax-adhesive, transport-regulated active fruit coatings
Biomimetic NIR-responsive pyroelectric platform for antibacterial therapy and enhanced biosealing
Silsesquioxane-functionalized strong wood aerogel for durable and energy-efficient buildings
abstract: Energy-efficient buildings demand high-performance insulation materials. Wood aerogels, with their intrinsic low thermal conductivity, high porosity, and good mechanical strength, offer exceptional potential as sustainable thermal insulators. However, their moisture sensitivity restricts the practical applications. To address this, we developed a silsesquioxane-functionalized wood aerogel composite through cold alkali treatment followed by methyltrimethoxysilane (MTMS) condensation, resulting in a hierarchical mesoporous wood structure with silsesquioxane particles integrated into cell walls and lumina fibril networks. This functionalization simultaneously achieves high specific surface area (261 m2/g), robust mechanical strength (compression yield strength > 4 MPa), and superhydrophobicity (surface contact angle > 170°, interior ~156°). The composite exhibits reduced moisture uptake and great thermal insulation. These attributes make functional wood aerogel a promising solution for nearly zero-energy buildings (NZEBs), where energy performance is paramount.

Sulfonated polysiloxane and polyborosiloxane synergistic flame retardancy for polycarbonate composites with preserved transparent and mechanical properties
Simultaneous stabilization of cadmium and arsenic in co-contaminated soil by ferrihydrite-humic acid microspheres: Effects and mechanisms

Yarrowia lipolytica as a cell factory for carotenoid synthesis: Metabolic engineering strategies and biomanufacturing prospects
Average metal-oxygen bond energy as a descriptor for perovskite cathodes: Reconciling the activity-stability trade-off for CO2 electrolysis
abstract: Solid oxide electrolysis cells (SOECs) face a critical bottleneck in developing robust cathodes for CO 2 electrolysis. Herein, we propose the average metal‑oxygen bond energy (AMOBE) as a simple, intuitive descriptor to unify the trade-off between activity and stability in iron-based perovskite cathodes. Using SrTi x Fe 1- x O 3-δ as a model, we tuned the AMOBE (−283.5 to −355.1 kJ mol −1 ) via Ti doping. Electrochemical evaluation reveals a volcanic relationship between activity and AMOBE with optimal performance at x = 0.3–0.4, corresponding to an AMOBE window of −(320–330) kJ mol − 1 . Mechanistic studies elucidate that weak M-O bonds facilitate active Fe nanoparticles exsolution but trigger phase decomposition and SrCO 3 formation, leading to rapid cathodic activity degradation. In contrast, excessively strong bonds over-stabilize lattice oxygen, improving the long-term stability, but hindering CO 2 activation and electronic conductivity. Therefore, the balance between activity and stability of iron-based perovskite cathodes is achieved within a narrow AMOBE window of −(320−330) kJ mol − 1 . The SOEC with the optimal cathode, SrTi 0.4 Fe 0.6 O 3-δ , were operated stably for >1000 h at 850 °C and 1 A cm − 2 with Faradaic efficiency close to unity. This work establishes AMOBE as a universal design criterion, moving beyond empirical trial-and - error and providing a clear roadmap for rational perovskite cathode design for SOECs.

title: Quantifying systematic kinetic bias in microwave-driven carbothermic reduction: Apparent non-thermal effects for ZnFe₂O₄-biomass pellets
abstract: Kinetic analysis of microwave-heated heterogeneous solids is frequently distorted by spatial temperature non-uniformity, yet standard methods rely on a single representative temperature. This work develops a quantitative correction framework utilizing the rate-equivalent effective temperature ( T eff ), effective reaction volume ( V eff ), and a conversion-temperature spatial correlation factor ( C αT ). Applied to the microwave carbothermic reduction of ZnFe₂O₄-biomass pellets, the framework integrates customized experiments with fully coupled COMSOL multiphysics simulations. The study demonstrates that using the hotspot temperature ( T max ) systematically underestimates the apparent activation energy ( E a ). This kinetic bias is dynamically modulated by endothermic heat sinks and a newly identified product shielding effect, where conversion-dependent electromagnetic weakening (consumption of the strongly absorbing biochar and pore formation via Zn volatilization) suppresses hotspot intensity. Across multi-power evaluations, standard Friedman analysis is underestimated by 49%; the combined T eff and C αT correction successfully recovered this value to within 12% of the model reference. Finally, a dimensionless scaling law is proposed for first-order bias estimation, alongside a screening criterion ( Φ ≪ 1 ) embedded in a practical workflow, enabling researchers to quantitatively isolate thermal artifacts before invoking non-thermal microwave effects.

title: Spatially differentiated regulation synchronizes interfacial activation and bulk conversion for fast and durable sodium storage
abstract: Conversion-type anodes are attractive for sodium-ion batteries because of their high theoretical capacities but suffer from unsynchronized interfacial reaction initiation and bulk conversion propagation, resulting in limited rate capability and cycling stability. Herein, we report a spatially differentiated regulation strategy for conversion-type anodes that integrates an electron-delocalized π-conjugated shell with a Se-bridged d-p-d coupled heterointerface to regulate distinct yet interconnected stages of the sodium-storage reaction. Specifically, the outer N-doped carbon shell constructs an interfacial reaction region with delocalized π-electron-mediated charge transport and stabilized electrode/electrolyte interactions. Meanwhile, the internal heterointerface functions as a conversion regulation region, where Se-bridged orbital coupling reprograms local electronic structures and lowers the energy barrier for phase transformation. Together, these spatially differentiated functional domains synchronize interfacial activation with bulk conversion, effectively eliminating the intrinsic kinetic mismatch of conversion-type anodes. As a result, the optimized electrode delivers an outstanding rate capability of 366.9 mAh g-1 at 10 A g-1, accompanied by negligible capacity loss after 1300 cycles. Moreover, the CoSe2/FeSe2@NC||NaNi1/3Fe1/3Mn1/3O2 full cell achieves a capacity of 262.7 mAh g-1 at 1.0 A g-1. This work establishes a spatially differentiated conversion chemistry framework for designing high-rate and durable sodium storage materials.

abstract: The development of novel bio-based chemicals is of critical importance for advancing the high-value valorization of lignocellulosic biomass. As emerging bio-derived chemicals, bio-based spirocyclic ketal esters represent a novel class of bio-based monomers featuring tunable symmetric terminal groups, with strong application potential in the fields of polyesters and polyurethanes. Herein, we developed a site-selective ketalization method to synthesize four bio-based spirocyclic ketal ester compounds with varying alkyl chain lengths from corncob-derived alkyl levulinates and pentaerythritol, using recyclable HZSM-5 zeolite as the catalyst. Benefiting from the MFI pore confinement effect and dual acid sites of HZSM-5, the reaction proceeds with high selectivity under mild vacuum conditions. Kinetic investigations performed at 85–105 °C reveal that the reaction follows pseudo-first-order kinetics; the apparent activation energy rises with extended alkyl chains, which is attributed to steric hindrance and increased desorption resistance. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations confirm that cyclization-dehydration is the rate-limiting step and elucidate the catalytic roles of acid sites. Furthermore, cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA) and techno-economic analysis (TEA) are conducted, providing theoretical reference for the process development of bio-based spirocyclic ketal ester production.

Influence of catalytic pellets on the electrical response and CO₂ conversion in packed-bed dielectric barrier discharge reactors
abstract: Catalytic packed-bed dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) reactors are widely investigated for plasma-assisted CO₂ conversion. Yet the role of catalytic pellets in shaping both discharge behavior and reactor performance remains only partially understood. In particular, it is unclear whether changes in CO₂ conversion arise from catalytic effects or from modifications to the electrical discharge induced by the geometry and dielectric properties. This work investigates the electrical response of a packed-bed DBD reactor using different packing materials with a wide range of dielectric and physicochemical properties. Peak, burning, and breakdown voltages are analyzed and compared with effective-medium approximations, geometric scaling, and a previously developed dimensionless framework. The results show that bulk dielectric constants alone cannot account for the observed electrical behavior. Although dielectric and geometric corrections partially improve trend consistency, significant deviations remain, indicating additional material-dependent effects related to plasma–surface interactions. A dimensionless scaling approach provides improved prediction of breakdown behavior across empty and packed configurations, suggesting its suitability as a unified reactor-scale descriptor. Finally, CO₂ conversion analysis shows that reactor performance is governed by coupled discharge–chemistry interactions. Importantly, higher dielectric constants of catalytic packing materials do not necessarily translate into improved CO₂ conversion, highlighting the limitations of dielectric-based design strategies.

abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) progression is closely associated with a ROS-amplified inflammatory microenvironment that promotes macrophage dysregulation, synovitis, and chondrocyte matrix catabolism. However, current antioxidant nanomedicines for OA are often constrained by metal-associated safety concerns, limited cartilage accessibility, and insufficient regulation of macrophage-chondrocyte inflammatory crosstalk. Herein, we report cyanidin-derived antioxidant carbon dots (CC-CDs) as a precursor-programmed nanoscale redox-modulating platform for preventing OA progression. Through a facile one-pot hydrothermal strategy, the intrinsic polyphenolic antioxidant motifs of cyanidin are integrated into an ultrasmall carbon framework, yielding CC-CDs with abundant surface functional groups, potent ROS-scavenging capacity, and superoxide dismutase-like activity. In vitro , CC-CDs suppress LPS-induced M1 macrophage activation, promote M2-associated polarization, and preserve matrix homeostasis in IL-1β-stimulated chondrocytes by restoring SOX9, COL2A1, and aggrecan expression while reducing MMP13 levels. In a murine OA model, intra-articular administration of CC-CDs attenuates synovial inflammation, reduces histological OA severity, preserves proteoglycan-rich cartilage architecture, and inhibits extracellular matrix degradation. Mechanistically, CC-CDs alleviate OA progression by suppressing TLR4/NF-κB signaling, as evidenced by reduced TLR4 expression and p65 phosphorylation. This study highlights bioactive precursor-engineered antioxidant carbon dots as promising nanomedicines and offers a microenvironment-oriented strategy for cartilage preservation and degenerative joint disease intervention.

abstract: Ion-conducting elastomers combine large deformability with charge transport but often exhibit trade-offs among mechanical robustness, self-healing, conductivity, and environmental stability. Here, we develop a partially reduced graphene oxide (GO)-reinforced ion-conducting elastomer through thermally induced ring-opening polymerization of α -lipoic acid in the presence of dopamine methacrylamide. Dynamic disulfide exchange and catechol-mediated interactions create a reconfigurable adhesive network, while GO nanosheets provide interfacial reinforcement and enhance heat transfer, photothermal conversion, and charge transport. The optimized elastomer exhibits a conductivity of 1.03 × 10 −3 S m −1 , high elasticity, cyclic durability, robust adhesion, and efficient recovery under thermal treatment and solar irradiation. GO-mediated photothermal heating accelerates network reorganization and restores the mechanical integrity and electrical response of damaged samples. The coupled charge-transport network generates stable and repeatable resistance changes under deformation, enabling strain sensing of complex human motions. The elastomer also maintains signal fidelity in aqueous environments and supports real-time underwater signal transmission. Its antibacterial activity and favorable biocompatibility further support potential use in skin-contact and biointerfacing applications. By integrating dynamic covalent exchange, mussel-inspired adhesion, and photothermally active nanosheets within a single network, this work provides a materials-design strategy for mechanically resilient, healable ion-conducting elastomers for wearable electronics and operation in wet environments.
